en: *Śrī Sekoddeśaṭīkā*: Homage to Kālacakra! Having ascended the palace of the penetration of the stainless Buddha-dharma, which pacifies all obscurations, I offer homage with my two-fold body to that Blessed One. Like a cloud drawing water from the ocean, I have drawn forth the water of his words from the ocean of the *Vimalaprabhā* and other treatises, and offered it here according to my devotion, for the sake of the ritual performance of the drama that benefits the world.
O wise ones, resort to this pond of the sixfold secret methods of instruction for the purpose of obstructing craving.

Sucandra said: Śrī Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of Secrets, who dwells in Āḍhakavatī; he who is the sovereign of the great realm of Śambhala consisting of ninety-six crores of villages situated to the north of the Śītā River; whose lotus-feet are saluted by the lords of millions upon millions of villages—those born from the lineages of the ninety-six great kings, who are emanation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of gods, asuras, and nāgas, and who wear crowns bound with great jewels; who, through his mastery of all the languages of sentient beings, acts as the compiler of the Dharmas spoken by the Tathāgatas and is thus the listener for all Tathāgatas; and who, due to the abandonment of the sixteen lunar digits of obscuration, possesses the stainless radiance of the moon—and is thus "Beautiful" (*su*) and "Moon" (*candra*), hence Sucandra.

In this context, "secret" (*guhya*) refers to the Vajrayāna, which is superior to the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; he is the sovereign (*adhipati*) therein by virtue of being the compiler of its teachings. Furthermore, according to worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), "secret" refers to *yakṣas*, and he is the sovereign of those, hence "Lord of Secrets" (*Guhyādhipati*).
Externally, the word "cremation ground" (*āḍhaka*) refers to a collection of corpses.
Because of its association with that [yakṣa], the cremation ground is called Āḍakavatī;
in it, there are always yakṣas who harass sentient beings and create many obstacles. Their oppressor is the Great Yakṣa Lord residing in Āḍakavatī, like a lord of deer in the forest.

The cessation of twenty-one thousand six hundred and thirty-six inhalations and exhalations within one's own internal continuum is the *āḍhaka*; that which possesses this is the *āḍhakavatī*, the Dharmameghā (Cloud of Dharma) stage. Residing there is the Lord of Yakṣas, the subduer of the Māras, the lords of ignorance, and the obscurations of meditative attainment;

he who sets forth the Dharma for all sentient beings through the lion’s roar of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, each in their own respective language, is the Lord of Secrets, the glorious Vajrapāṇi. It is his emanation body, King Sucandra, who makes this request.
As it is said in the Root Tantra: "With the full moon in front, the full moon-sun behind, darkness to the left, and the face situated at the tail to the right—
this is the commitment known as Trailokyavijaya, the crusher of Māra."
In that [assembly], the Teacher, facing eastward and seated upon a jeweled lion-throne,
filled the three worlds with arrays consisting of five-colored rays of light;
the Lord was honored by Bodhisattvas, Mārās, and the lords of the gods.
With various kinds of divine flowers, with enchanting divine perfumes,
with divine jewel-lamps, with divine incense produced from fragrant substances,
and with various kinds of divine offerings of grain and nectar-like fruits.

The Bodhisattvas, gods, and others, having prostrated again and again with their five limbs touching the ground before the Buddha, the Leader of the Three Worlds, [honored him] with divine and variegated ornaments, divine garments, yak-tail whisks, bells, mirrors, banners, and divine, cloudless parasols, all adorned with crowns.
Seated upon their respective seats, those bodhisattvas and gods, who sought the meaning of what they had heard of the Mantra Vehicle and some of whom had attained the higher cognitions (abhijñā),
were all joyful and satisfied in their intentions; with their minds, they reflected as follows:
"The teaching of the Mantra Vehicle which was previously given by Dīpaṅkara must now be performed for us by Gautama, the current Sage. Therefore,
[this work] called Śambhala, produced by Vajrapāṇi..."
King Sucandra arrived at the glorious Dharmadhātu temple;
having first performed a circumambulation of the Teacher’s two lotus-feet,
he worshipped them with jewel-flowers and prostrated again and again.
With palms joined in reverence, Candra stood before the Perfectly Awakened One as the requester of the tantra and the compiler of the Teacher’s word;
O Teacher, by virtue of being the one who teaches correctly.

That which is about to be described—consisting of the sevenfold [substances] beginning with water, such as the *kumbha* (vase) and so forth, being threefold—is the "Unsurpassed" (*anuttara*), that is, the Supreme Immutable (*paramākṣara*).
Thus, it is called an "initiation" (*seka*) because by means of it, the body and so forth are sprinkled (*sicyate*) and rendered stainless and free from obscurations; hence it is an initiation.
Tell me that:

mundane accomplishment (*laukikasiddhi*) is sovereignty extending up to the Akaniṣṭha realm; supreme accomplishment (*uttarasiddhi*) is the state of perfect buddhahood (*samyaksambuddhatva*) through the attainment of the twelve stages (*dvādaśabhūmi*), resulting from the abandonment of all obscurations of the propensities (*vāsanā*), afflictions (*kleśa*), and the knowable (*jñeya*). This is stated in brief for that purpose.

Because he is engaged in favoring those people afflicted by the five degenerations—hair, ritual, beings, craving, and lifespan—the Blessed One said [this], as it will be explained in detail in the *Sekapaṭala* and the *Jñānapaṭala*. He is called the "Blessed One" (*bhagavān*) because he possesses *bhaga*, which is characterized by qualities such as sovereignty, since he has purified the six elements.
As it is stated in the *Mūlatantra*: "Of complete sovereignty, beauty, fame, glory, wisdom, and purposeful effort—these six are remembered as *bhaga*."
The thirty-six qualities, such as mastery over the pure elements beginning with earth, are proclaimed to reside in those six limbs.
It is also stated in the *Hevajra*: "Bhaga is said to be 'breaking,' because it breaks the afflictions, the Māras, and so forth;
and since those afflictions are to be suppressed by wisdom (*prajñā*), therefore it is called wisdom."
"In what location, in which maṇḍala, and where situated, surrounded by what assembly, did the Blessed One [teach]? Thus he asked. The Blessed One replied:

In the Śrīdhānya, the place where the teaching of the definitive mantra-system is given, the abode of great bliss, situated within the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajra Realm upon a vajra-lion throne, surrounded by a host of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, wrathful deities, gods, and goddesses, with his lotus-feet worshipped by the three realms, having entered the supreme primordial *dhruva-samādhi*,
he is the syllable *vaṃ*, whose nature is body, speech, and mind, in that abode of great bliss.
In the *dharmadhātu*, which has the characteristic of space, the supreme unchanging moment (*paramākṣara-acyutakṣaṇa*) is called "time" (*kāla*);
that itself is vajra-gnosis.

The wheel (*cakra*) of that time consists of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases free from obscuration; it is the unity of the three realms of existence, the object of knowledge free from obscuration.

That very body of the Blessed One, which consists of wisdom and skillful means, is called the Great Maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu; it possesses all forms and all sense faculties, has the nature of the drop (bindu), and sustains the universal illusion.
Seated upon a vajra lion throne characterized by the syllable *E* or by the mandalas of the immeasurable, indivisible moon, sun, and fire,
it is stated in the Root Tantra: "Just as the Teacher taught the method of the Perfection of Wisdom on Vulture Peak,
so too was the teaching of the Dharma proclaimed in the Mantra system at Śrī Dhānya."
From what place and from what scripture was that tantra taught? In what location, by which assembly of people, and for what reason [was it taught]?
The method of the Perfection of Wisdom was [taught] on the great mountain Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Having delivered this unsurpassed Mahāyāna to the Bodhisattvas,
the Tathāgata then dwelt together with the Bodhisattvas and others in the great caitya, the mandala of the Dharmadhātu.
In the sky that is non-inert, luminous, and providing no space for obstruction;
in the delightful realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), the abode and dissolution of all things,
the teaching of the tantra serves as the means for men to attain merit and wisdom.
The letter E is proclaimed as the illumination of the sky, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
The syllable Vaṃ, the array of the Sugatas, is perfectly situated within the letter E.
Furthermore, in that very same [text]: "In the realm called *Erahasya*, or in the *bhaga*, the *dharmodaya*, or the lotus, the Vajrī is said by me in other tantras to be seated upon a lion throne;
he is Vaṃvajrī, Vajrasattva, Vajrabhairava, and Īśvara."

Heruka, Kālacakra, and so forth, beginning with Ādibuddha— these are known by various names for different objects. I have explained the locus as having the characteristic of being the support (ādhāra), and that which is supported (ādheya), according to the diverse dispositions of sentient beings.
"The Omniscient One, the Holder of the Vajra, the Teacher, the Buddha, seated upon the lion throne,
is the expounder of the Kālacakra, having been requested by you, Sucandra.
Thus ends the introductory summary beginning with "Listen, Sucandra."
Regarding the Blessed One’s reply concerning the purpose of the consecration (*sekārtha*),

[it is stated that] the consecration and its purpose are supreme because they are the means for the bliss of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-sukha*), which is the supreme immutable (*paramākṣara*). Thus, even though it was not explicitly requested, he explains the movement of the channels (*nāḍī-sañcāra*) and so forth with the words "the movement of the channels," etc.,
referring to the upward and downward movement of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds within the six channels, such as *lalanā*, according to the sequence to be described.
Regarding "saṅkramaṇamāyāma": *āyāma* is the complete restraint (*āsamantād-yamana*) derived from the verbal root *yam*, which means "to cease" or "to restrain."
The entry of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds into the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*) occurs through the cessation of both movements;
this is stated briefly as a summary.
In every tantra, whether of the Yogins or Yoginīs and so forth, there are three types of summary (uddeśa),
as well as detailed exposition (nirdeśa).
Among these, the summary is stated by its own name alone.
The second is the brief indication (pratyuddeśa), the third is the detailed instruction (nirdeśa); thus, the detailed instruction is also explained by its own name.
The second is the *pratinirdeśa* (detailed explanation),
the third is the *mahānirdeśa* (great explanation),
and the recitation of the tantra consists of these two: the *uddeśa* (brief statement) and the *nirdeśa* (detailed explanation).
In that regard, the recitation by way of summary refers to the entire condensed tantra,
such as the *Śrī-guhyasamāja* consisting of eighteen hundred verses; the recitation by way of detailed exposition refers to the teaching of the complete root king of tantras,
such as the *Śrī-guhyasamāja* consisting of twenty-five thousand verses.

Thus, by way of the summary (pratyuddeśa), the commentary (pañjikā) on the *Laghutantra* is here intended as the exposition (nirdeśa) and the detailed exposition (pratinirdeśa); therefore, the commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Mūlatantra* is likewise [intended] by way of the great summary (*mahoddeśa*) for the *Laghutantra*.

Here, the *Mahānirdeśa* (Great Exposition) is intended as the instruction; by means of this *Mahānirdeśa*, there is a commentary (*ṭīkā*) upon the Root Tantra. Furthermore, these three—the *saṅgīti*, the *pañjikā*, and the *ṭīkā*—must be composed by those who have attained the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), namely, those who have acquired the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of their own and others' former births, and the miraculous power of traveling through space. They must not be composed by mere scholars whose mental continuums are impaired by the practice of dry logic.

"By those who have turned away from the pleasures of internal study that is to be personally realized"—by these sixfold headings and so forth, according to the stated sequence, this *Ādibuddha-tantra*, titled *Kālacakra*, is "pure," meaning completely purified; this is the connection with what is to be explained hereafter.
Likewise, the phrase "purified by the fourfold vajra-yogas" is to be connected everywhere.

By means of vajra-yogas whose nature consists of the pure dharmas, mantras, and formal configurations, which take the form of gradual integration into a single flavor with the sublime abodes (brahmavihāras)— namely, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and the lack of volitional effort, as well as compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity— [one attains liberation].

Smeared with the impurity of passion that is difficult to restrain, overcome by the deep sleep of the darkness consisting of the five sense-faculties and the ego, and possessing the waking state characterized by the perception of manifold conceptual states—both real and unreal—produced by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), [one is liberated] by those who destroy the path of this waking state through the forms of the *svābhāvika*, *sāmbhogika*, and *nairmāṇika* [bodies].
Therein, due to the absence of intrinsic nature, there is emptiness; the being of that emptiness is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Here, the object of knowledge—the past and the future—is empty; the vision of that [emptiness] is existence, which is emptiness. It is profound because of the non-existence of the past and the future, and it is vast because of the vision of the past and the future.
The cognition characterized by that [emptiness] or the cognition which apprehends it is the liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*).
Purified by that, and due to the exhaustion of the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*), there is the imperishable great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
That which restrains (*ruṇaddhi*) this bliss (*kaṃ*) is the Gnosis-Vajra (*jñānavajra*), characterized by compassion (*karuṇā*).
That very sahajakāya, consisting of wisdom and means, is called the pure yoga;
[terms such as] "sign," "Buddha," and "enlightenment" are the conceptual mind which is the cause,
and because of its emptiness, there is an absence of cause.
Therefore, that for which no sign (*nimitta*) exists is "signless knowledge" (*animitta-jñāna*), which is the liberation through the signless (*animitta-vimokṣa*).

Purified by that, through the exhaustion of deep sleep, free from the duality of permanence and impermanence and so forth, having the nature of loving-kindness (*maitryātmaka*), and characterized by non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpātmaka*) as it brings about the welfare of the world through the radiation of the two bodies—such a mind is the Mind-Vajra (*cittavajra*).
That itself is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), consisting of wisdom and means (*prajñopāyātmaka*), and is called the Yoga whose essence is the Dharma (*dharmātmā yoga*).

From the signless (animitta) itself comes the absence of discursive reasoning (atarka); from the absence of discursive reasoning, there is no directed application (apraṇihita)—that is, no directed application such as "May I become a perfectly awakened Buddha" and so forth; that which possesses this is the liberation of the undirected (apraṇihita-vimokṣa).
Purified by that, the unassailable sound— which is imperishable due to the exhaustion of dreams,
consists of the voices of all sentient beings, and is characterized by the joy of mantra—
is the "mantra" because it gladdens all sentient beings through their various voices and serves as a protection for the mind; it is the Vajra of Speech, and that itself is the Saṃbhogakāya.

The mantra-yoga, which consists of wisdom and means, is so called because, due to the absence of aspiration, there is no volitional construction (*abhisaṃskāra*). That which is characterized by the white and red vital winds (*prāṇāyāma*) and consciousness is the "liberation through non-construction" (*anabhisaṃskāra-vimokṣa*).

Purified by that, and through the exhaustion of the waking state, [the yogin] pervades with infinite, infinite emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) that lead to the path which is the antidote to the afflictions (*kleśa*). Having forms such as the fierce, the passionate, and the peaceful, yet remaining unmixed, the Vajra Body is essentially equanimity (*upekṣā*).
That very emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), consisting of wisdom and means, is the "configuration yoga" (*saṃsthānayoga*).

As it is stated in the *Vimalaprabhā* in the commentary on the first verse: "That very innate body (*sahajakāya*), purified by the liberation of emptiness, is the wisdom-vajra, the omniscient one, consisting of wisdom and means; it is the 'pure yoga' (*śuddhayoga*)."

That very *dharmakāya* is said to be the *yoga* consisting of the nature of phenomena (*dharmātmaka*), whose essence is wisdom and means (*prajñopāyātmaka*), which is the *jñānakāya*, the vajra of mind purified by the signless liberation (*animittavimokṣa*).

That very [body] is the *saṃbhogakāya*, said to be the *mantrayoga* whose essence is wisdom and means, which is the vajra of speech (*vāgvajra*) purified by the wishless liberation (*apraṇihitavimokṣa*), having the form of the sun and lotus-petal-like eyes.

That very [body] is the *nirmāṇakāya*, the *saṃsthānayoga* whose essence is wisdom and means, which is the vajra of body (*kāyavajra*) purified by the liberation of non-conditioning (*anabhisaṃskāravimokṣa*), with eyes as long as lotus petals. Thus, [it is attained] by means of the four awakenings (*catuḥsambodhi*).

By means of the characteristics of the single-moment awakening (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodhi*), the five-aspect awakening (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*), and the twenty-aspect awakening (*viṃśatyākārābhisambodhi*) within the Net of Illusion (*māyājāla*):

therein, according to the process of birth from the womb, when the *ālayavijñāna*—which has become the unified essence of the two drops of the mother and father—is about to arise in the secret wheel of the mother, its experience of exclusive bliss for a single moment and its body being of a single form like a rohita fish, that is the single-moment awakening. However, when there is the experience of the five cognitions consisting of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of form and so forth for one who is still in the womb, with the five fingers drawn in like a tortoise, that is the five-aspect awakening.

Then, when for each of the five cognitions (*pañcajñāna*) there is a differentiation of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the four elements beginning with earth, and the body is also complete with twenty fingers, that is the "Awakening in Twenty Aspects" (*viṃśatyākārābhisambodhi*).
Then, having emerged from the womb, the perception of infinite phenomena like a net of illusion is the "Awakening through the Net of Illusion" (*māyājālābhisambodhi*).

By contrast with these, the immutable drop (*bindu*), consisting of pure gnosis (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), is the Vajrayoga of the Gnosis-Vajra of the Svabhāvikakāya, Vajrasattva; because he is perfectly awakened in a single moment regarding the manifestation of all objects, it is the "Awakening in a Single Moment" (*ekakṣaṇābhisambodhi*).

In this context, through the exhaustion of the wheel of breaths characterized by twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths, it is stated in the Root Tantra as well: "The birthplace of the Lords of Jinas occurs when the mind is established in a single moment in the syllable, the Great Breath; when the vital wind has reached its end, the divine sense-faculties arise and the collection of fleshly sense-faculties perishes."

"When the natural abode is lost and the divine abode is perceived, O King of Kings, I see everything; there is nothing that is not always seen by me. Thus, he is the Dharmakāya, the Mahāsattva who is the yoga of the mind-vajra, possessing supreme unchanging bliss. Because he is perfectly awakened through the five aspects (*pañcākārābhisambuddhatvāt*), he is the "Perfect Awakening in Five Aspects" (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*). Here, characterized by the five wisdoms such as the mirror-like wisdom and so forth, consisting of the elements beginning with earth and the aggregates beginning with form, and having the nature of the cessation of the five maṇḍalas, he is essentially the union of wisdom and means.

That very Bodhisattva, the union of the speech-vajra of the *saṃbhogakāya*, possesses the meaning of truth in twelve aspects; he is the benefactor of Bodhisattvas and the teacher of Dharma through the voices of all sentient beings. Because he has attained perfect awakening in twenty aspects, he is the "twenty-aspect perfect awakening.

Here, this should be understood as existing through the cessation of the twelve transitions (*saṃkrānti*), characterized by the absence of obscuration regarding the five sense faculties, the five objects, the five action faculties, and the five actions of the action faculties.

That very emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is the yoga of the body-vajra (*kāyavajrayoga*), the commitment-being (*samayasattva*). Through the realization of the sixteen-fold reality, it is the primordial benefactor; its body is pervaded by infinite nets of illusion (*māyājāla*), and because it is perfectly awakened through the net of illusion, it is the "perfect awakening through the net of illusion" (*māyājālābhisambodhi*).

Here, it should be understood that the sixteen bodies, characterized by infinite and boundless various illusory emanations, arise simultaneously from the cessation of the drops (*bindu*) such as bliss and so forth.

However, at the stage of the arisen [path], there are four practices distinguished by the weak, medium, intense, and extremely intense degrees of the ten signs beginning with smoke; these are categorized by the aggregates characterized as form, perception, feeling, formations, and consciousness;
by the elements characterized as earth, water, fire, air, space, and consciousness;
by the sense bases consisting of body, tongue, eye, nose, ear, mind, smell, form, taste, touch, sound, and the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*); and by the sense fields.

Due to the plural number, [the six organs] beginning with the anus, feet, hands, speech, genitals, and skin are [associated] respectively with excretion, movement, grasping, speaking, emission, and the discharge of semen;

through these, purified by Vairocana and the others, there are the six families known as the World, the Inner Self, Empowerment, Means, and Gnosis. These reveal the meaning of the purification of worldly beings, the accomplishment of mundane siddhis, and the supreme unchanging gnosis, by means of the two truths—the mundane and the supramundane.

The word "ādi" (beginning) signifies that which has neither beginning nor end; he is "Buddha" because he has awakened to all phenomena (*dharma*) without error; thus, he is both the "Beginning" and the "Buddha," hence "Ādibuddha."
The meaning is that he is devoid of arising and passing away;
and in the *Nāmasaṅgīti* it says: "The Buddha is without beginning or end, the primordially awakened one, without causal succession."

He whose form is compassion and emptiness, who is Time (Kāla) and whose nature is conventional reality (saṃvṛti), is called the Wheel of Emptiness (Śūnyatācakra); he is Kālacakra, the non-dual and the immutable. By the designation of each individual syllable: from the letter *kā* comes the peaceful cause; from the letter *la*, dissolution indeed occurs here.
He made the mind unshakable by means of the syllable *kra* through sequential bindings.
This is its meaning:

the cause is said to be the body of bodhicitta. It is peaceful, free from conceptual construction due to the cessation of the waking state, and the Nirmāṇakāya is at the forehead through the cessation of the *kāyabindu*.
This being so, the Sambhogakāya is at the throat through the cessation of the *vāgbindu*, which consists of the dissolution of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) due to the cessation of the dreaming state.

In the states of waking and dreaming, the mind wanders among objects such as sound; it is restless, subject to fall, overcome by darkness (tamas), and undergoes transformation through the eighteen elements (dhātus).
Its bondage is the departure of darkness;
it is the cessation of deep sleep through the restraint of the *citta-bindu*, which is the *dharmakāya* in the heart. Why is this so? It is said:

The sequence beginning with the letter *kra* refers to the descent of the drops (*bindu*) of body and so forth; their binding is through innate bliss (*sahajasukha*), which is the exhaustion of the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*).
Due to the cessation of the drop of gnosis (*jñānabindu*) situated in the vowels at the navel, there is the "innate body" (*sahajakāya*); thus, he consists of the four bodies.

He alone is the Blessed One Kālacakra, whose nature is wisdom and method (*prajñopāya*), described in terms of the relationship between gnosis and the object of gnosis. Thus, the gnosis of immutable bliss, which is the cause for the destruction of all obscurations, is called "Time" (*kāla*).
Skillful means consists of compassion and has the nature of the six superknowledges.
The wheel of the world (*jagaccakra*) is the aspect of the knowable; the knowable is the wheel characterized by the infinite phenomena of the three realms.
That very [wheel] is wisdom, whose nature is emptiness and whose nature consists of all aspects. The unity of these two is called the *Kālacakra*, as it is stated in the *Śrīkālacakra* as well.

The infinite Buddha-fields, the elements with their immeasurable qualities such as space and so forth, the threefold existence here consisting of stability, arising, and destruction, all sentient beings within the six realms of rebirth, the Buddhas, the wrathful deities, the gods and others, the Bodhisattvas together with their consorts, and this wheel of the Victor—even the three worlds—belong to that one Śambhu alone. The two verses beginning with "In the beginning" are clear.
Now, he indicates the seven empowerments with the words beginning with "It is said."

Here, for the sake of instructing beginners who have not studied other tantras and are unskilled in the three watches (*tri-yāma*) and so forth, some of the procedures beginning with the seven initiations (*sapta-seka*) are extracted from the *Śrītantra* and the *Vimalaprabhā*.
Among those, first, the procedure for the protection of the disciple (*śiṣya-rakṣā-vidhi*) is stated.

Having performed the protection of the disciple at the head, heart, crown, navel, throat, and the glorious secret lotus by means of the Vajras of Body, Speech, and Mind belonging to the two families beginning with the Jinas, I shall likewise draw this mandala of the Lord for the sake of the liberation of all beings—including those made of clay and so forth, as well as books—by means of the glorious vowels prescribed in the revealed [tantras].

In this context, having first performed a protection for the disciple and others, one should subsequently gather the disciples and so forth. Here, the protection is performed by the deities of the Jina family and those belonging to both families: the syllable *ū* on the head, *ī* at the heart, *ā* on the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*), *au* at the navel, *ṛ* at the throat, and *a* at the secret place.
These belong to both families through the distinct [protections] of body, speech, and mind.
Thus, having performed the protection of the books with the manifest and fixed *śrī-svaras*—namely, *ai*, *ṛ*, *u*, and *e*—one should then request the Buddhas:

"For the sake of the liberation of sentient beings, I am causing the mandala of the Lord Kālacakra to be drawn, even though it is difficult; therefore, O Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, grant your empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) to the disciples and others."
The rule for the request [for teaching] is the rule for protection.
Now, the vases are described:
thus, there are crystal jars, those made of excellent silver, those of precious skull-cups, those called copper, golden jars of manifest and fixed dimensions, and those made of wood or clay.
For pacification, the vases are made of crystal; for nourishment, silver; for killing, human skulls; for driving away and causing enmity, iron; for subjugation, gold;
for attraction, copper; for paralyzing, clay; and for bewildering, wood—these are the ten vases.
Now, the characteristics of the jar for the purpose of pacification (śānti) and nourishment (puṣṭi) are stated:

it is circular, said to be eighteen finger-breadths (aṅgula) in width, twenty finger-breadths in height, with a lip of one finger-breadth, a neck of six finger-breadths, and an opening of eight finger-breadths; these, white as the moon, are for pacification and nourishment, and no others.
Here, the vases (*kalaśa*) are said to be eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in circumference at their necks;
they are twice that height, meaning from the bottom of the vase-body to the edge of the comfortable lip (*sukhoṣṭha*), they are twenty finger-breadths in height.
"With two-finger-breadth lips" means those whose two lips are measured at two finger-breadths each.
They have lips two finger-breadths thick from the starting point of the mouth;
their necks are six finger-breadths long and their mouths eight finger-breadths wide.

Having divided the portion of the mouth from the upper lip to the lower lip into three parts of eight finger-breadths each, we shall determine the opening of the throat with two parts and the thickness of the two lips with one part.
And those jars for the rites of pacification (*śānti*) and nourishment (*puṣṭi*) should be white like the moon; no others should be used.

In the absence of crystal or silver jars, earthen jars—black ones or rootless ones—should be smeared with rice flour or sandalwood paste and made white. Likewise, it was stated by the Blessed One in the *Mūlatantra*:
"For the rite of killing (*māraṇa*), one should cause human skulls to be blackened by smearing them with the charcoal powder from a cremation ground and human fat."

For the rites of eradication (*uccāṭana*) and inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), [the images] have long necks eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length, curved and with thin limbs, twelve finger-breadths in circumference, twenty-four finger-breadths in height, one finger-breadth for the lips, and six finger-breadths for the mouth. For subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*karṣaṇa*), however, they should be fashioned by the artisan according to common worldly practice.
For the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*), they are short, with their circumference equal to their height.

They are sixteen finger-breadths [in height], with necks four finger-breadths [wide] and mouths six finger-breadths [wide]. "Thick lips by two finger-breadths" means they should be taken as described for all rites—such as rites of pacification (śānti), subjugation (vaśya), and so forth. This is the rule for the jars.

Then, one should consecrate the vajra-vases with these mantra syllables: Oṃ haṃ hāṃ hiṃ hīṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ vajrapadmāmṛtaghaṭasuviśuddhadharmadhātusvabhāvasarvadharmān suviśuddhadharmadhātusvabhāvāṅkuru kuru svāhā.
One should place the victory flask (vijayakalaśa) in the center of the mandala after offering perfumes and other substances; this is the consecration of the flask (ghaṭādhivāsana).
Then follows the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the disciples.

At all times—initially at the time of requesting the mandala, in the middle during the preparation of the ground and so forth, and finally at the time of entering the mandala—one should construct the mandala, give a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*), and then perform the protection; this is the procedure therein.

For one who has bathed and put on clean clothes, having prepared a mandala on that very ground according to the rites for pacification and so forth, one should place a twelve-finger-long tooth-stick made of udumbara wood or from another milky sap tree upon his head, bind a garland of flowers around it, and worship it with perfumes and other offerings; then, while he faces the east, the stick should be given to him with this mantra.

"Oṃ āḥ hūṃ ho haṃ kṣaḥ! O Vajradantakāṣṭha, you who are the cause of the nature purified by the four liberations and the four purities; grant the bliss of speech, mind, and gnosis! Purify, purify the impurities of the teeth! Svāhā! Having given the tooth-stick with this mantra, one should observe where the tooth-stick, when thrown upward during the subsequent consecration, falls upon the maṇḍala. Whichever direction it falls toward, the expansion of activities and so forth situated in that direction will be accomplished for that person. This is the ritual procedure for the tooth-stick.

Then, having led the disciple into the mandala on the ground, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the six families with the syllables *uṣṇīṣe guhye oṃ āḥ hūṃ hoḥ haṃ kṣaḥ* upon the head, throat, heart, navel, crown, and secret place. One should then exhort Vajrasattva with these mantra words:

*Oṃ a ā aṃ aḥ, O Vajrasattva, Great Bliss, Vajra Kālacakra! Be present before the disciple; be satisfied; be the granter of boons; perform, perform the consecration of body, speech, and mind, svāhā!* This is the ritual procedure for the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the disciple.
Now the worship of the deities is described:

having performed a manifold worship according to one's own capacity— consisting of jewels, gold, flowers of Indra, various vajra-cloths, perfumes, incense, lamps, bells, mirrors, canopies, various fruits, banners, and so forth, along with dance and music— the excellent disciple offers a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) at the feet of the preceptor for the sake of purification, as prescribed in the tenfold supreme manner.

Here, having performed the visualization of the deity according to the previously stated procedure, one should then unify the *jñānacakra* with the *samayacakra* and offer the *argha* and other oblations using the previously mentioned mantra-words.

Then, for the purpose of worship, first taking scents, sandalwood, and so forth, one should worship the central deity (*nāyaka*) and the others upon the mandala formed on the forearm with the thumb and ring finger.

In all acts of worship and all ritual activities, the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ) should be placed at the beginning of the name; it is understood that in every individual rite, such as those for nourishment (*puṣṭi*), the name is followed by the word *svāhā*. At the end of the name, the word *namaḥ* is used.
Thus are the mantra words for the deities to be worshipped in all rites, as follows in the Root Tantra:
Oṃ buddhāya namaḥ | Oṃ dharmāya namaḥ |

Oṃ, homage to the Guru, the Buddhas, and the Bodhisattvas; such is the procedure for worship.

Then, having performed the tenfold worship as prescribed in the Tantra—consisting of precious gems such as sapphire and others, excellent flowers, various types of incense, garments of five colors, perfumes, incense, lamps, bells, mirrors, canopies, diverse fruits, banners of five colors, dances, and musical instruments.

In this way, the disciple, having performed the aforementioned worship according to his own capacity, then constructs a mandala at the base of the preceptor’s feet and offers a dakṣiṇā for the sake of purification. He offers himself as a substance along with his wife, sons, daughters, and maiden sisters born of the same lineage. Then he should entreat the Guru with gold and flowers, saying: "Today, terrified by the fierce cycle of existence, I have gone for refuge to the Jinas; through the purity of body, speech, and mind, I take refuge at the lotus-feet of you who remove the fear of worldly existence. Having thus caused the mandala to be made, he should request the Guru.

With the three purities—the purity of body, speech, and mind—one gives away one's own substance, including sons and daughters; if one has no daughter of one's own, one may give a maiden born of the same lineage or another. Having thus given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one then performs the formal request (*adhyeṣaṇā*) and the aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).

"From this very day until the limit of enlightenment, I have attained refuge in the Jinas; with the purity of body, speech, and mind, I take refuge at the lotus feet of you two who remove the fear of cyclic existence. Thus one should supplicate the Guru after having a maṇḍala made with gold and flowers.

Then one makes the aspiration: "I shall carry the vajra, the bell, the mudrā, and the Guru upon my head; I shall give gifts to the desired Vajra; I shall protect the samaya of the Supreme Jina here in the Jewel; and I shall maintain the commitment here in the Wheel."

I perform worship to the sword in the family of the manifest lotus; I maintain the vow in the family that gives birth to the Victors for the sake of the liberation of sentient beings; I generate the awakening mind;
and I hold the vajra, the bell, the mudrā, and the guru upon my head. Abiding in the desired Vajra family, I take this commitment:
I shall practice generosity.
Abiding in the Jewel family, for the sake of the accumulation of merit, I shall give the tenfold gift;

namely, iron, jewels, food, cattle, horses, elephants, daughters, wealth, land, beloved wives, and my own flesh—this is considered the tenfold gift. Having accomplished the *cintāmaṇi*, I shall give it away; thus I maintain the vow of the Supreme Victor in this mandala.

Abiding in the Wheel family (*cakrakula*), one makes the vow: "I shall protect the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth, the cow, the fire, and the aggregate of the elements and sense faculties (*skandhendriyasamūha*)," and performs worship with a sword (*khaḍga*).
Abiding in the Sword family (*khaḍgakula*), one makes the vow: "I shall perform worship with all necessary implements for the assembly of gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas, as well as for others.
Abiding in the Lotus family (*padmakula*), which is the family of the manifest lotus (*sphuṭajalaja*).
In the contact with the clearly manifest lotus through union with women of all castes and those of no caste, I make this aspiration for the accumulation of ethical discipline:

"I shall maintain the vow of celibacy for the sake of the liberation of sentient beings. Standing upon the single-pointed vajra of the family that gives birth to the Victors, I shall generate the awakening that is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā), which consists of emptiness and compassion.

Having bathed, anointed with perfumes, and endowed with vows and observances, one should place white mustard seeds and a tooth-stick on the eastern ground; having empowered them with the vajras of the supreme Jinas, they should be given.

Furthermore, nectar should be placed upon the tongue according to the pledges of the supreme Jinas. For the purpose of inducing possession, incense should be offered while reciting the single-syllable *hūṃ* mantra of the Lord of Wrath, accompanied by the *arala* rhythm, as an exhortation.

When this vow has been made, the Guru, requested for the consecration, shall seat the disciple—who has bathed, is anointed with fragrance, and is endowed with vows and observances—on the eastern ground outside the mandala. For the sake of accomplishment, he should empower a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) seven times with the previously mentioned ritual using the "vajras of the best of Jinas," namely with these syllables: *ĀḤ HŪṂ*. Having caused the disciple to lick it, he should cast it into the mandala.
In whichever direction it falls, that particular course of action for him will succeed; thus, the previously mentioned rites of pacification and so forth are accomplished in the eight directions.

Then, having poured three handfuls of water into his mouth and performed the purification, one should place a neck-cloth upon the mandala and lead the disciple to the eastern ground. Thereupon, one should place the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) upon his tongue by means of the commitments (*samaya*) of the Excellent Jinas—the five nectars and the five lamps—after first having prepared incense with those very same substances. That same incense is for the purpose of the descent of the deity; its mantra is the single syllable *HŪṂ*, accompanied by the *arali* [mudrā].

With this mantra, *oṃ arararara lalalala vajrāveśaya hūṃ*, one performs the incitement of the Lord of Wrath, which means the descent of wrath (*krodhāveśa*). By reciting this ten million times and performing a fire offering (*homa*) of one million, one should perform the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*); it brings about a descent of wrath similar to that of [the deity's] remembrance. Its characteristic sign is as follows:
"Possessed by the King of Wrath, threatening the host of Māras with his own weapons in hand"—
here, when the King of Wrath has entered the disciple, he makes that which he kills— whether stationary or moving— into a hundredfold fury with his hands adorned by weapons;
and whomsoever he threatens, that host of Māras who obstructs the Dharma, he causes to fall to the ground and brings to a state of motionlessness.
Likewise, one dances the Vajra-dance with various movements such as the *pratyālīḍha* stance and so forth;

here, that disciple who previously did not know any characteristics of dramatic dance (*nāṭya-lakṣaṇa*), being possessed by wrath, performs the Vajra-dance with various movements in the intermediate space. Then, when he performs laughter, it is mixed with the sound "Haṃ," which strikes fear even into the enemy—the host of Māras.
Thus, [it applies to] that disciple who was previously ignorant.
Possessed by wrath, he sings with a voice unapproachable for humans and other beings,
as it is stated in many other tantras;
therefore, one possessed by the King of Wrath becomes shameless and fearless by virtue of the quality of his wrathful nature.
Furthermore, other deities are also gentle; thus, the deities of the eyes and so forth are gentle—this is the rule regarding the possession of wrath.
Here too, the ten fundamental natures of the ten other wrathful deities should be understood in detail through the binding of mudrās.
The rule is that whichever sign gives rise to which deity, that becomes its hand-mudrā, and by means of that, the deity is to be known.
Other characteristics of possession have not been stated here for fear of prolixity;
now, the pacification of possession and so forth is described.

After the possession has ceased, one should perform protection for the head, heart, crown, navel, throat, and private parts with the Victors residing in their respective stages, using the three vajras of oneself.

When the disciple has been given his body [anointment], dressed in yellow garments, and his eyes have been covered, his entry here should be performed for the sake of concealment; and those vows that lead to the supreme state should be bestowed upon him. This is when the disciple is presided over by the wrathful deity.
Then the preceptor should ask whatever matter is intended;
having consecrated a flower with the three syllables Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ, it should be placed upon [the disciple's] head,
whereupon [the spirit] abandons its possession and returns to its own place.
Thus one becomes free from possession;

thereafter, for one who is free from possession, protection is performed on the head according to the statement "by the Victors," using the syllable *Oṃ* on the head, the syllable *Hūṃ* on the heart, and the syllable *Haṃ* on the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*), by means of the three vajras of the method— body, speech, and mind.

Thus, by means of the syllable *ho* at the navel, the syllable *āḥ* at the throat, and the syllable *kṣaṃ* at the secret place— these being the three vajras of body, speech, and mind belonging to the Wisdom Consort— one should understand that here,
regarding the domain of the body, speech, and mind vajras of both [the male and female deities], the long *hūṃ* syllable is the Speech Vajra.
Having performed protection wherever else the short *cittavajra* is located, the entry of the disciple— clad in yellow garments and with eyes covered— into this mandala should be effected. First,
for the sake of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), there is the conventional truth beginning with the vows and ending with enlightenment, which is the accumulation of merit and so forth.
The meaning of "for that purpose" (*tadartham*) is as follows: those [gifts] have "gone to the supreme goal" (*pravaragatigatāni*).

The "supreme ones" (*pravara*) are the Tathāgatas of the Fortunate Aeon (*bhadrakalpa*), beginning with the seven starting with Vipaśyin and ending with Śākyamuni. Their "goal" (*gati*) consists of the accumulations of merit, ethical discipline, and wisdom.
Those gifts which have gone to that goal are "those that have gone to the supreme goal. It is the rule of the Tathāgata that these must be given by the teacher to the disciple.

In that regard, the Blessed One said that until the attainment of awakening, one must abandon these five: violence, falsehood, another’s wife, another’s wealth, and likewise the drinking of intoxicants; for in this saṃsāra, these evils are like a vajra-noose that destroys one’s own roots of virtue.

"Whoever was the teacher of gods and men at any given time, in his name this command of the Lord of the Universe—which destroys the fear of worldly existence—must be bestowed and indeed observed by you as well.
You must renounce violence, untruth, another’s wife, another’s wealth, and likewise the drinking of intoxicants; these are the five vows, which means they are the rules."
Why? Because in saṃsāra, those five sinful actions are the "vajra-noose" that destroys one's own roots of virtue;
therefore, they must not be committed—this is the rule.

To whom? To Viśvabhartṛ, the Tathāgata who appeared at that time as the teacher of the gods and humans; by his name, this command of Viśvabhartṛ, which crushes the fear of existence, must be given and must also be observed by you.

Just as it has been ordained by the Tathāgata that sons and daughters of noble family should protect the accumulation of merit, one who observes the five precepts must not gamble, eat forbidden food, recite evil words, kill cows, children, women, or men, or commit the five heinous crimes against the Teacher of the Three Jewels.
Betrayal of friends, lords, and the teacher of the three worlds (the Buddha), as well as the destruction of those who trust in the Saṅgha,
and attachment to the sense faculties— these are the twenty-five vows of the Lord of the World;
thereafter, whatever else he desires may be granted.

In that regard, one should not commit these five secondary sins (*upapāpa*): gambling, eating with those of mixed caste (*sāvadyabhoja*), reciting false speech as previously mentioned, the practice of the *bhūtas*, and the rites for ancestors, sacrifices, Vedic injunctions, the religion of the Daityas, and the religion of the Mlecchas. Likewise, among the ten [sins] beginning with the first of the preceding and following groups, one should never commit the first five killings:

the killing of a cow, the killing of a child, the killing of a woman, the killing of a man, and the "killing of another" which is the violation of a statue, stupa, or the like belonging to the Teacher of the Thirty Gods and Men.

Likewise, one should not commit these five acts: betrayal of a friend, betrayal of a lord, betrayal of a teacher, betrayal of the community, and betrayal of one who trusts. Furthermore, "attachment of the senses" refers to attachment to forms, attachment to sounds, attachment to smells, attachment to tastes, and attachment to tactile sensations.

Thus, by the rule of Vajrasattva, the Lord of Beings, the twenty-five vows must be observed by the disciples; these are to be bestowed by the Vajrācārya upon the disciples at the time of initiation—this is the rule for the bestowal of the vows. Now, the entry into the maṇḍala is described: having consecrated a single flower with the *śrī-mantra*, it should first be placed in the hollow of the hands (the lotus-cup) and rotated three times, after which the flower is released from the hollow of the hands into the maṇḍala.
O Lord of Men, in whichever place a beautiful flower falls, that is surely his family;
thereafter, the threefold consecration—here, the supreme one—should be bestowed.
First, after the granting of the vows, one should cover the face with a yellow cloth for all ritual actions.
For the rites of pacification and so forth, using a fine cloth of the color corresponding to the deity, one should recite this mantra:

*oṃ dvādaśāṅganirodhakāriṇe hūṃ phaṭ*. Then, having restrained the eyes and other senses, one should first circumambulate the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) three times within the maṇḍala. Thereafter, at the eastern gate, the preceptor stands in the form of the central deity.
If the deity has arisen within the maṇḍala in the *pratyālīḍha* stance, then the preceptor also stands and bestows the initiation (*seka*) upon the disciple.
Then, once [the master] is seated, he who is seated gives [the initiation].

Thereupon, having sprinkled the head of the disciple entrusted by the spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) with water from a conch shell while reciting the three syllables *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*, one should place a single flower—empowered seven times—into the hollow of his cupped palms as a purification through the offering of a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*). Then, from the hollow of his cupped palms, the casting of the flower upon the *vijaya* flask at the entrance of the mandala should be performed.
Since flowers and such should not be offered on the ground of dust—
as offering them would cause the removal of the dust and, by destroying the established mandala, result in the breaking of the stupa— therefore,
for the sake of examining the family (kula), the throwing of flowers should be performed upon the Victorious Vase (vijayakalaśa) at the eastern gate of the outer mandala.

Otherwise, how could the flower thrown by the disciple fall [upon its own deity] within the thousand-hand mandala? Having first bypassed the *vajrārcis*, even the *vajrajvālā* extends there for one hundred and twenty-five cubits (*sapādahastaśata*). How then, without the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the deity, would the flower fall upon the directions of the families after crossing that [obstacle]?
Therefore, having made the five symbols in the *vijaya-kalaśa*, the throwing of the flower should be performed therein.
Therefore, one should understand that the scents and so forth are for the outer maṇḍala, while the powder-ground is for the powder-maṇḍala and the body of the Blessed One;
one should cause the blindfold to be removed simultaneously.

Then, having first cast a flower and subsequently prompted [the disciple] with this mantra—*Oṃ, open the divine senses, svāhā!*—and having thus performed the opening of the eyes, the deity residing in that place where the well-blessed flower, consecrated with the three syllables, falls, becomes his *kuladevatā*. It is the rule that through her, the accomplishment of the *karmamudrā* is attained.

Then, having shown him his family deity (*kuladevatā*), afterwards the sevenfold consecration (*saptābhiṣeka*)—consisting of water and so forth, being threefold here just as [the lower ones] are with the vase (*kalaśa*) and so on—should be bestowed; after worshipping the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), the unsurpassed [consecration] to be described later is to be given. This is the rule of the Tathāgata for the preceptor (*ācārya*).
Now, the procedure for the sevenfold consecration is stated:

the king should be bathed by the Nāgas with four vases made of jewels, gold, or clay, containing medicinal herbs and perfumes, which are the "Victorious" (*jaya*) and "Most Victorious" (*vijaya*) vases belonging to the deities.

The supreme Guru bestows the Vajra and the Bell— along with the divisions of the crown, the Buddhas, and the Śaktis— as well as the vows of the Sun and Moon, which are to be joined with their respective sense objects.

Having bestowed the Vajra and Bell with equal measure through his most excellent compassion, he should impart the pure Dharma and the clear command of the Lord of Jinas regarding the Wrathful Ones, Maitrī, and the others.

In this case, "by the Nāgas" refers to eight [vases]: four victory-vases (*jayaghaṭa*) and four invincible-vases (*vijayaghaṭa*); or, in the system of five vases, five victory-vases and five invincible-vases; or, in the system of four vases, three victory-vases and three invincible-vases. These are made of jewels and gold, or in their absence, of clay, provided they contain gems and are infused with medicinal herbs and fragrances.

In that regard, the medicinal herbs previously mentioned should be collected in the sulphur-pouch (*gandhakakṣapuṭa*) according to their respective parts, such as the eyes and so forth; from among the twenty-five, five should be taken by the Master as available, according to the procedure taught in the Root Tantra.
Regarding this, the Blessed One said:
"O King, one should cast the medicinal herbs into the sulphur-pouch in sequence."
The [deities] beginning with Brahmā are assigned to the five groups of five parts, starting from the pupils of the eyes, the fire, and so forth: Brāhmī, Nārāyaṇī, Raudrī, Īśvarī, Parameśvarī,
Aindrī, Lakṣmī, Vārāhī, Kaumārī, and likewise Carcikā.
She is known as the earthly, the watery, the luminous, the airy, and likewise the sky-faring;
she is remembered as the mother, the sister, the daughter, the sister’s daughter, and the maternal aunt;
and she is the Brāhmaṇī, the Kṣatriṇī, the Vaiśyā, the Śūdrī, and the Ḍombī.
Thus, these herbs, which grant supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and bestow great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*), are always beneficial;
likewise, *brāhmī* is *brahmadaṇḍī*, and *nārāyaṇī* is *viṣṇukrāntā*. Each part [is so designated].
Raudrī is the portion of Rudra’s matted hair; the well-known Īśvarī is the portion;
the goddess Devatālī is the portion.
Thus ends the first fivefold placement (*pañcanyāsa*):
*aindrī*, *indravāruṇī*, *āg*,
*lakṣmī*, and *āg* [as] *lakṣmaṇā*.
Vārāhī is the portion of Vārāhakrāntā;
Kaumārī is the portion of the pericarp; Carcikā is the portion of the lower calyx.
Thus is the second fivefold placement (nyāsa):
Pārthivī, Māṣalī, Bhāgā,
Vāruṇī, and Rudantī.
The portion called *jyotis* is radiant;
the portion of Vāyu is modest;
the portion of Khecarī is formless.
Thus ends the third pentad:
Mātā is the portion for the son’s paramour; Bhaginī is the portion for Sahadeva.
Putrī is the portion; Kṛtāñjali is the portion; Bhaginī is the portion; Bhāgineyā is the portion; Ajakarṇā is the portion; Svasā is the portion; Mohanī is the portion; Vaṭapatrikā is the portion.
Thus ends the fourth fivefold nyāsa:
Brāhmaṇī is the portion of the *vṛhatī* plant,
and Kṣatriṇī is the portion of *bhṛṅgarāja*.
One part of *yaṣṭimadhu* from a Vaiśya woman,
one part of *kaṇṭakārī* from a Śūdra woman,
and one part of *mayūraśikhā* from a Ḍombī woman.
Thus, in the fifth pentad-assignment (*pañcaka-nyāsa*), the collection of grains and crops is as follows in their respective order:
*dhānya*, *mahādhānya*, *māṣa*, white *śaṇa*, and black sesame—this is the first pentad; *kodrava*, *mudga*, *kalāya*, white sesame, and wheat—this is the second pentad.
The third group of five consists of moṣṭha, tripuṭā, black mustard, barley, and māṣa beans.
The fourth group of five consists of lentils (*masūrikā*), white mustard, *kaṅgu* grain, *tuvarikā*, and *varvaṭikā*.

The fifth group of grains consists of linseed (*alasī*), *varaṭī*, *varṇa*, *lūlaya*, and black chickpeas (*kṛṣṇacaṇaka*); these should be taken as they are available in the section on the *kakṣapuṭa*. These constitute the five groups of five.
In this context, the portions are equal to the number of pills.

From these, one should take gems belonging to the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra classes; likewise, diamonds, sapphires, rubies, moonstones, and emeralds are the primary red stones. Similarly, there are metals: gold, silver, copper, steel, iron, and magnetite. Furthermore, the intermediate gems are pearls, coral, royal silk, sword-crystals, six-dot crystals, and *ṣaḍvinduka*. Likewise, the inferior ones are rock crystal, *jīvaja* (living-stone), *dohalikā*, and green gems. These should be taken according to one's means.

Now, for the gods and nāgas, the jewels used in the great jewel-consecration of a universal monarch (ājñācakravartin) are of five colors; in their absence, there is a rule that fragrant flowers of five colors may be used. Here, for those who are poor, a green gem is used in the victorious conch.
The eastern and western jars of victory and triumph are blue in color;
the eastern and southeastern jars are black; the southern and southwestern jars are red.
White [powder] is in the jar of the north-eastern direction,
yellow in the jar of the western-north-western direction; likewise, iron, magnetite, steel, tin, silver, and gold.
Likewise, the medicinal herbs are one part each; in the *jayavijaya* jar they are two parts, and in the eastern fire-pit [they are likewise].
The [lines] are three parts long in the south and west,
four parts long in the north and east,
and five parts long in the west and northwest.

Likewise, by means of the division of pills (*guṭikā*), there are grains (*sasya*), as well as the aforementioned fragrant substances for the *kakṣapuṭa*—thus, having placed the metals, jewels, forest herbs, grains, and fragrant substances into jars, one should again bind a packet (*pohalikā*) with those twenty-five [substances] and cast it into a conch full of water that has been victorious. With that, one should consecrate [the disciple] at the five places of birth: on the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*), the shoulder, the joint of the right arm, the joint of the left arm, and likewise on the buttock and the joint of the waist. Then, for the purification of the family deity (*kuladevatā*), there is the mantra for casting flowers (*puṣpakṣepa*).
Oṃ sarvatathāgatakulaviśodhani svāhā. With this mantra, the preceptor should cause the disciple to release the flower.
With this mantra, the opening of the eyes [is performed]:
Oṃ divyanayanam udghāṭayāmi svāhā.
Then, beginning with the presiding deity of the maṇḍala of the family deity (*kuladevatā*), he should show the entire maṇḍala.

Then, having performed the purification of the family at the eastern gate, the preceptor (*ācārya*) leads the disciple with his left hand; together with the Action-Vajra-holder (*karmavajrin*), they perform a circumambulation and lead him to the northern gate. There, for the sake of purifying the body, he takes water from all the ritual jars (*kalaśa*) with the mantras of the goddess Tārā, pours it into the victorious conch (*vijayaśaṅkha*), and performs the water-consecration (*udakābhiṣeka*). Furthermore, he should consecrate him at the five places of birth with this mantra:
*oṃ ā ī ṛ ā lu pañcadhātuviśodhani svāhā*.
Then, during the crown consecration (*mukuṭābhiṣeka*), one should consecrate [the disciple] at the five places of birth with this mantra:
*oṃ ai ṛ u lu pañcatathāgatapariśuddha svāhā*.

Then, one should bind upon him a crown of jewels and gold or a cloth crown. Thus, by these two consecrations, through the purification of the elements (*dhātu*) and the aggregates (*skandha*), the purification of the channels (*nāḍī*) occurs.

Having performed the purification of the body on the *kāyavajra* ground, one should then lead the disciple by way of a clockwise circuit back to the southern gate for the sake of purifying speech. Having consecrated the disciple at the five places of birth, one should perform the ribbon-consecration (*paṭṭābhiṣeka*) with this mantra: *oṃ a ā aṃ aḥ ha hā haṃ haḥ ho keṃ daśapāramitāparipūraṇi svāhā*.
Then, one should bind a jewel ribbon, a golden ribbon, or, if these are unavailable, a garland of flowers upon the forehead.
Thereafter, during the vajra and bell consecrations, one should consecrate [the disciple] at the five places of birth with this mantra:
"Oṃ hūṃ hoḥ, O Purifier of the Sun and Moon, svāhā! Then, placing the vajra and vajra-bell upon the head, one should perform the consecration with water from a conch shell.

Having thus purified the Speech-Vajra (vāgvajra) by means of these two consecrations, and having placed the vajra on the thumb, one should again circumambulate clockwise; then, for the sake of purifying the Mind-Vajra (cittavajra), one should perform the consecration at the five places of birth at the eastern face as before.
The Vajra-vow initiation is performed with this mantra: *oṃ a ā e ai ar ār o au al āl viṣayendriyaviśodhani svāhā*.

Then, having offered flowers upon the ears and other sense organs, one is again consecrated during the Name Initiation at the five places of birth with this mantra: *oṃ ha hā ya yā ra rā va vā la lā caturbrahmavihāraviśuddha svāhā*.
Thereafter, having bound a flower garland around the hands and feet—in the absence of bracelets, anklets, and so forth—one should perform the prophecy through the Name Initiation.

Having established [the disciple] as "Amukavajrastha," and then, for the sake of purifying gnosis (*jñānaviśuddhi*), having purified the mind-vajra (*cittavajra*) and led the disciple back again by way of the right-hand circuit through the two empowerments, one should empower him at the western face in the five locations with the empowerment of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakrābhiṣeka*) by means of this mantra: *oṃ haṃ kṣaṃ dharmacakrapravartaka svāhā*.

Having bestowed the empowerment and purified the vajras of body, speech, mind, and gnosis through the seven empowerments, the preceptor then places the vajra and vajra-bell in the hands of the disciple. With the two and a half verses beginning with "O [Name]vajra, by these two," and "The preceptor, having given the vajra-bell, should cause the pure Dharma to be bestowed out of supreme compassion," he should act as follows: "In the Vajra family, one should indeed commit the taking of life; in the Sword [family], untruthful speech; in the Jewel [family], one should steal the property of others; and likewise in the excellent Lotus family, one should take the wives of others."

Alcohol, lamps, and the Buddhas—each with their respective objects—are to be utilized within one’s own mandala; the eyes and so forth are to be honored on the full moon of Kārtika; one’s own wives are not to be despised;

and for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings, they are to be offered at one’s feet. This body, which is the means of accomplishment, must not be protected by you [in a worldly way], for Buddhahood does not otherwise occur even in infinite kalpas, as spoken by the Jina.

Water is the goddesses Tārā and the rest; here, the Conquerors are the crown; the powers are the hero’s turban; the vajra-bell, the sun, and the moon are the vows; and the objects of the senses are the yoga of loving-kindness and the rest under those names.

"The splendor of the awakening of command, which crushes the fear of cyclic existence and is permeated by Kālacakra— these seven empowerments, which remove the stains of defilement, are to be bestowed in the maṇḍala.
Having thus performed the ritual of the seven empowerments in the maṇḍala, the preceptor should then contemplate the empowerment of the Buddhas for the disciple,
for the sake of determining seniority and so forth.

The fifth is the Vajra-vow initiation (*vajravratābhiṣeka*), which is the purification of the sense faculties such as the eyes with respect to objects such as forms, and the thorough cleansing of the year-long [observances] and so forth; it is called the "Vajra-vow" because it brings about the attainment of the *mahāmudrā* siddhi through the restraint of ordinary objects.

The sixth is the Name initiation (*nāmābhiṣeka*), which is the bestowing of a name such as "Amuka-vajra" with the intention that the castes, such as Brahmins and others, are of a single essence; it consists in the perpetual purification of passion, hatred, and so forth by means of the fulfillment of the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), beginning with loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

The seventh is the empowerment of authorization (*anujñā-abhiṣeka*), which brings about the accomplishment of Buddhahood; it is for the purpose of teaching the most secret Vajrayāna through the distinction between the conventional and the ultimate, according to the inclinations of the infinite realm of sentient beings.

These seven empowerments are not to be bestowed elsewhere than upon a powder mandala (*rajomaṇḍala*), such as one made on cloth and so forth; however, the [first] six, beginning with the vase empowerment (*kumbha*), may be bestowed even without the construction of a mandala.

Having explained the seven empowerments—which consist of the lower conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) and serve as the steps to the palace of mundane and supramundane accomplishments—among the eleven empowerments previously indicated, [the author] now introduces the three empowerments that consist of the yogic conventional reality, which accomplish mundane siddhis and accord with the ultimate truth, beginning with the word "Kumbha":
"Until ten years of age, she is of one kind, appearing in ten forms, visible and touchable; therefore, the oceans of nectar should be embraced, served, and obtained."

The twenty [mudrās] held above are extremely terrifying, being portions of the *krodhas*, *bhūtas*, and *asuras*; six and four are for the purpose of consecration (*sekārtha*), bestowing the fruit of equal bliss, while the others are for the purpose of meditation (*bhāvanārtha*).

That which is the first touch of the glorious Wisdom (*prajñā*) upon the breast is itself the "Vase Consecration" (*kumbhaseka*); it becomes the "Secret Consecration" (*guhyābhiṣeka*) through the tasting and gazing at the moon-holder (*śaśadhara*). Having purified [the disciple] with all the Buddha-families (*jinakula*) and their limbs and faces, the mudrā should be given to the disciple by the Guru, having made even the Victorious One (*jina*) a witness therein.

Having enjoyed with passion a beautiful maiden of twelve years, adorned with all ornaments and resembling molten gold, by means of his own vajra-jewel consisting of wisdom and method; and having recognized her as being possessed of passion, one should place the vajra, together with the seed-syllable, into the mouth of the disciple for the sake of purification. Thereafter, one’s own mudrā should be given, or alternatively another who is endowed with the path of smoke and so forth, yet who is terrified, distracted in mind, deaf, under the control of another, afflicted by disease, or recently delivered.

Those who are prone to anger, stubbornness, greed for wealth, falsehood, and quarreling, or who are deficient in their own limbs, should be avoided by a skillful preceptor during the Wisdom Empowerment (*prajñābhiṣeka*), O King. However, those previously mentioned who are devoted to the Buddha and uphold the commitments (*samaya*) of the Guru should always be honored.

Now, regarding the procedure for the Higher Empowerment (*uttarābhiṣeka*): the triad beginning with the flask (*kalaśa*) is called the Higher Empowerment; here, it is for the purpose of the flask and subsequent empowerments.

One should avoid a maiden as a *mudrā* until she reaches ten years of age, because the single *prajñāpāramitā* becomes tenfold through the purification of the [perfections] beginning with generosity (*dāna*) for each successive year; furthermore, until the falling out of the teeth occurs, it is the *jñānadhātu* due to its imperishability,
and after the falling out of the teeth, it is the *ākāśadhātu*.

Thus, by means of the two elements, that maiden of unbroken womb is to be seen, touched, and worshipped by him; therefore, beginning from the eleventh year after the tenth year, she is to be embraced until her twentieth year. Together with the six [elements], four are to be cultivated, beginning with the wind element;
hence, the wind element is present in the eleventh year.
In the twelfth [month] fire,
in the thirteenth water, and in the fourteenth earth— thus there are four.
In the fifteenth [day] there is sound; in the sixteenth, touch; in the seventeenth, taste.
In the eighteenth [moment] there is form;
in the nineteenth, odor; in the twentieth, the dharma-element.

Thereafter, from twenty years onwards, the mudrās become supremely terrifying; being portions of the wrathful ones, spirits, and asuras, they are— starting from the twenty-first year after the twentieth year, for each successive year respectively— extremely dark blue.
Atibalā,
Jambhī,
and Mānī.
Stambhī, Mārīcī, and Cundā.
Bhṛkuṭī, Vajraśṛṅkhalā, and Raudrākṣī are the ten wrathful deities.
Then, from the thirty-first year, there are eight elemental portions: Carcikā and Vārāhī.
Raudrī, Aindrī, and Brāhmaṇī.
Mahālakṣmī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
From thirty-nine years [of age], eight portions of asuras are Śvānāsyā and Sūkarāsyā.
She with the face of a tiger, she with the face of a jackal, she with the face of a garuḍa.
Ulukāsyā, Gṛdhrāsyā,
and Kākāsyā— for forty-six years, for the purpose of meditating on the mudrās.
Furthermore, regarding the meaning of initiation (*sekārtha*), there are six and four [initiations] that bestow the fruit of equal bliss;
starting from the fire element up to the dharma element,
the rule is that they are to be received at the vajra-position of the wind element.
Here, the higher initiation (*uttarābhiṣeka*) is twofold:

one is for the purpose of introducing sentient beings [to the path], for the thorough knowledge of the path, and for the authority to hear the tantras; the other is for the sake of conferring the status of a Great Master (*mahācārya*) and making one a teacher.

Therefore, in the preliminary consecration (*pūrvābhiṣeka*), a maiden of twelve years or more—free from defects such as timidity or distraction—and who has been ripened by the disciple, must be offered to the guru.
Then, having performed the supplication and so forth, the disciple requests the guru with the praise to be described below.
Thereupon, the pleased guru causes the touching of the breasts according to worldly convention; that itself is the vase consecration (*kalaśābhiṣeka*) of his own consort (*mudrā*).

Then, having performed the secret worship (*guhyapūjā*), he gives the nectar (*amṛta*) to the disciple and causes him to gaze upon the lotus of the consort (*mudrā*). By means of that tasting and gazing at the one who holds the moon (the consort), the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*) occurs. Thereafter, in the wisdom-knowledge initiation (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*), having formed the five-family garland (*pañcakulakalāpinī*) with the seed-syllables beginning with *oṃ*, the consort should then be given to the disciple by the Guru for the purpose of embracing her hands and engaging in union. Having made the Victor Vajrasattva the witness, [the Guru should think]: "So that this unfortunate being may be authorized for the teaching of the tantra to disciples, for the drawing of the mandala, and for the proclamation of the tantra in his own abode and so forth."

First is the rule for the initiation for introducing the disciple: thus, by means of laughter, the master [bestows] the Guhya initiation through the purification of the deity via the bliss of semen characterized by duality; by means of gazing, the Pāṇivyāpti initiation through the purification of the deity via the threefold nature; by means of the embrace of hands, the Dvandva initiation through the purification of the deity via the fourfold nature; and by means of the bliss of semen characterized by the fivefold nature, [the initiation is bestowed]. Thus, according to worldly convention, there are four types of initiation for the purpose of introducing sentient beings.

Then, once all the tantras have been heard and understood along with their commentaries, the ten vidyās as described in sequence for the sake of attaining the status of a great sovereign (mahādhipati) should be offered by the householder disciple to the guru;
regarding this, the Blessed One has spoken in the Root Tantra:
The sister's daughter, one's own daughter, the sister, the mother, the mother-in-law, the wife of the maternal uncle,
the wife of the father's brother, and the father's sister.
One's own mother’s sister, one’s own wife of excellent form,
and the ten vidyās beginning with Tārā and ending with Dharmadhātviśvarī— all born of one's own lineage— must be offered by the disciple who desires liberation at the time of initiation.
If the disciple does not offer these vidyās to the guru, it is for the sake of protecting the family lineage.

At that time, O King, the consecration (seka) should not be given by others who dwell in the household; it should be given by those other women of the Śūdra caste who have been consecrated in the maṇḍala,
and by the Guru, to the monks and novices.
The ten [mudrās] born from the end of the Dharmadhātu are, in order: the Śūdrī, Kṣatriṇī, Brāhmaṇī, Vaiśyā, Ḍombī, Kaivartī, Naṭīkā, Rajakī, Carmakārī, and Caṇḍālī, beginning with Vāyavyā.
"The Great Vidyās are fully proclaimed as bestowers of the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.

Thus, according to the sequence stated, the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), the ten masteries (*daśavaśitā*), the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), and the ten powers (*daśabala*) become purified by these [Vidyās]. Therefore, for the sake of exercising sovereign power, the ten mudrās should be bestowed upon one who desires the rank of a Maṇḍala Master; such is the rule of the Tathāgatas.

Having thus mastered the ten mudrās, the disciple then requests permission from the guru: "O Blessed One, who has attained all the pāramitās, what should I do now? Thereupon the ācārya says: "Taking this wife of yours, go among the ten [mudrās] and together with her, make my request."
And for the monks and novices, a Caṇḍālī woman should be made their own wife;
then, having taken her according to the guru’s injunction, they both construct two maṇḍalas with flowers such as gold-colored ones, and thereafter they make the formal request.
Homage to you, Kālacakra, who destroys all obscurations;
homage be to you, the body of gnosis, filled with supreme unchanging bliss.
That which is the unchanging bodhicitta is the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion.
Therefore, O Protector, show me favor now;
together with my wife, children, and others, I am forever your servant until the very seat of enlightenment. I have no other refuge.
To the disciple who had thus requested [the teaching] together with his wife, the satisfied master, having removed all her ornaments, causes Śabdavajrā to embrace him;
for a householder, however, [he causes her to embrace] the mother of his wife.
Then, to the east, Tārā.
Pāṇḍarā is in the south,
Māmakī in the north, and Locanā in the west.
Sparśavajrā is in the southeast,
Rasavajrā is in the southwest,
and Rūpavajrā is in the northeast.

In the northwest, one should arrange the circle of Yoginīs, beginning with Gandhavajrā, naked, with disheveled hair, and holding skull-cups and flaying knives in their hands, together with the nine Vidyās in their proper sequence;
thus is the sevenfold prior consecration by means of water and the other [substances].

Then follows the Higher Consecration (*uttarābhiṣeka*). The Higher-Higher Consecration (*uttarottarābhiṣeka*) is performed with the common action-seal (*sāmānyakarmamudrā*). For the purpose of offering the seals by those born of the *śūdra* caste and others previously mentioned, one should bathe a monk (*bhikṣu*) or a novice (*śramaṇera*) with ten or eight jars, as well as with the *jaya* and *vijaya* [victory] vessels. Among those [women], one should bathe a householder with six seals and four jars, as well as with the *jaya* and *vijaya* vessels. From among those nine [women], one should consecrate him with his own wife using one seal and one *vijaya* jar, according to the previously stated procedure.
Then, one should present the consort for the purpose of bestowing the vase-consecration (*kalaśābhiṣeka*).

Here, having—by means of the deity-yoga consisting of wisdom and method—enjoyed a beautiful maiden endowed with all ornaments, resembling molten gold, twelve years of age and up to twenty years old, with his own vajra-jewel; and having recognized her as being full of passion and possessing the power of the *rajas*, he should cast even the vajra, together with the seed-syllable, into the mouth of the disciple for the sake of purification during the successive consecrations.

Afterwards, the seal (mudrā) who was embraced by the ācārya—or else the wife of his son—the ācārya himself approaches; then, when the moment for the consecration (seka) has arrived, he should hand over his own wife to the disciple again. Having bound the disciple’s eyes, the Guru [takes] the nose of the Prajñā; then, through the knowledge of the wife, the ācārya should hand over his own seal. This is the procedure for the consecration everywhere in the Great Sovereignty (mahādhipatya).

If there are ten mudrās, then the disciple should offer whichever one he is capable of desiring, from two ghaṭikās after midnight until sunrise; thereafter, he should dismiss the gaṇacakra, and having dismissed it, he should give the *saṃvara* to the disciple:

"That which has been described by me conventionally (*saṃvṛtyā*) as the characteristic of the innate (*sahaja*) ending with the *virama*, which ends with the three moons—that is what occurs through the ultimate (*vivṛtyā*)."
Because bliss is revealed for yogins through the Unfallen One, this Great Bliss must be protected by you.
This was stated in the Root Tantra,
even in the context of the action seal (*karmamudrā*) and the passion for the wisdom seal (*jñānamudrā*).
The great bliss that must be protected, the bodhicitta, should be established by those of firm vows; one should not abandon the bodhicitta,
but rather meditate upon the entire triple world as a reflection in a mirror.
By protecting this very [precept], one attains Buddhahood in this very life;

endowed with the equipment of ethical discipline and possessed of merit and wisdom, one reaches the ten perfections and becomes a Perfectly Awakened One existing in the three times. By means of this, all the Perfectly Awakened Ones have set in motion the Wheel of Dharma.
Beyond this there is no higher knowledge, which is the sovereign of the three realms, inseparable from emptiness and compassion, for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of oneself and others.
If you, my son, maintain the vow of all the Protectors, then you shall attain perfect awakening, empowered by all the Buddhas.
