If, with your mind overcome by passion, you do not maintain your vow after having taken it in the presence of your husband, then you shall go to the Raurava hell.
When the bodhicitta, having become soft in mind and so forth, is about to be emitted, one should then grasp it outside the lotus with one's own tongue, having recognized the mudrā.

Having thus bestowed the vow upon the disciple, the disciple also, having given the teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*) and having again performed the mandala, should pray: "May the Blessed One graciously perform the ritual of consecration (*seka*) for me. Then the Guru should address the disciple:

"Listen, my son! Just as, according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), the bliss characterized by the sixteen joys is common to all sentient beings, yet it has emerged—through more than one hundred and twenty-one verses—as the supreme primordial Buddhahood."

By means of the [mantras] beginning with *mañjuvajreṇa kāmākṣobham*, one effects the unshakeability of desire; the fullness of the world enters into one's own mind. The Full (Pūrṇā) flows as a drop from the lotus of full-blazing flames, having melted the moon-holder (the semen) from the head. Embraced by the letter *Āṃ* and *ṆṬR*, it naturally bestows excellent bliss at the end of the three emissions of the drop (*bindu-mokṣa*). This consists of the bliss of light, touch, and union, and the distinctions of joy (*ānanda*) and so forth.

First, even by the mere sight with the eyes, it produces the bliss of desire for men; later, during the full union, it produces supreme bliss once again within one's own body. Flowing as a flame-drop (*jvālābindu*), she rejoices with the vajra of the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*) in the lotus; at the end of the three drops, she brings about the vajra of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) which has reached the state of emission (*kṣara*).

The first is the union with the fourfold [state] known as *kāmānanda*, characterized by the desire for the syllable; it is indeed the arising of power (*śakti*). The second is *paramānanda* (supreme bliss). Then there is *jvālā*, *bindu*, and *ghūrṇa*; the third is *viramānanda* (bliss of cessation). *Oṃ*, *ṇṭrā*, *nāda*, and *nidrā* constitute the fourth, which is *sahajānanda* (innate bliss).

In this world, desire causes agitation in the mind of every living being; from that, the first bliss arises, and thereafter it reaches fullness. The state of fullness occurs at the forehead due to the fullness of the *bodhicitta* through the embrace of wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth; this is the second, supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).
Then, from the head—the state of fullness—the state of the flame flows as the drop (*bindu*); having caused the moon-bearer to flow, it produces the third, the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*).

Then, at the time of the *auṃ* and *ṇṭra* states, at the conclusion of the drops (*bindu*) of body, speech, and mind, and at the moment of the emission of the four drops, one brings about innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). Thus, by means of the five groups of five digits (*kalā*) beginning with the first lunar day (*pratipad*), which consist of the natures of space, wind, fire, water, and earth, and are named Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā, and which possess the qualities of these vowels: *a, i, ṛ, u, ḷ, ka; ā, e, ar, o, al, ca; ha, ya, ra, va, la, ṭa*.
Thus, the fifth is full of ānanda,
the tenth is full of paramānanda,
and the full moon day (pūrṇimā) is full of viramānanda.
Innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) is the sixteenth digit (*kalā*), the gathering (*samāhāra*) of all elements (*dhātu*), the meeting (*melāpaka*), the assembly (*samāja*), and the vow (*saṃvara*); thus,
passion (*rāga*) is the white phase of the bodhicitta.

Dispassion is the dark side, as it is said in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*: "Great passion beginning with dispassion, possessing all colors, blazing with light; seated in the vajra-posture of perfect awakening, upholding the Dharma of the Buddha’s assembly."
Thus it is:
possessing all forms yet formless, holding the sixteen-fold half-and-half bindu; partless, free from the fear of mental construction, he holds the pinnacle of the fourth dhyāna.
Such is the rule of the Blessed One;
the knowledge of Mahāmudrā should be understood in detail through the exposition in the fifth chapter, and it has not been elaborated upon here.

Now, the four yogas of the sixteen joys (*ānanda*) are described, beginning with the words "desires" (*kāmāḥ*). Here, for all sentient beings, there is the yoga of body, speech, mind, and gnosis (*jñāna*), distinguished by the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (*turya*).
These joys, according to their divisions, are sixteen.
In that context, "desires" refers to the bliss of the body; "bliss" refers to the bliss of speech; and "trembling" refers to the bliss of the mind.
By the designation "syllable" (*akṣara*), there is bliss-consciousness (*jñānānanda*);
thus, through these four, the yoga of bliss is one.
Likewise, by "fullness" (*pūrṇā*), there is the supreme bliss of the body (*kāyaparamānanda*).
In this context, by the power of meter, the three beginning with supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) are [respectively] speech, mind, and gnosis-vajra; thus, "supreme bliss" refers to speech,
and that which arises from it is the supreme bliss of the mind (*cittaparamānanda*).
"Power" (śakti) is the supreme bliss of knowledge;
this is the second yoga.
"Flame" (jvālā) is the cessation-bliss of the body.
"Viramānanda" refers to the cessation-bliss of speech; "ghūrṇa" refers to the cessation-bliss of mind;
and "bindu" refers to the cessation-bliss of gnosis—this is the third yoga.
Likewise, *ā~ ṇṭrā* is the sahajānanda of the body; *sahajānanda* is the sahajānanda of speech;
and *nidrā* is the sahajānanda of the mind.
"Nāda" is the innate bliss of gnosis (*jñānasahajānanda*).

Thus, the body is fourfold; the body is fourfold through the divisions of the emanation (*nirmāṇa*), enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*), dharma, and essential (*svābhāvika*) bodies; speech is fourfold; mind is fourfold; and gnosis is the fourth.
Thus, the sixteen varieties of bliss (ānanda) are to be seen in detail in the Śrītantra; such is the rule that the innate (sahaja) is the sixteenth bliss.

Having indicated the three types of empowerments that accomplish mundane siddhis, he speaks of the eleventh empowerment—the uncommon cause for supramundane siddhi—with the words "again," and so forth.

"Great wisdom" refers to the great mudrā to be described, whose nature is non-conceptual intention; through the cultivation of that, the gnosis arises, which is the great immutable great bliss—this is the eleventh empowerment.
In the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara* as well, only eleven consecrations are taught; for it says:
"First by the water-consecration, second by the crown-consecration, third by the ribbon-consecration, and fourth by the vajra and bell."
The fifth is the empowerment by one's own master, while the sixth is the name-empowerment; the seventh empowerment is the command of the Buddha, and the eighth is the vase-empowerment.
The ninth is by means of the secret consecration, and the tenth is from the wisdom consecration; through the application of the Vajra of Reality, one should bestow all the vajra vows.
The Teacher himself explains this ritual of consecration; the preceptor must not be disparaged, nor should one transgress the command of the Sugata.

Thus, because of the Lord’s explicit statement that "the eleventh consecration is the principal one through the application of the *tattva-vajra*," the fourth or the eleventh consecration should be understood by the wise as being distinct.

Accordingly, these four—the vase and so forth—have names that correspond to their etymologies: the "leaking" (*kṣara*), the "non-leaking" (*akṣara*), the "vibration" (*spanda*), and the "non-vibration" (*niḥspanda*).
The passage beginning with "kāya" and so forth is easy to understand.

Likewise, those known as the "child," "mature," and "old" [types of consorts] are designated as "wisdom" (prajñā). From the age of twelve up to twenty, for her who is pleasing to one's own mind and fit for initiation, the emission of the *bodhicitta* occurs through touch.

Through the descent of the stream of white nectar from the four-petaled *uṣṇīṣa*-lotus onto the pericarp of the sixteen-petaled lotus in the forehead, there occurs an experience of bliss consisting of physical bliss (*kāyānanda*), the bliss of yoga (*yogānanda*), mental bliss (*cittānanda*), and the bliss of gnosis (*jñānānanda*).
Because he has received the first initiation, the yogin consecrated by the breasts is called a "child" (*bāla*);
then, by the slight agitation of the vajra, the bodhicitta is emitted.

From the thirty-two-petaled lotus of the heart to the pericarp of the eight-petaled lotus of the throat, that experience of bliss consisting of the supreme bliss of body, the supreme bliss of speech, the supreme bliss of mind, and the supreme bliss of gnosis—which exceeds even the preceding [stages]—is the mature secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*).

Then, through intense swinging, [the seminal essence] becomes mobile; by its arrival from the navel-lotus of sixty-four petals to the secret lotus of thirty-two petals, and by the movement of the clear fluid—known as *spanda*—which resides at the tip of the fifteenth lotus of the lunar semen, all the way to the hollow of the *vajra*-jewel, there arises an experience of bliss consisting of the physical *viramānanda*, the verbal *viramānanda*, the mental *viramānanda*, and the gnosis-*viramānanda*. This is the "increased" (*vṛddha*) Wisdom-Gnosis Initiation, known as Mahāmudrā.

The disk arising from the sky is born from her through the passion known as the meditation on the internal and external essences; it is called "motionless" because the external vibration of the *vajramaṇi* has been arrested.

That which is the nectar of the moon, characterized by non-emitted bliss, consists of the body-innate joy (*kāyasahajānanda*), the speech-innate joy (*vāksahajānanda*), the mind-innate joy (*cittasahajānanda*), and the gnosis-innate joy (*jñānasahajānanda*). This is the fourth initiation, termed "Great Gnosis" (*mahājñāna*), which is further designated by the phrase "that again in that manner."

He is the *Prajāpati* because he brings about the manifestation of the five Tathāgatas, the five goddesses, and so forth, from the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so on—which possess obscurations—just as copper and other metals are transformed into the appearance of gold through the attainment of unobscured supramundane gnosis (*lokottarajñāna*).
He is the *Tāyin* (Savior) because of his possession of *tāya*, which is the proclamation of the path seen by himself; thus [he is] the Tathāgata and others.
The establishment of the body and so forth for the yogi who has realized the supreme unchanging gnosis (*paramākṣara-jñāna*) is taught in the *Śrī Kālacakra*.
The body becomes transparent, unimpaired by atoms, and arises equal to space, fully endowed with the [major] marks and so forth;
the entire threefold world, transparent and free from obscuration, appears like a dream.
Speech, pervading all directions through various languages pleasing to others, moves at all times embraced by the innate (*sahaja*), the mind being filled with true bliss. Thus.

This very non-dual, imperishable, and upward-streaming [consciousness], by proceeding in sequence through the secret place, the navel, the heart, and the throat, receives four names beginning with Vajrasattva;
reaching the forehead, it is called the fourfold yoga known as Viśuddha and so forth;
and reaching the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa), it is named Kālacakra—thus there are six beings.

Now, he states the instruction on the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), which is the uncommon cause for supramundane accomplishment (*lokottarasiddhi*), beginning with the words "one should perform the practice of this very [yoga]," and so forth;
for it is as follows:

Beginning with "By inconceivable appearances" and ending with "the universal image is luminosity," the first limb of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*), called withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), is indicated;
by the verse beginning with "covered and uncovered," the limb of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is indicated;
and by the verse beginning with "When the image has been seen, then... the limb of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is indicated.
By the statement "one should place the vital breath (prāṇa) in the drop (bindu)," the limb of meditative concentration (dhāraṇā) is also indicated.
Regarding the two limbs beginning with recollection (anusmṛti), their indication should likewise be inferred as appropriate, by virtue of the capacity of that [preceding] indication for its purpose.

Furthermore, the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga) has been taught by the Blessed One in the *Samājottara* through the methods of general indication, detailed explanation, and specific re-explanation, as the means for achieving the supreme accomplishment characterized by perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
The siddhis beginning with invisibility are proclaimed as the common siddhis;
the wise call the supreme siddhi the means for attaining the state of a Buddha.
The fourfold means has been described by Bodhivajra; it is always praised in all the Yoga Tantras for the sake of yogins.

The first is the procedure of service (sevāvidhāna), the second is the near-attainment (upasādhana), the third is indeed the attainment (sādhana), and the fourth is the great attainment (mahāsādhana).
Service is of two kinds, distinguished as ordinary and supreme;
the ordinary is performed with the four vajras, and the supreme through the six limbs.
First is the realization of emptiness; second is the gathering of the seed-syllable;
third is the accomplishment of the image; and fourth is the placement of the syllables.
By means of these four vajras, the service— the common sādhana—
must always and in every way be performed with the nectar of gnosis.
Having performed service through the six-limbed yoga, one should accomplish the supreme practice; otherwise, the highest siddhi will certainly not arise.
Withdrawal, meditation, breath control, concentration, recollection, and absorption— this is called the six-limbed yoga.
The withdrawal of all ten sense organs from their respective objects in every respect, directed toward the cessation of desire, is declared to be *pratyāhāra*.
In brief, through the application of the five Buddhas, the conceptualization of the five desires is called "meditative concentration" (dhyāna); that meditative concentration is of five kinds.
Applied thought, sustained thought, joy, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind— these five are the constituents of dhyāna.
In all the secret tantras, various [topics] have been proclaimed:
the arising of the three secrets, reasoning, investigation, and their practical application.
The third is characterized by joy, the fourth is the gathering of bliss;
the fifth should be known as one's own mind, wherein the exertion of knowledge and the object of knowledge has ceased.
Consisting of all Buddhas, peaceful, established in all desires,
the breath consists of the five gnoses and has the nature of the five elements.
Having emanated it in the form of a sphere, one should visualize a great jewel of five colors at the tip of the nose; this is known as *prāṇāyāma*.
Having meditated on one's own mantra in the heart, one should place the vital breath (prāṇa) within the bindu; having restrained the senses, one should hold the jewel—this is known as dhāraṇā.
When the mind has entered the vajra of cessation, the apprehension of signs arises in five ways; that sign has been taught by Bodhivajra.
First is the appearance of a mirage, the second is the appearance of smoke,
the third is the appearance of fireflies, and the fourth is a blazing lamp.
The fifth, however, is the constant light, resembling a cloudless sky;
one should expand that stable [light] through the vajra-path within one's own elements.
Having meditated upon that which is to be recollected, one should cause it to radiate forth in its very form; this is to be known as "recollection" (anusmṛti), for therein a manifestation arises.
Having briefly withdrawn all phenomena through the meditative absorption of wisdom and means, one should visualize them within the central image by means of the yoga of the mass.
The instantaneous accomplishment of knowledge is designated as "samādhi";
having perfected withdrawal (pratyāhāra), one is empowered by all mantras.
Attain the knowledge of meditative absorption and subsequently achieve the state of the five superknowledges;
through breath control (prāṇāyāma), this is certainly observed by the Bodhisattvas.
Through the power of *dhāraṇā*, Vajrasattva shall constantly enter [the practitioner];
from the union with *anusmṛti*, a circle of light arises.

The brief explanation of these verses, beginning with "Service is indeed by the nectar of gnosis," is stated as follows: "When there is mere mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there shall be freedom from obscuration."

It is called *sevā* (service/devotion) because it is served by those seeking liberation and practiced repeatedly. What is that? It is the limb of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the limb of meditation (*dhyāna*), extending up to the vision of the reflection of the smoke and other signs. That indeed is the supreme *sevā*; it must be performed and accomplished through the nectar of knowledge—that is, solely through the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*). "In every way" (*sarvataḥ*), "with one's whole self" (*sarvātmanā*), and "always" (*sadā*)—that is, at all times; the particle "eva" is used for emphasis. This is indeed the six-limbed yoga known as the "Nectar of Knowledge."

He provides the detailed explanation and further clarification of the introductory terms beginning with "pratyāhāra" (withdrawal) through the verses starting with "daśānām. In this context, "indriyāṇi" refers to the sense organs and their objects; "teṣāṃ daśānām indriyāṇām" means of those ten sense organs. Their "svavṛttiḥ" (own-functioning) is their persistence or operation within their own self, which is their state of mere existence. This is their svavṛtti.

The meaning is that one's own function (*svavṛtti*) is the non-cessation of the activity of grasping objects, which consists in the engagement of the objects and the subject with the state of being an object.

Abiding therein is "abiding in one's own function"; it is not, however, an activity proceeding by way of the nature of the grasped and the grasper. He states this very point by means of the designation of "perception" (*pratīti*) regarding the "intake of desires" (*kāmāhāra*).

Desires (*kāma*) are so called because they are desired or longed for; these are the objects such as forms and so forth. The "taking up" (*āharaṇa*) of these by means of the sense faculties is the "food of desire" (*kāmāhāra*).

With regard to that food of desire, the withdrawal (*pratinivṛtti*)—aiming at the grasping of objects such as forms by means of the sense faculties beginning with the eye—is declared to be "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*).

It is the non-engagement with external objects such as forms, wherein, by means of the sense faculties beginning with the eye, there is the vision of all phenomena as unconstructed through the support of emptiness within oneself, like a young girl seeing a reflection in an empty mirror.
The meaning is that this is stated as the limb of withdrawal (pratyāhāra).

He states the second limb with the words "five," and so forth. The term "five" is an elliptical expression for both [the five objects and the five senses]; thus, "the five desires" refers to all phenomena (*bhāva*) consisting of the stable and the moving.
"By means of the application of the five Buddhas" means by means of the application of all the Buddhas.
By their very nature, all phenomena are impelled by all Buddhas and consist of all Buddhas in brief.

Regarding those phenomena which consist of all Buddhas, that vision which— free from conceptualization and the delusion of discursive thought— is a continuous flow perceived within the yogi’s own personal experience as a single form reflecting the three times and the three realms, is called wisdom (*jñāna*).
He will explain this very same meaning through the following exposition: "consisting of all battle, peaceful, and established in all desires.
Furthermore, that meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is fivefold, according to the divisions of "investigation" (*vitarka*) and so forth, beginning with the "three secrets" (*guhyatraya*).

The three secrets consist of body, speech, and mind, pertaining to the three times and the three realms. Their simultaneous arising—understood as the realization and awakening that they appear merely as the manifestations of the three realms in the form of the gross aspects of a *caitya*—is the "arising of the three secrets.
That itself is *vitarka* (initial inquiry), and *vicāra* (subsequent investigation) is its application.
In that [state], *vitarka* is the mental application (*ābhoga*) toward its object;
*vicāra* is the grasping of the specific qualities of beings, whether stationary or moving, such as jars, cloths, and so forth;

and *sukha* is the gathering of pleasure, which is a state of mental well-being (*saumanasya*) resembling joy (*prīti*), serving as the cause for directing the mind toward all those objects of *vicāra*.
From all entities whose minds have been elevated, there arises the attainment of happiness; the gathering of happiness caused by physical pliancy is one's own mind, and so forth.
This is the arising of the knowledge of the sixfold active consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, with respect to the objects of knowledge, from form up to the dharma-sphere.
The arising of knowledge and the object of knowledge ceases;

the one-pointedness of mind characterized by the emptiness of the grasped and the grasper is called "one's own mind. Such a mind consists of all Buddhas; it is peaceful through the subsiding of conceptual constructions such as the grasped and so forth; it is established solely in emptiness as the mere appearance of the triple world; and it is not established in any desires.
"All desires" and "all states of being" are established and situated here in the form of a single manifestation that is non-different from itself; thus, it is called "established in all desires."
He states the third limb: "The five gnoses," and so forth.
The five gnoses are the five Buddhas, Akṣobhya and the others.
The five aggregates, consciousness and the rest, possess the nature of the five maṇḍalas of Lalanā.
That breath consisting of those [elements] is in the left nostril.

Here, by the term "five elements" (pañcabhūta), the five constituents—earth and so forth—are meant, which possess the nature of the five mandalas of the rasanā. Breath having that nature is that which possesses the nature of the five elements.
Having emitted [the breath] from the left nostril in the form of a *piṇḍa*, the *piṇḍa* consists here of the nature of the right and left mandalas within the central channel, the *avadhūtī*.
And that vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*), having been emitted in the form of a *piṇḍa*, [is placed] at the tip of the nose.
Here, by the word "nose" (*nāsikā*), the pericarps of the lotuses of the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown are meant.

Having expelled that vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*), one should direct it toward the tip of the nose and visualize it through the center of the pericarp by means of the left and right lotus petals. This very vital breath, flowing solely through the middle channel due to the cessation of the two flows of the left and right, is called the "five-colored great jewel," as well as "breath control" (*prāṇāyāma*) and "vajra-recitation" (*vajrajāpa*); it is to be recited with the tongue-tip not touching the palate.
He states the fourth [method]:

Thus, because it serves as mental protection, one should meditate on one's own mantra—the vital breath (prāṇa)—from the pericarp to the pericarp within the heart; then, having reached the point of the drop (bindu), which is the forehead, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) there and restrain [the breath].

One should hold the jewel together with the senses once it has been restrained; one should make it free from coming and going. This is known as *dhāraṇā*, and it is declared to be the limb of concentration (*dhāraṇā-aṅga*).

The two and a half verses beginning with "nirodhavajra" are to be understood as belonging to the branch of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). The reading "āraṇā" [instead of "ānāpāna"] is due to the oral instruction of the guru, intended to exclude the reading found in books.
It is called "nirodha" (cessation) because things are ceased therein.
That which is both cessation and a vajra is "nirodhavajra," the path of the avadhūtī.
When the mind has gone there [to the heart] and the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) is [stabilized], the apprehension of signs (*nimitta*) arises;
that is, the apprehension—the manifestation—of signs such as smoke and so forth is born and produced.
The statement regarding the reverse order of the first and second signs, however, is for the purpose of explaining [the practitioner's] dependence upon the Guru.

Having made it firm and motionless through the limb of *dhāraṇā*, one should raise the *caṇḍālī*—the "great jewel" (*mahāratna*)—from the navel-cakra. By way of the vajra-path, she rises through the central channel to the *uṣṇīṣa*-cakra within the *khadhātu*. Having risen there, she causes the syllable *haṃ* to flow; then, by means of the four drops (*bindu*) of body, speech, mind, and gnosis, distinguished as the [four] joys (*ānanda*) and so forth, she leads them to the pericarp of the lotus at the tip of the *vajra*-jewel. This is the instruction of the Guru: that after *dhāraṇā*, the *caṇḍālī* blazes spontaneously.
He states the fifth limb:
"Having meditated," and so forth.

Having meditated upon and stabilized by means of the two limbs of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one should cause that conventional truth—which consists of the appearances of the three realms—to radiate in its form through recollection (*anusmṛti*).
One should cause that form—which is the form of conventional truth—to expand;

one should perceive it as pervading the entire expanse of space. "Recollection" (*anusmṛti*) should be understood as the vision of the three worlds in their entirety throughout all three times; this is the meaning of "the object of knowledge for the limb of recollection.
For this very reason, he says: "A manifestation arises therein."
Thus is the appearance of the triple world;
therein, it arises as the limb of recollection.
He states the sixth limb,
beginning with "wisdom" (*prajñā*) and so forth:
through the union of wisdom and means, by way of the sequence beginning with *niṣyanda*, when the lotus of space arises, by virtue of immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*).

Because the object of knowledge and the knowledge itself have become unified, in the state of purity, one should—in brief, by way of summary—withdraw and dissolve all entities, both stationary and moving, which exist in the form of appearances, into a single nature consisting of the luminosity that is supreme, uncontaminated great bliss, by means of the yoga of the "pill" (*piṇḍa*).

Just as mercury, having consumed all metals and ores, takes on a single perfected form, one should meditate upon and behold the image (*bimba*) whose nature is conventional truth within that luminosity of the single flavor of supreme, uncontaminated great bliss.
This is its detailed explanation.
"Instantly," and so forth.
The instantaneous perfection and realization of knowledge—the non-duality of the two truths—is called "samādhi," which is designated as a limb of meditative concentration (*samādhyaṅga*).

In the *Kālacakrottaratantra*, however, the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) has been very clearly explained by the venerable Mañjuśrī as follows: "The cultivation of emptiness through the ten powers [of the Buddha] is taught via the six [limbs] beginning with withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). Furthermore, at night there is the yoga of smoke and so forth, and during the day, that of the lamp and so forth in the sky.

By means of withdrawal, the yogi perceives the forms of the three times situated in the expanse of the sky; therein, by means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he makes the mind firm, having abandoned external entities."

By means of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should cause the vital wind to flow at night when the moon and sun have departed; then, by means of the limb of meditative retention (*dhāraṇā*), one makes it free from inhalation and exhalation within the drop (*bindu*).

Through recollection (*anusmṛti*) in the void, great rays of light issue forth from one's own reflection like those of the moon; through meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the seminal essence (*śukra*) proceeds to the head, completely filled with the bliss of purity.
Thus [it is said].
Now, he explains the fruit of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the subsequent stages with three verses beginning with "Having attained withdrawal" (*pratyāhāraṃ samāpadya*).

Having stabilized the vision of the images of the three realms through the sequence of signs such as smoke by means of the limb of withdrawal (*pratyāhārāṅga*), when the vision of the image has become stable through withdrawal, then the yogi is empowered by all mantras and bestows boons and so forth through his speech.

"Having attained the knowledge of meditation" (*dhyānajñānaṃ samāpadya*): when, by means of the limb of meditation (*dhyānāṅga*), the mind is fixed upon the image and one becomes one whose eyes do not blink.
Then one comes to possess the divine eye;
in this same way, one comes to possess the divine ear and so forth.
One shall attain the state of the five superknowledges.
Regarding the phrase "by means of breath-control" (*prāṇāyāmena*):

when the yogin becomes free from the paths of the moon and the sun and always carries [the breath] through the central channel, then, being purified by breath-control, he is beheld and praised by the Bodhisattvas.
"By the power of *dhāraṇā*, the empty image (*śūnyatābimba*) is certainly the object (*grāhya*), and Vajrasattva is the subject-mind (*grāhakacitta*); he should enter [into it].
By the power of *dhāraṇā*, through the cessation of the coming and going of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), they become one and the same.
This is due to the union with *anusmṛti*."

When there is the union of recollection (*anusmṛti*), which is the embracing of the image (*bimba*) and the state of the mind being free from all conceptual constructions, then a stainless circle of light (*prabhāmaṇḍala*) arises;
from the pores of the skin, five rays of light radiate forth. This occurs simply through mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
In this context, that imperishable bliss which arises through the oneness of the mind of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject is called "samādhi.
Mastery over that [bliss] is its immovability; from that, there comes the state of being free from obscurations (*nirāvaraṇatva*).
The meaning is that the state of being free from obscurations occurs solely through mastery over the luminous gnosis characterized by supreme imperishable gnosis.
Following that, there is the realization of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) whose nature is the true method (*bhūtanaya*), characterized by the non-duality of the two truths;
this constitutes the sequence of the fruition.
This has also been stated in the *Śrī Kālacakra* and explained in detail in the *Vimalaprabhā*, as follows:

Withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is the Lord of Jinas, which is tenfold; meditation (dhyāna) is Akṣobhya; breath control (prāṇāyāma) is Khaḍga; furthermore, retention (dhāraṇā) is Ratnapāṇi; mindfulness (anusmṛti) occurs in the Ḍombī [mudrā] and is Padmadhara; and the glorious samādhi is Cakrin. Each one is further divided into five types because they are differentiated by the vowels and consonants beginning with 'A' and 'Ka'.
Thus [it is said]. This is its meaning:
in the practice of the withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth, "Jinendra" refers to the aggregate of gnosis (*jñānaskandha*).

Furthermore, the aggregate of knowledge (*jñānaskandha*) is tenfold according to the distinction of signs (*nimitta*), being differentiated by the perception of smoke, mirages, fireflies, lamps, flames, the moon, the sun, Rāhu, the crescent, and the point (*bindu*).

Meditation (*dhyāna*) is indeed Akṣobhya; it is tenfold as the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), for meditation consists in the unification of the ten objects and subjects within the universal image (*viśvabimba*).
And breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) is tenfold, known as Khaḍgī; this is the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
This is because of the state of the left and right mandalas having become unified as one.
Furthermore, the tenfold *dhāraṇā* is "Ratnapāṇi," which is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
The *dhāraṇā* of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is tenfold according to the distinction between its movement to and fro within the lotuses of the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown.

In the *ḍombī*, the central channel (*madhyamā-nāḍī*), there are ten states according to the divisions of desire (*kāma*): anxiety (*cintā*), longing (*kāṅkṣā*), fever in the limbs (*jvara-aṅga*), dryness in the lotus-face of the beloved (*vara-mukha-kamala-śuṣira*), the onset of madness (*unmāda*), reeling (*ghūrṇā*), delusion of the mind (*mano-vibhrama*), intense fainting (*tīvra-mūrchā*), [the appearance of] smoke (*dhūmādyā*), and [the state of] the Thunderbolt-bearer (*vajrin*). These ten states of living beings within their bodies are manifest; in the world, they are the fixed manifestations of the God of Love (*manmatha*). Who is the Victor (*jina*)? And who is Desire (*kāma*)? These are the tenfold Samādhis: Śrī, Samādhi, Cakrī, and Vairocana—the tenfold Samādhi resulting from the cessation of the ten winds.
Thus, the Blessed One is one whose *nirvāṇa* is non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*), meaning he is like the wind from which [the breaths] flow.
Now, the characteristics of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs of yoga] are stated:

withdrawal is the non-functioning of the ten objects and their subjects within the body; discernment (*prajñā*), reasoning (*tarka*), investigation (*vicāra*), delight (*rati*), and immovable bliss (*acala-sukha*) are meditation (*dhyāna*), as well as one-pointedness of mind.

Prāṇāyāma is the stumbling of the two paths; the entry of the vital breath into the central channel is its arrival at the *bindu*. Indeed, the entry of the vital breath occurs when both movements have ceased, and concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is one-pointedness of mind.

The vision of the Caṇḍālī that occurs within the body and in the sky is indeed *anusmṛti*; through the power of the bliss of the immutable (*akṣara-sukha*), which consists of wisdom and means, there is *samādhi* upon the image of gnosis (*jñāna-bimba*). This practice of the Sustainer of the Universe (*viśvabhartṛ*) is threefold according to the divisions of "mild" and so forth.
There are three *mudrās* with three measures, by virtue of the three types of movement, belonging to the goddesses of karma, conceptualization, and gnosis.

Here, what is called *pratyāhāra* (withdrawal) is the non-engagement of consciousness with the ten objects and subjects within the body, while its engagement with the object of the image of emptiness occurs through the other five [senses], such as the eye and so forth.
Likewise, in that very same image, "wisdom" (prajñā) is the illumination;
"reasoning" (tarka) is the grasping of the object;
and "investigation" (vicāra) is the determination of it.
"Rati" is attachment to the *bimba*;
"immovable bliss" (*acala-sukha*) is the unification of the mind with the *bimba*.
Thus, meditation (*dhyāna*) is of eight kinds according to the distinction between the grasped and the grasper.
Here, what is called *prāṇāyāma* is the deviation from the left and right paths, their cessation, and entry into the central path; it is of ten kinds due to the cessation of the ten mandalas.
Here, "in the bindu" means the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the forehead.
"Struck by both paths" means devoid of going and coming;

this is the *dhāraṇā* of the vital breath at the forehead, called "one-pointedness of mind. It is the gazing upon Caṇḍālī within the sky of the abode of the three worlds; that is the tenfold *anusmṛti* previously described.

"By means of that which consists of wisdom and method" means that, through the state of being merged into one with the object of knowledge and the knowing subject, one enters into the knowledge-image (*jñānabimba*) by virtue of non-emitting bliss; thus, she too becomes tenfold according to the names of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth. In this way, the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) is the means of accomplishment.

This means of accomplishment (sādhana) of Kālacakra, the Sustainer of the Universe, is threefold according to the divisions of soft (*mṛdu*) and so forth; there are three mudrās and three measures (*mātrā*) by virtue of the three types of movement.
Thus, the movement of the bodhicitta is the soft measure, and the movement of vibration (*spanda*) is the middling measure.
The movement of the *niṣpanda* is the highest degree;
thus, the *karmamudrā* bestows the bliss of the unchanging (*akṣara*),
while the *jñānamudrā* bestows the bliss of vibration (*spanda*).
Mahāmudrā alone bestows the bliss of immobility;
thus, the meditation on the three mudrās has been taught by the Blessed One through the yoga of the six limbs.
Therefore, the yoga of the six limbs should be meditated upon by the yogin for the sake of attaining buddhahood.
Now, for the sake of accomplishing the image of emptiness, the gaze is described:

during the stage of service (*sevā*), there is the tenfold yoga of the Wielder of the Wheel (*cakrin*) in the sky with the wrathful gaze; during the stage of near-accomplishment (*upasādhana*), there is the six-limbed yoga with the gaze of the Destroyer of Obstacles (*vighnāntaka*) directed toward the path of the sky;

during the stage of accomplishment (*sādhana*), there should be the three-syllabled yoga of the drop of the moon produced by wisdom within the jewel of the vajra, characterized by bliss, non-decay, and the single state of peace; and here, in the stage of great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*), there is the yoga of gnosis (*jñānayoga*) which is the innate (*sahaja*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "here, service" (*iha sevā*) and so forth:
"service" (*sevā*) refers to the cultivation of the signs such as smoke (*dhūmādinimitta*). Within that service, "initial yoga" (*ādiyoga*) is the grasping of the signs such as smoke by the mind;
and that [yoga] is of ten kinds, as it occurs together with the conviction (*sampratyaya*) regarding smoke and the other signs. Therefore, it is tenfold.
And that [sign] of the one possessing the wheel, namely the gaze of wrath of the Uṣṇīṣa, is the sign of the unblinking upward gaze;
it is fourfold in connection with the night and sixfold in connection with the day.
Then, the image itself, up to the limit of the image, becomes the limb of service through withdrawal and meditation; this is the view of Vighnāntaka.
Vighnāntaka is Amṛtakuṇḍalī; his gaze is directed toward the unblinking state, reaching the forehead.

With that gaze, which has entered the path of nectar for Vighnāntaka, one should perform the six-limbed practice (*ṣaḍaṅga*)—by the word "and" (*ca*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and concentration (*dhāraṇā*) are included—once the reflection (*bimba*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) has been perceived. This is the *upasādhana*.
Regarding the phrase "of the moon-drop created by wisdom" (*prajñāsṛṣṭendubindoḥ*):

here, it is that which is both created by the passion of wisdom (*prajñārāga*) and is the moon-drop (*indubindu*), thus "the moon-drop created by wisdom. Even for that moon-drop of bodhicitta created by wisdom, when it has entered the jewel of the vajra, there occurs the yoga of the three syllables. [This occurs] in the secret place, the navel, and the heart; it should be in the practice (*sādhana*). Thus, it occurs in the third limb of practice.
In this way, the limb of practice is to be performed.
"Peaceful by virtue of bliss not being lost" means that the single moment of the bodhicitta, through its bliss not being lost, is called "peaceful."
"Sahaja" refers to the "yoga of gnosis" in the *Mahāsādhana*;
it is the oneness of the mind with immutable bliss,
and it is the fourth limb of the *Mahāsādhana*.

Thus, in the means for accomplishing gnosis, there is the four-limbed deity-accomplishment through the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), according to the previously explained sequence for accomplishing both the mundane and the supramundane.
Now, the entry into the appearance of this very mind is described:

by those whose minds are unattached to space, with unblinking eyes, having entered the vajra-path, there is seen from emptiness smoke, a mirage, a clearly manifest stainless firefly, a lamp, a flame, the moon, the sun, and the vajra; and within that, the supreme digit, the drop (*bindu*), and the form of the Buddha—the manifold *saṃbhogakāya* free from sense objects.

In this Mantra Vehicle and the Pāramitā Vehicle, there are two ways of practicing yoga: practice in space and practice in an open area. One who would attain yoga in space should, at night in a windowless room in total darkness, fix the mind on space; having abandoned all thoughts and become empty with a one-pointed mind, he should examine for one day and behold the signs beginning with smoke. With unblinking eyes, he has entered the Vajra Path.

In this context, having entered the central life-force (*madhyamā-prāṇa*), with minds unattached to space, eyes unblinking, and having entered the vajra-path, one perceives through the yoga of night: from emptiness alone, smoke, a mirage, a clearly manifest stainless firefly, and a lamp. Then one sees the cloudless sky. Then, from that sky, through the yoga of day, the flame of the self-arisen one born of space—the great fire of the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*)—is seen in the very same cloudless sky. Thus, Vairocana is the great radiance, the light of wisdom, the illuminator, appearing like the moon.
The lamp of the world, the sun; the torch of wisdom, the vajra-Rāhu;
of great splendor, luminous, the supreme lotus of lightning.

The King of Vidyās, the Lord of Supreme Mantras, the Binduka—this tenfold sign was taught by the Blessed One through the night yoga in the *Samāja* and other tantras, and through the day yoga and the terminology of intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣā*) in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*.
Therefore, [it is said]: "The King of Mantras, the accomplisher of great purpose," which refers to the vision of reflections such as jars and cloths in all their aspects.

In the center of that, within the *bindu*, the form of the Buddha is to be seen, free from sense objects due to the absence of anything to be perceived and the absence of conceptual construction; from that, through the union with the form, the sound of the unstruck (*anāhata*) is heard—
thus is the *nirmāṇakāya* [manifested] from the appearance of form.
The meaning is that the *saṃbhogakāya* appears as sound.

The yogin should gaze at the sky with a steady stare when it is free of clouds, until a black line (*kṛṣṇarekhā*) is seen flickering like a lotus-stalk in the *kālanāḍī*. Within that [line], one's own mind—devoid of objects, possessing all colors and all forms, and as unclouded as the sun in water—is the image of the Omniscient One; it is not another mind, but the mind itself.

In this regard, during the daytime yoga, the yogi should look at the sky free from clouds with a fixed gaze during the forenoon and afternoon, keeping his back toward the sun; otherwise, the darkness caused by the sun's rays will arise, and due to that obstruction, he must observe daily until a black line, the size of a hair, shimmering and stainless, is seen within the *avadhūtī* known as *Kālanājī*. Within her resides the image of the Omniscient One—the entire threefold world, like the sun in water, unclouded, possessing all colors and all forms. This is one’s own mind, devoid of objects; it is not another mind, for there is no such thing as "knowledge of another's mind. It is the mind itself that is the "other mind."

In that regard, first, the manifestation of one's own mind is seen by the Tathāgata with the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*); through the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and so forth, the knowledge of others' minds is seen. Thus, it is said in the *Dharmasaṃgraha* that the Blessed One possesses five eyes.

In this way, through the sequence of knowledge, the fleshly eye, the divine eye, the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*), the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*), and the gnosis-eye (*jñānacakṣus*) will arise by the power of cultivation;
thereafter, for the Omniscient One, there is nothing whatsoever that remains unseen.
This six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga) has also been taught by the venerable Vajrapāṇipāda:

"In this context, withdrawal (pratyāhāra) is the non-engagement with external objects such as form and so forth; it is the engagement of the visual consciousness and other faculties with internal objects by means of the divine eye and other divine faculties. It is the vision of all phenomena within the unconstructed [state] by taking emptiness as the object within oneself; it occurs in emptiness like a reflection seen by a young girl in a mirror. Thus, withdrawal is the limb [of yoga] because of the vision of the images of the Buddhas of the three realms."
Then, "meditation" (dhyāna) refers to the state when all phenomena are seen as empty; "wisdom" (prajñā) is the engagement of the mind with them;
"initial inquiry" (vitarka) is the mind's grasping at entities; and "sustained investigation" (vicāra) is the mind's application toward that grasping at entities.
Delight (*rati*) is the fixing of the mind upon all phenomena;
immovable bliss (*acalasukha*) is the attainment of happiness from all phenomena.
Thus is the fivefold limb of meditative absorption (*dhyānāṅga*).

Then, what is called *prāṇāyāma* is the blocking of the left and right paths of the *lalanā* and *rasanā* channels, such that the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) flows perpetually through the central path of the *avadhūtī*.

Through the yoga of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*), one performs inhalation with the syllable *oṃ*, retention with the syllable *hūṃ*, and exhalation with the syllable *āḥ* within the *avadhūtī*.
The yogi performs [this] by means of the nature of the moon, sun, and Rāhu; this is the limb of *prāṇāyāma*.

Thereafter is the limb called *dhāraṇā*: the non-emergence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) from the mandalas of Mahendra (earth), Varuṇa (water), Agni (fire), and Vāyu (air) at the navel, heart, throat, and forehead, and the entry of the vital breath into the *bindu*—this is the limb of *dhāraṇā*.

Then, "recollection" (*anusmṛti*) is the vision of one's chosen deity in the form of a reflection, free from conceptual construction; from that arises a circle of light (*prabhāmaṇḍala*) whose nature is the radiance of many rays;
and from that, the pervasion of the triple world whose nature is the radiance of many forms—this is the limb of recollection.

Then, "concentration" (*samādhi*) is the unification of the mind within that attainment of immutable bliss which arises from devotion to one's chosen deity; this mind, free from subject and object, is called a limb of concentration by the Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, the instruction on the initial cultivation of the six limbs is stated here in other tantras.
Here, in the *Śrī-samāja-uttara*, it is said: "service," "near-attainment," "attainment," and "great attainment."
The Blessed One himself has said this:
"During the time of service (*sevā*), one should diligently visualize the form of Mahoṣṇīṣa;
but during the time of the subsidiary practice (*upasādhana*), one should visualize the form of Amṛtakuṇḍalī."
One intent on yoga should meditate upon the form of the deity during the stage of accomplishment (*sādhana*);
however, at the time of the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*), one should meditate upon the all-pervading Lord Buddha as the image.

Thus, here, in another intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣā*), the Blessed One’s promise is as follows: having established the *uṣṇīṣa*-image— the image of the Buddha— within the *dharmodayā* in space throughout the three realms without exception, one should meditate upon the *cittavajra* during the time of service, at the first stage, by means of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), and stabilize it through the limb of meditative concentration (*dhyānāṅga*).
Abandoning all other thoughts, one should examine this for a single day;
if no conviction arises therein, then my word is false.
Thus it is said.

Here, "conviction" (pratyaya) refers to smoke and so forth as the cause, and not anything else such as mantras, which could be accomplished in a single day by means of which conviction would arise. Therefore, practitioners of mantra, having abandoned the notions of existence and non-existence and having rendered [the mind] supportless, a profound, objectless conviction arises in the void; that conviction is cultivated by the yogin as smoke and so forth—this is the rule of the Tathāgatas.
"Likewise, one should accomplish the three worlds by means of the instruments (karaṇas) and the conjunctions of bondage.
One should accomplish the reflection of the Buddha—the three worlds—by means of the instruments, such as the eyes and so forth; that very instruction is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru.
In that regard, according to the Guru's instruction, it is to be known through experience that first the yogi sees smoke in the sky, not a mirage.
Then there are the mirages;
afterwards, that very same [vision] consisting of smoke and so forth, free from conceptual construction, like a *pratisenā* (magical reflection).

Thus, in the *Samājottara*: "The first sign is smoke; the second is the mirage-sign; the third is the firefly-sign; the fourth is the lamp-sign; and the fifth is the sign resembling the cloudless sky."
In the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara* as well, the Blessed One has said;
regarding that, the Blessed One further stated:
"In the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*, that which is caused by omniscience is the catalyst for proceeding toward the proximity of the accomplishments (*siddhi*)."
"Subsequently, there is the appearance resembling an illusion, the appearance resembling a dream, moment by moment," and so forth.

Because of these words of the Blessed One, some will say that the realization of the meditation on the signs such as smoke occurs at the time of attaining siddhi; all of them are violators of the Blessed One’s promise.
They are detractors of the Blessed One’s statement: "Having abandoned all thought, one should examine the realization for a single day."
At the time of accomplishment, the mundane signs such as smoke and so forth are not like an illusion or a dream;
for here, they possess the actual capacity for actions such as burning through smoke, flames, and the like, and likewise there is even a rain of saffron, flowers, jewels, gold, and so on.
Therefore, the signs such as smoke arise from the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*).
Likewise, the Blessed One said in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*:
"Therefore, one should again meditate upon the six limbs equal to self-consecration;
afterwards, one should perceive one's own sign through the sequence of the forward-order procedure."

In this context, what is called "self-consecration" (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) is the vision of the relative truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*). Through withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), the signs (*cihna*) appear like clouds, smoke, and so forth; and that is first seen up to the appearance of a lamp, and thereafter as cloudless, stainless space.

In the *Māyājāla*, within the chapter on meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the Blessed One has also taught another six signs, beginning with the flame and ending with the drop (*bindu*). They are as follows:
"The self-arisen one born from space, the great fire of the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*)."
Vairocana is the great radiance; he is the illuminator of the light of gnosis.
The lamp of the world, the torch of knowledge, of great splendor and radiant;
the fierce King of Vidyās, the Lord of Mantras, the King of Mantras who accomplishes the great purpose.

Thus, by means of these two verses, the Blessed One has spoken of the subsequent sign in the *Māyājāla* through the language of intentional terminology (*sandhyābhāṣā*). That which arises from the previously mentioned cloudless sky is the manifestation that emerges from space; it is the self-arisen (*svayambhū*) [deity] from the mind free of all conceptual construction.
In this context, "the fire of the wisdom-knowledge" (*prajñājñānānala*) refers to the manifestation of flames.
Vairocana is the "Great Radiance," which is the manifestation of the moon; he himself is the "Radiance of the Light of Gnosis. The "Lamp of the World" is the manifestation of the sun.
"The torch of gnosis" is the appearance of Rāhu;
"of great splendor and luminous" is the appearance of lightning;
and "the King of Vidyās, the fierce Lord of Mantras" is the appearance of a drop (bindu) in the form of a blue lunar disc.

"The King of Mantras, the accomplisher of great purpose"—this refers to the manifestation of all phenomena of the three realms in every aspect, which is seen by the yogi through the withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) as being equal to the appearance of a magical illusion or a dream, by means of the instruments of the eyes and other faculties.

Then, by the binding of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and through these instruments joined with the [proper] bindings, one should accomplish the three worlds—characterized by desire, form, and formlessness—and consisting of the nature of both the stable and the moving.
Likewise, the Blessed One said in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*:
"The entire threefold world, including all that is moving and unmoving, without exception or remainder, is accomplished; as many as there are beings with vajra-bodies in all the world-systems."

"Thus, by means of the cultivation of the six-limbed yoga (ṣaḍaṅgayoga)," such is the rule of the Blessed One. Likewise, the Blessed One said in the *Śrīsamāja*: "In the absence [of objects], there is an absence of cultivation; cultivation is not truly cultivation."
Thus, existence would not be becoming, and the act of contemplation is not perceived.
Thus:
in the absence [of objects], the cultivation [of the mind] in a cloudless sky is withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). That very thing is the absence of cultivation in the absence [of objects].
"Meditation is indeed no meditation.
Thus, in the absence of the meditation of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), that meditation occurs in the cloudless sky;
it is "no meditation at all."

"Because it is devoid of conceptual cultivation"—this is the meaning: that entity which is perceived through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) would not be an entity, because one perceives the existence and non-existence of entities in the past, future, and present beyond conceptualization.
Therefore, the Blessed One’s statement is that conceptual cultivation is not found within the cultivation of withdrawal.
And this cultivation was also taught by the Blessed One in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
For example: Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the venerable Subhūti: "Noble Subhūti, whoever here shall attain yoga in this perfection of wisdom, what will he attain through yoga?
Subhūti replied:

Kauśika, he who would attain yoga in the perfection of wisdom will attain yoga in open space; Kauśika, he who thinks that one should train in the perfection of wisdom is one who desires to attain yoga in open space.
The meditation on Mahāmudrā is said by the Blessed One to be like a reflection or an illusion in a cloudless sky.
Thus, through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the branch of service (*sevāṅga*) is described.
Thereafter, by means of the terminology of "symbolic language" (*sandhyābhāṣā*), wind is spoken of through the designation of the form of Amṛtakuṇḍalī.
And that is of five kinds;
thus the Blessed One said in the *Samājottara*:
"The breath consists of the five jewels and is presided over by the five Buddhas."
Having emitted it in the form of a mass, one should visualize it at the tip of the nose.
Thus:

here, by the term "five jewels" (pañcaratna), the *rasanā* possesses the nature of the five maṇḍalas; the five elements, beginning with earth, and the breath composed of them constitute the "five-jeweled" [breath] in the left nostril.
Likewise, the five Buddhas are the *lalanā*, which possesses the nature of the five maṇḍalas; these are the five aggregates, beginning with consciousness.
The breath presided over by them is [inhaled] through the left nostril.
"Having expelled it in the form of a *piṇḍa*"—
here, the *piṇḍa* refers to the state of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*) within the central channel, the *avadhūtī*, which is not composed of the right or left mandalas.
Having exhaled that vital breath (prāṇavāyu), one should visualize it in the form of a sphere at the tip of the nose.
Here, by the word "nose" (nāsikā), the pericarp of the lotuses at the navel, heart, throat, forehead, and crown are meant;
one should cause [the breath] to descend to its tip.
One should meditate on the tip of the nose;
from the pericarp to the center of the pericarp, not to the petals of the left or right lotus.
Thus, the vital breath (prāṇa), having been restrained in the form of a mass at the location of the point (bindu).

By that very means, its retention (*dhāraṇā*) is described. Thus, the secondary practice (*upasādhana*) is performed by means of the disk of Amṛtakuṇḍalī with these two limbs. That same secondary practice is called the "vajra-recitation" (*vajrajāpa*).
"It should be recited with the middle [channel] as the undivided limb" means by means of the undivided instrument;
that is, there is no movement of the vital breath through the left or right [channels].
When the image of the *uṣṇīṣa* has been seen, the mantra-practitioner should thereafter perform *prāṇāyāma*;

this is the instruction of the Guru. The twilight language (*sandhyābhāṣā*) is to be understood through its alternative terminology. Now, the preparatory practice (*upasādhana*) consisting of *prāṇāyāma* and *dhāraṇā* is described.
Then, regarding the statement "the image of the deity in the sādhana":

here, by the power of *dhāraṇā*, the yogi perceives the blazing *caṇḍālī* located at the navel—free from all obscurations, resembling a *pratisenā* (magical reflection), the *mahāmudrā* emitting clouds of rays from infinite Buddhas, and resplendent with a halo of light.
He describes that *anusmṛti* as the *sādhana*, establishing the rule: "At the end of *dhāraṇā*, the yogi should meditate upon the *caṇḍālī*."
Then, by the flame of her gnosis (*jñānārcis*), the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), bases (*āyatana*), and so forth are incinerated and become unified as one.
The consciousnesses and the elements, such as earth and the rest, which reside in the left and right channels and possess the nature of the mandalas, enter the lunar mandala in the forehead.

Thereupon, when the moon has been melted by the flame of gnosis of Caṇḍālī, that bodhicitta descends in the form of a drop (*bindu*) through the states of bliss (*ānanda*), supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), and the cessation of bliss (*viramānanda*) into the throat, heart, navel, and the secret lotus.
Then, from the *vajramaṇi* up to the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).

Alternatively, by means of the nature characterized by the stages of diversity (*vicitra*), maturation (*vipāka*), refinement (*vimarda*), and the signless (*vilakṣaṇa*)—thus, when that bliss which is full of sixteen digits (*kalā*) and situated within the *maṇi* bestows happiness through the power of meditation, it is merely an illustration; for in its true nature, the pleasure born of the two organs does not equal even a ten-thousandth part of the supreme immutable bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*).
In this context, that state which is the abiding in immutable bliss (akṣarasukha) and consists of coemergent joy (sahajānanda) is an indescribable state unknown to novice yogins;
it is called by the Bodhisattvas the "samādhi of emptiness," and not merely a worldly pleasure that follows the path of nihilism.

Thus, through the yoga of the six limbs, Buddhahood is accomplished for yogins: service (*sevā*) occurs by means of the five nectars and so forth, the oceans and vajras, the recitation of mantras and so forth, and the withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth; near-attainment (*upasiddhi*) occurs through the nectar born of the vajra-lotus;

the practice of meditation (*sādhana*) occurs through the cultivation of the state of equal flavor within the lotus of the three vajras by means of joy (*ānanda*) and so forth; and indeed, the great attainment (*mahāsādhana*) arises as the non-emission [of semen] during union with wisdom (*prajñā*) through the subtle yoga.
Here, the beginner must first perform the service (*sevā*) according to the ritual procedure for accomplishment; this service is performed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and so forth.

Externally, the "five nectars" are excrement and so on, while by the word "and so forth" are meant cow-products such as urine; having consumed these, the service is performed for the sake of pleasing the deity. Internally, the five nectars are the five aggregates (*skandha*).

By the word "first," the five sense-faculties are the five lamps; their independent service is the abandonment of craving for the body and material things. By that service, the deities become bestowers of boons, not by consuming [the substances] in secret and so forth—this is indicated by the phrase "by the oceans and the vajras."
Indifference toward the enjoyment of the body, indifference toward the enjoyment of speech, and indifference toward the enjoyment of the mind.
The meaning of "brahmacarya" (celibacy) is the restraint of body, speech, and mind, characterized by service that is indifferent to the pleasure of falling away [from the spiritual state].
By means of this, the deities become bestowers of boons.
"Not through longing for existence or enjoyments" means by means of mantra-recitation and so forth; here, "mantra-recitation" refers to the restraint of the vital breath (prāṇasaṃyama).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [is meant] the yoga of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*). Constant service through that [yoga] causes the deities to become granters of boons;
the deities are not [pleased] by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), nor by mechanical restraint (*yantrila*), nor by verbal chatter—this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Furthermore, according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), recitation (*jāpa*) and so forth should be performed with a rosary and the like for the sake of ordinary accomplishments (*sāmānyasiddhi*).
Now the *upasādhana* (near-attainment) is described, beginning with the words "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth.

Here, for those in the cycle of existence (*saṃsārin*), "food" (*āhāra*) refers to the grasping of objects such as forms by means of the sense organs, such as the eyes; the abandonment of that is called "withdrawal."

In the image of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimba*), the apprehension of other objects such as form by means of other [senses] like the eye and others consisting of flesh and so forth is the *upasādhana*; likewise, meditation (*dhyāna*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and concentration (*dhāraṇā*) constitute the *upasādhana* through the nectar born of the vajra-lotus that is not emitted. According to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), this is the accomplishment of the *upasādhana*; according to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), it is through the external emission of the deity.
Now, the *sādhana* is described, beginning with "Bliss" (*ānanda*) and so forth.

In this context, Ānanda, the three vajras—the drops (*bindu*) of body, speech, and mind—attaining a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) with the lotus constitute the *sādhana*; the meaning is that the abiding of these drops occurs in the navel and the secret place.

Such is the *sādhana*. Thereafter comes the *mahāsādhana*: when non-falling bliss arises through union with the Wisdom Consort (*prajñā*), then indeed it is the *mahāsādhana*. Regarding the "subtle yoga," it is called the *mahāsādhana* because of the conjunction of the semen (*śukra*) within the *suṣumnā* channel above; this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Furthermore, according to the *neyārtha* [interpretation], the rule is that wisdom (*prajñā*) and the dharma [semen] are on the tip of the nose, like a mustard seed and so forth; in this way, the great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*) comes to be.
Now, the service (*sevā*) and other stages are described according to the divisions of "mild" (*mṛdu*) and so forth:

first indeed is the awakening to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), then the gathering of the moon-drop, and from that, the arising of the image (*bimba*); thereafter follows the placement of syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*) by means of the most excellent families of flavors.

This is the common service (*sāmānyasevā*); the accomplishment (*sādhana*) by means of the ocean and the vajra is the intermediate [practice], and here the method is fourfold, being likewise soft or firm according to the limbs of accomplishment.

Thus, in this stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), first there is the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatābodhi*), because at the end of death for living beings, upon the abandonment of the aggregates (*skandha*), there is the grasping of the aggregates belonging to the portion of rebirth.

That intermediate state, which is the single vision of the three worlds characterized by emptiness, is indeed certainly called "void. Then, after that moment, there is the "gathering" (*saṅgraha*) of the lunar drop (*candrabindu*).
Here, "gathering" refers to the seizing of the seminal drops within the mother's womb by the *ālayavijñāna*.

Then, from the grasping of the planets such as Venus (*śukra*) and so forth, there is what is called "the arising of the image" (*bimbotpatti*); by means of these concise terms, this refers to the completion of the embryo (*garbha*), which is to say, the completion of the body.

Then, "by the families of excellent fluids" refers to the arrangement of the letters (*akṣara-nyāsa*) for the eyes and other [senses] via the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), and the engagement with objects such as form (*rūpa*).
Thus, even in the practice of deity yoga (*devatā-sādhana*), the beginner (*ādikarmika*) should cultivate this single conceptualization.

This is the common service (*sāmānyasevā*) by means of the "ocean and vajras," that is, through the accomplishment of the vajras of body, speech, mind, and gnosis. The middling practice is the accomplishment of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Here, the method consists of four parts:
the limb of service, the limb of near-accomplishment, and likewise the limbs of soft and firm accomplishment, according to the rule that it extends until the age of sixteen.

In this context, [the stages are as follows]: the infant (*mṛdu*) is one whose hair has grown; the middle child (*madhyabāla*) is from the eruption of teeth; the youth (*kumāra*) is from the falling out of teeth; and from the re-eruption of teeth until the age of sixteen and beyond, he is mature (*prauḍha*), due to being a progenitor of sons and daughters.
Thus, the yogi should meditate upon the fourfold limb of all deities; such is the rule of worldly truth (*laukikasatya*).
Now, the accomplishment of the Buddha-image by means of ultimate truth is described:
here, first is the realization of emptiness;
in darkness, nothing at all should be conceptualized.
Then, "the gathering of the lunar drop" refers to the apprehension of the signs beginning with smoke up to the point of the drop;
"and from that, the arising of the image" means that from that drop comes the manifestation of the universe, which is the arising of the image— thus it is said by the lineages of the excellent Rasas.
The "placement of syllables" (*akṣaranyāsa*) by means of the six families free from obscuration is the cessation of the limited aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth; thereafter,
through the attainment of the stages (*bhūmi*), there occurs the distinction of the "mild" and other levels, until one becomes the sovereign of the twelve stages.

Therefore, the rule is that he who knows the meaning of the Truths in twelve aspects, who knows reality in sixteen aspects, and who is awakened by the twenty aspects of perfect enlightenment, is the supreme omniscient one; now, the fruit of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs of yoga] is being stated.

Through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), the yogi, freed from sense objects, is empowered by all mantras; thereafter, O Lord of Men, he becomes a possessor of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*). Purified by the yoga of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and purified by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), being devoid of the moon and sun, he is honored by the Bodhisattvas. Through the power of retention (*dhāraṇā*), he enters the abode that destroys the Māras and the afflictions (*kleśas*); and through the power of recollection (*anusmṛti*), there arises the stainless mandala of light from the reflection of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*). Therefore, purified in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he accomplishes the body of gnosis (*jñānadeha*) within a few days.

If that desired accomplishment does not arise for practitioners of mantra through withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other [limbs of yoga], then by means of the practice of *nāda* and the restraint of the *bindu* within the jewel of the *kuliśa*, one should achieve it.

O Lord of Men, when the yogi becomes purified here by means of withdrawal and becomes stabilized by the *bimba*, he is then empowered by all mantras; through his speech he grants boons and so forth, and subsequently he becomes a possessor of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*), being purified through the yoga of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

In this context, when one becomes one whose eyes do not blink, then one truly possesses the divine eye; likewise, one becomes purified through meditation and purified through breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). When the yogi is devoid of the paths of the sun and moon, and always flows through the central channel (*madhyamā*), then, being purified by breath-control, he is honored and praised by the Bodhisattvas—this is the meaning. He enters the "power of the fire," which is the image of emptiness (*śūnyatā-bimba*) that destroys the Māras, the afflictions (*kleśas*), and so forth; he enters the mind of the grasped and the grasper through the power of retention (*dhāraṇā*), and by the cessation of the coming and going of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he becomes unified as a single essence.

"Completely purified through recollection" means that when the mind’s embrace of the reflection (*bimba*) is free from all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it becomes pure; at that time, a stainless circle of light (*prabhāmaṇḍala*) arises.
Furthermore, by the word "also," rays of five-colored light flash forth from the pores of the skin, emerging from the reflection of gnosis—that is, from the reflection of emptiness.
Therefore, "pure in samādhi": here, the imperishable bliss that arises through the oneness of the mind of the apprehended and the apprehender is called "samādhi";
being pure in that samādhi—having attained purity and stainlessness—he succeeds in a few days, three fortnights, or three years.

The rule for withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is as follows: one becomes a Bodhisattva who has attained the body of gnosis (*jñānadeha*), characterized by [the powers of] faith, strength, mastery, and so forth.
Now, *haṭhayoga* is described:

here, when the reflection (*bimba*) has been seen through withdrawal and the other [preliminary practices], and the moment of the imperishable (*akṣarakṣaṇa*) arises while the vital breath (*prāṇa*) remains unrestrained, then—by means of the forceful practice of the resonance (*nāda*)—one should cause the breath to flow through the central channel (*madhyamā*). By arresting the drop of the thought of awakening (*bodhicittabindu*) within the jewel of the "Vajra of the World," which is Wisdom (*prajñā*), one should accomplish the moment of the imperishable through the motionless state (*niṣpanda*); this is *haṭhayoga*.
The practice of *nāda* is taught right here:

that power (*śakti*) which travels upward from the center of the navel to the supreme state, the end of the twelve, the end of the digits (*kalā*), when restrained at the navel, resembles lightning and fire; rising in the form of a staff, it moves with a soft and graceful gait from one wheel (*cakra*) to another within the central channel (*madhya-nāḍī*) until, by force, it touches the aperture of the crown (*uṣṇīṣa-randhra*), like a needle piercing through the outer skin.
At that time, one should forcefully impel the *apāna* upward; having pierced the *uṣṇīṣa*, it proceeds to the supreme city once the pair of winds has been restrained.

Thus, through the awakening of the *vajra* in the mind along with its object, one attains the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*). Subsequently, she becomes the Mother of the Universe for yogins, whose nature is the five higher knowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).

Furthermore, the mind becomes the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), and its tenfold manifestation is itself the consecration (*seka*) in this immersion, which resembles the reflection in a mirror like the stainless moon.

Therefore, he is the glorious Guru in whom this fourth state—the innate (*sahaja*), imperishable (*akṣara*), and indeed unswerving from the bliss of *nirvāṇa*—resides within his heart and mouth, which are the Buddhas’ faces.
Here, "wisdom" (*prajñā*) and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) correspond respectively to the apprehending mind and the object of that apprehending mind.

The tenfold appearance of smoke and so forth, which is the manifestation of the mirror-like object of perception like a reflected image (*pratisenā*), is itself "knowledge"; the meaning is that it is the apprehended mind.

Thus, just as one’s own eye is reflected in a mirror, so too is one’s own eye the object of perception (*grāhya*). Wisdom (*prajñā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) are the "consecration" (*seka*); "immersion" (*majjana*) therein means that the entry of the perceiving mind (*grāhaka-citta*) into this perceived mind (*grāhya-citta*), which is the non-engagement with external objects. This is called withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and fixation (*dhāraṇā*) within the six-limbed yoga.

From that immersion, there arises the bliss of nirvāṇa, which is unchanging (*acyuta*), innate (*sahaja*), and imperishable (*akṣara*). It is the fourth bliss, transcending the states of the child, the adult, and the vibration (*spanda*); it surpasses worldly analogies and is free from the conduct of the three worlds—this is the meaning.

That which is free from laughter, momentary touch, embracing, the grasping of hands, and sexual union; free from the causes of the *karmamudrā* and *jñānamudrā*; characterized by the manifestation of all aspects within emptiness—this is the Buddha-vajra, the Gnosis-vajra. The meaning is that the venerable Guru Vajradhara is he in whose heart this resides, who has cultivated it as his own personal experience of bliss, and who exists at all times for the purpose of imparting it to disciples.

Now, the summary of yoga is stated: the entry of the vital breath into the center; the binding of the movements of the sun and moon in the right and left [channels]; the mind fixed upon the supreme bliss during the application of the mudrā; the awakening of the vajra;

the lotus, or the sound of the vajra, or the splashing of water from one's own hand for the sake of bliss; and the non-emission of the seed—that is bliss, which removes the fear of death—this is the mouth of the glorious Guru.

In this context, first the yogin must effect the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the central channel (*avadhūtī*) by which he perceives the signs; this is called the first "body-vajra face" of the venerable Guru Buddha. Thereafter, the rule is that the binding of the vital breath—consisting of the movement of the moon through the left channel—must be performed together with the sun through the right path;
this is the second "speech-vajra," the breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*).
As for the mind, it is attached to the image (*bimba*) during the engagement with the mudrā.
The bodhicitta melts; this is the third [state], the mind-vajra, which has reached supreme bliss and is the awakening of the vajra.
Now, if bliss does not arise through the door of the *bimba*, then the lotus or the sound of the vajra should be applied gradually.
If even then it is not obtained, then [the practice] should be performed for the sake of increasing bliss, and not for the sake of causing a fall.

Thus, the abandonment of the seed becomes that bliss which removes the fear of death; this is the fourth face, the face of knowledge, belonging to the glorious Guru—this is the rule for the practice of yoga.
Now the destruction of the five mandalas is described:

earth dissolves into water, water likewise into fire, fire into wind, and wind into space; and space proceeds into the signless, which is tenfold. The sign proceeds into the omniform, which is the cause of the supreme immutable bliss and the effect of gnosis. From gnosis, O Lord of Men, the firm accomplishment arises for men in this very life.

In this context, when the practitioner has unwinking eyes and, with a wrathful gaze, is empty-minded and focused on the visualization, then—whether on the left or the right—"earth" is an indicative term (*upalakṣaṇa*). When the yogi performs the meditation during the flow of earth on the right, this is the procedure;
it is not, however, performed during the flow of the left channel according to the sequence beginning with the mandala of space.
Therefore, when the vital breath (*prāṇa*) flows through the left or the right, it is called that very mandala because it possesses those characteristics.
Thus, when the vital breath moves from the earth-mandala in the right channel to the water-mandala,
and so on up to the gnosis-mandala (*jñānamaṇḍala*), it proceeds through the left channel starting from the space-mandala (*ākāśa*).
Thus, the tenfold sign proceeds as emptiness; the sign beginning with smoke proceeds to the image of all aspects; and that very image proceeds to immutable bliss.
