That same gnosis is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); from this gnosis, there arises firmness, the accomplishment of traveling through space and so forth, and sovereignty over the three realms. O Lord of Men, for men in this very life, such is the rule for entering the path.

Having explained in detail that each successive initiation depends upon the preceding one through the words of the *Śrī Kālacakra*, the *Vimalaprabhā*, and other texts, and having established that even the supramundane initiation (*lokottara-seka*) must be preceded by the mundane initiations, [the author notes] that it is caused solely by the yoga of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-yoga*). Having extensively demonstrated the yoga of the six limbs through the very words of the *Śrī Kālacakra* and other scriptures, he now begins to explain the subject at hand, starting with "Now, its accomplishment" (*asyaiva sādhanam*), etc.: "The yogin should effect the accomplishment—that is, the manifestation—of this very fire of omniscient gnosis (*sarvajña-jñāna-agni*), which burns away all afflictive and cognitive obscurations (*kleśa-jñeyāvaraṇa*) without remainder, by means of smoke and the other signs."

By what kind of [reflections]? By those reflections which are well-known in all the Root Tantras, the Condensed Tantras, and the definitive-meaning (*nītārtha*) sūtras such as the *Āryaprajñāpāramitā*, because they appear suddenly in emptiness; by those reflections which are inconceivable due to the cessation of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*); by those signs (*nimitta*) which are the prior forms of the fruit of reality (*tattvaphala*); by those images of that wisdom (*dhī*), which is the insight (*prajñā*) whose nature is emptiness devoid of subject and object; by those appearances of yogic direct perception (*yogipratyakṣābhāsa*) which are equal to the sky because they are unstained by external or internal impurities, and because they are unmarked by the stains of conceptual constructions such as existence and non-existence.

Transcending existence and non-existence, because it is self-cognizable by the yogi, and because it is the nature of the appearance of emptiness— white in form, pervading all external and internal objects, free from the accumulation of even a single atom of dust, and consisting of an unartificial, marvelous, and non-substantial state in all its aspects— this [appearance] arises immediately after the appearance of clouds. It is the appearance of emptiness, characterized by the objects of cognition within one's own mind.
As it has been stated:
"The first appears like a cloud; the second resembles smoke.

Likewise, the forms of moving water and mirage, as well as the forms of fireflies and a lamp, are well known; these four signs occur in the darkness of a windowless room, and thus involve both the yoga of night and the yoga of space.

As it is stated in the *Śrīsamāja* and other texts: "By reversing the order of the first and second [stages], when the mind has entered the vajra of cessation (*nirodhavajra*), the apprehension of signs arises:
first, in the form of a mirage; second, resembling smoke."
The third has the appearance of a firefly; the fourth is a blazing lamp;
and the fifth is constant radiance, resembling a cloudless sky.
Then, preceded by a radiance resembling a cloudless sky, there appears the form of a horse, blazing with the appearance of emptiness; then follow the well-known appearances of the moon and the sun,
the light of Rāhu, and the appearance of a black jewel.
*Kala* is the appearance like a flash of lightning;
*mahābindu* is the appearance in the form of a blue lunar disc that illuminates all that is moving and stationary.

These six signs arise from the light of a cloudless sky and so forth, and thus constitute the yoga of open space (*abhyavakāśayoga*). Then, accompanied by the vision of the Buddha-image consisting of the *sambhogakāya* entering into their midst, there occurs in a single instant the luminosity of the universal image (*viśvabimba*), which—like water in the palm of one's hand—is transparent and perceives all forms such as pots and cloths.
"With eyes both closed and open" means:

with eyes half-opened and suspended in the intermediate space, one should meditate upon—that is, stabilize through the limb of meditation—that non-conceptualized image which, like a dream-image, exists in the void of space devoid of subject and object; that image is the image of the universe. This is stated in the *Jinajananī* (Prajñāpāramitā) in the *Madhyamā* version as "the samādhi named Jewel-Light," "the samādhi named Jewel-Lamp," and "the samādhi named Perceiver of All Aspects," and so forth;
and in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*: "Directly perceived by all Buddhas, the flame of gnosis, self-radiant."

And by the venerable Ārya-Nāgārjuna: "Those whose intellect has transcended existence and non-existence and is without support—they alone perceive the profound meaning of conditions, which is itself without objective basis."
Even by means of woolen garments and such, other signs are to be known by the yogi who has attained light; these are the unfailing indicators of success, just as smoke is for fire.
It causes stiffness of the eyes and bending of the head,
a state of numbness in the mind and mental factors, and a sense of voidness for those who perceive emptiness.

Others also [have said]: "When that half-eye was fashioned in the stainless sky, from the heart deeply moistened by the throbbing, vast compassion, there suddenly arose—unbreakable by the conceptualization of existence, non-existence, both, or neither—the lineage of all dharmas beginning with emptiness."
Likewise,
being free from the beginning and the end and relying solely on the middle,
he who remains there should avoid that light of his which consists of ten aspects.
In this context, the realization of the intermediate state (*antarāla*) through the grace of the Great Guru has been proclaimed for the meritorious.
Indeed, this is declared from the *Yogīśvara-vajragīti*; it bestows the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
As stated by the venerable Saraha: "The fool [does not know] the measure of the intermediate state."
The net of delusion was torn asunder; having questioned the Guru, you shall know.
In the first stage, one's craving for objects of desire is purified, and the eye of vision is restrained whenever it seeks after them.
Thus—why speak so much? This is the measure of the Dharma:
open your eyes, O friend, and see the peace found within;
know that the sky is far away. Look, O Bhusuku, at the form of emptiness!
O Bhusuku, there are incomparable blossoms;
take these priceless, invaluable flowers!
These flowers are of many colors.
Thus, in the forest of the void, the two blossoms are in full bloom; likewise, the Śambara-blossom is free from attachment, its nature being established in non-abiding,
liberated from both existence and non-existence, and possessing a perfectly pure form.
Thoughts are dispelled by non-thought;
like a lamp flickering in a lattice window, they seek peace; yet in the chest, the stars of the *bhusuku* remain ignited.
Śānti says: When the full moon rises at dawn, stealing away the darkness,
the body that was closed in slumber opens its eyes.
With intense compassion, beating the hand-drum,
today, O King, the king of the sky [the wind] blows from both the left and the right, scattering dust.
Kānhu says: In the interval, the path is revealed by experience; O fool, let the hidden treasure be released from the city and not from the outside.
The blossomed *paścaphullas* have withered,
and the *ākhaṭacīas* have become devoid of bees; why then, O people, do you look on with indifference?
Having tied up the moon and bound the sun,
she laughs; having made peace with the lamps herself, O friend, she looks upon the sky as her own courtyard.
Greatly distressed by the profound Dharma,
he was unable to see anything at all in the darkness of night; yet, if flowers were to bloom upon the peak of the sky, [he would see them].
Śānti says:
If one who is skilled in the Dharma can, at a single moment, simultaneously control the mind, the breath, and the eyes, then even a mistake will be corrected instantly.
In this [work], the jewels of the Jina’s virtues are extracted;
herein lies the entirety of the Tathāgata’s speech, free from various conceptual constructions and beyond thought.
If the intermediate space were clearly perceived by the eye,
then all the lords of the worlds would be attached there along the tenfold path.
Devoid of all characteristics of his own mind, he was revealed by the world with its doors wide open;
then the wind began to blow through the midst of it.

For those who are bound, there are two types of perception: direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). Here, that which has the deity as its object is twofold. Direct perception arises from the realization of reality, like [the vision of] the manifold *saṃbhogakāyas* in the sky like a rising sun.

Inference pertains to what is not directly perceived; it is a conceptualization based on unreality, like a corpse, which is to be viewed in paintings and the like for the sake of meditation by yogins whose intellects have matured.

In this world, according to the disposition (*āśaya*) of sentient beings, the perception of yogins—whether direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*)—may both have the deity as its object. Of these two, direct perception and inference, that which is direct perception arises from the yoga of reality produced by the instructions of the path of a true guru; it is free from the stain of all conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Like a star in the sky, it appears as the manifold *saṃbhogakāya* of Kālacakra. It is perceivable by the eye of flesh and so forth, resembling an illusion or a dream, and consists of the three realms of existence within the three paths. Here, first of all, the beginner yogin perceives the universal image (*viśvabimba*) with the eye of flesh, even without the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).
Then, by means of the divine eye through the power of the limit of the superknowledges; then, by means of the Buddha-eye through the power of the limit of those free from passion;
then, by means of the wisdom-eye through the power of the limit of the Bodhisattvas.
Then, by means of the eye of knowledge, through the power of the Tathāgata’s perfect awakening and because of being completely liberated from all substrates of existence,
the five constituents of the Tathāgata, beginning with flesh, are thus described in relation to the vision of emptiness.

Other sentient beings are like those blind from birth regarding the object of the vision of emptiness; this is the rule for the cultivation of reality. Furthermore, when establishing what is not reality, that which is neither perception nor inference—being a conceptualization based on non-reality like a dead body—is what should be shown in paintings and the like.
Because there is a total absence of the vision of reality, like a corpse or a dead body,

one should draw the maṇḍala circle or the painted images of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas— just like figures carved from wood— for the sake of meditation by dull-witted beginner yogins who require a fixed form to behold; such is the rule for the cultivation of conceptualization.

Therefore, when existence has dissolved into the cloudless sky, when the Lord, the master of the vital breaths, has entered into the dream-self, and when the host of inhalations and exhalations has ceased and the life-wind is stilled,
that most radiant expansion of light which issues forth from the very body of the masters of yoga and pervades the three worlds, having destroyed all darkness— of this,
the dull-witted indeed imagine it to be the destruction of the intellect following the dissolution of the world-cycle.
From this very [work], the wise derive an indescribable joy that surpasses even the heavens; for now, during the springtime, the Śabara woman, her hands full of blossoming forest fruits,
sports in the absence of her husband.
"By the cessation of the movement of the animal-eye [the senses], through the instruction of the true Guru, the wind [prāṇa] becomes still.

Even for a mind that possesses the form of the universe throughout the three periods of time, there is no "existence" (bhāva) in the form of past objects and so forth, because those [objects] do not exist and because they have transcended the nature of atoms. Yet, even if there were existence of the past and so forth, why would there be a total absence of all description (sarvopākhyāviraha) regarding the mind? To this he says: "Because of the vision of the image as non-conceptualized" (bimbe 'kalpitadarśanāt).

Because, when the mind has the form of the universal image (*viśvabimba*), there is indeed experienced a vision free from all conceptual construction, a direct perception that cannot be denied by the power of non-existence;
and it is said in the *Mūlatantra*: "Transcending existence and non-existence, the exhaustion of being and non-being, non-dual, beyond the nature of atoms, and devoid of empty phenomena."
The vajrayoga, free from eternalism and nihilism and devoid of causal continuity,

exists when this world of mental fluctuations and saṃsāra has reached a state of total non-existence; it is like a reflection appearing in mirrors and the like, contemplated by the practitioner and designated by the term "pratisenā," even for those of expansive intellect who have fallen into the abyss of delusion.

One should not perceive that which is non-substantial (*avastujā*) in a mirror—that is, the insentient nature of thieves and so forth—as it is said in the *Pratisenāvatāra-tantra* that the descent of the *pratisenā* occurs in mirrors, swords, the thumb, lamps, the moon, the sun, water-vessels, and the eyes, all of which are non-substantial things. Likewise, in the *Dharmasaṃvara*, it is stated that the yogin of reality, having attained the path of non-conceptualization, perceives the past and future within the void (*śūnya*), which is the reflection of all aspects. Regarding this *pratisenā* that is being seen, its existence—which is characterized by appearance—is not a [real] existence; that object does not exist. Why? He says: "Because of seeing the meaning of the voidness of objects."

That object, which is empty of—that is, devoid of—the nature of a collection of atoms as its substance, is the appearance characterized by manifestation; the perception of it occurs through non-conceptual direct perception. Since objects consisting of a collection of atoms, such as those of the past and so forth, do not exist, the object characterized by manifestation exists [as a mere appearance]. Indeed, even in the world, an object is seen despite being without a real substratum, just as in the case of illusions, dreams, and magical displays.

He states this very point in the passage beginning with "asati" and so forth: and that production of non-conceptual, non-erroneous knowledge is like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) because it accomplishes the fulfillment of all aspects of the world.

Now, one might object: "How can that which is without an objective support (anālambana) accomplish the welfare of the world? For how could it arise without an object? To clarify this through an example, he says:
"Unseen," and so forth.

Previously, only the maiden—whose eyes are empowered by the mantra and who remains in that state—sees the thief and others; however, the practitioners of *pratisenā* go to that place and see what was described by the maiden with their ordinary eyes.
This is the intended meaning.

The yogin, whose eyes and vision are empowered by the mantras of the perfected ones' instructions—like a young maiden, with the moon of his *bodhicitta* unerring—perceives the supramundane reality (*tattva*) that is untaught and inaccessible to ordinary beings.
And he says that this is always free from all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), such as existence and non-existence, beginning with the words "If... and so forth.
One does not see with the eyes of another—those produced in the forehead and so forth—nor even with one's own eyes at other times, because [the object] is not seen [then].

By this analogy of the *pratisenā* (magical mirror-image), the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the yogin is in every respect unborn due to the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This is established like the perception of a son by a young girl in a dream.
And regarding this, the *Samādhirāja-sūtra* speaks of the knowledge of the Omniscient One:
"Just as a maiden might see a son born within her bed;
she would be exceedingly joyful when he is born, and distressed in mind when he dies—so too, through knowledge, are all phenomena seen as being like that."
That which is not seen, unborn, and unproduced by the maiden is her *jātaka* (birth-story), meaning it is as if it were produced.

Regarding the statement "prāṇāyāma": when such a reflection—resembling a dream or an illusion, the universal reflection (*viśvabimba*) in all its aspects—is perceived, then immediately thereafter one should perform *prāṇāyāma*, the restraint of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* winds, continuously and without interruption through the yoga of inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*).
To the question "In what [state]? he says:
"Upwards," and so forth.

Above and below the navel, in three channels each, there occurs the sequential restraint of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths; this is because *prāṇāyāma* obstructs the triad of elements, beginning with the body. As for the phrase "of what nature" and so forth: "in the moon" and so forth refers to the left, right, and middle [channels] above.
Below, in the middle, left, and right [channels],
there are three channels carrying the moon, sun, and Rāhu,
and three channels carrying feces, urine, and semen.
Likewise, in the channels carrying water, fire, and space;
in the channels carrying earth, wind, and the gnosis-element (*jñānadhātu*);
and in the other [channels], which are the birthplaces of the seventy-two thousand channels and thus constitute the various classes of beings (*jāti*).
"Beginning with 'Candra'... and so forth.
Above, the triad of channels beginning with Candra are body, speech, and mind;
below, the triad of channels beginning with feces (viḍ) are body, speech, and mind.
He states the conceptualization of the six families of these [elements],
beginning with "Candra" and so forth:
Candra is the water element (*toyadhātu*), which constitutes the body of *upāya*, the semen element (*śukradhātu*).

For the element of passion (*rajo-dhātu*) associated with wisdom (*prajñā*), the element of fire (*tejo-dhātu*) or speech becomes the day; for that very element of passion, the feces-channel (*viṣ-nāḍī*) is the body.
For the pervasive element of semen (*śukra-dhātu*), the urine-carrying channel is speech.
"Upward" refers to the Rāhu-carrying channel of the semen-element as the mind (*citta*); the semen-carrying channel of the element of passion is the mind.
"Upward and downward is the sixfold family (*ṣaṭkula*).

This is because the channels carrying water, wind, and space constitute the means (*upāya*), while the channels carrying earth, fire, and gnosis (*jñāna*) constitute the wisdom (*prajñā*). Death occurs within ninety-six years plus ten and a half months; this is the omen of death (*ariṣṭa*). He says that it arises from the upward and downward flow of the body due to excessive winds, according to the rule to be explained hereafter.

Regarding the channels of body and speech as appropriate—namely, the *lalanā* and *rasanā*, and the channels for feces and urine—when the lower channel of feces is blocked, death (*ariṣṭa*) occurs in the upper left channel (*vāmanāḍī*).
When the channel of urine is blocked, death occurs in the upper right channel.
This will be explained in detail later.
The word "that" (*tam*) and so forth is the enumeration; its explanation is "arising" (*utpāda*) and so forth.

"That" means there is no ill omen (*ariṣṭa*) regarding the two channels that carry the semen. "That" means the wind in the two semen-carrying channels consists of arising [from the womb], exit from the womb, death, staying, and being in a healthy state.
Not only do the two semen-carrying channels flow during the three times of arising and so forth, but so too does the *avadhūtī*.

Furthermore, due to the similarity in the revolution of the twelve zodiacal signs (*lagna*), at the junction of the transition (*saṅkrama*)—when the Sun moves from the left nostril, consisting of the Aries sign and so forth, to the right nostril, consisting of the Taurus sign and so forth—and during the equinox (*viṣuva*), the central channel (*madhyamā*) flows. This is indicated by the verse beginning with "When the sign rises" (*lagnodya*); because the Moon and Sun flow equally, it is called the equinox (*viṣuva*).
He states the number of equinoxes with the verse beginning with "Fifty-six" (*ṣaṭpañcāśat*).

Combining inhalation and exhalation as a single unit at the junction of one *lagna*, it carries fifteen hundred and twenty-five breaths. Thus, in one day and night, at the junction of twelve *lagnas*, it carries six hundred and seventy-five breaths.

Those very breaths—amounting to twenty-one thousand six hundred that all sentient beings carry within their bodies—which the *lalanā* and *rasanā* channels carry, they carry reduced by six hundred and seventy-five.

Having multiplied the sixty-three hundred and seventy-five breaths of the middle channel per day by thirty-six thousand—the number of days in a hundred years—and then dividing that product by twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths per day, one obtains eleven hundred and twenty-five days; these, when divided by three hundred and sixty days (the number of days in a year), result in three years and three fortnights.

That which is the left [channel] above is indeed *candra* (moon); it is the *iḍā*, the carrier of water, having the nature of the Tathāgata Amitābha. To its right, however, is the *piṅgalā*, known as the other; it is the *rasanā*, the carrier of fire, having the nature of Ratnasambhava. Below, in the center, is the *viṇnāḍī* (feces channel), the carrier of earth, having the nature of Vairocana. But the left one below is the *sūtranāḍī*, the carrier of wind, having the essence of Amoghasiddhi. Above, in the center, is the *rāhunāḍī*, the carrier of emptiness, having the nature of Akṣobhya.
That same left channel below, the semen-channel (*śukranāḍī*), which carries gnosis and has the nature of Vajrasattva, unites with the feces-channel (*viṇnāḍī*) above by way of the moon-path.
Likewise, because they possess a single cavity, the thread-channel (*sūtranāḍī*) unites with the sun.
Thus, during the four periods beginning with birth, the semen-channel unites with Rāhu.

The *avadhūtī* which extends from the navel to the upper [cranial aperture] has two names: *suṣumnā* and *tamovahinī*. That which flows downward carrying semen (*śukra*) has two names: *khagamukhā* and *śaṅkhinī*. Emerging from the pericarp of the five lotuses beginning with the navel, the *avadhūtī*, whose vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) has departed [from its ordinary course], sequentially carries the five elements beginning with earth. Among these, in the lotus of the navel are the five qualities of earth, characterized by smell, form, taste, touch, and sound.
In the lotus of the heart, water has four qualities, characterized by form, taste, touch, and sound.
In the lotus of the throat, fire has three qualities, characterized by taste, touch, and sound.
In the lotus of the forehead, air has two qualities, characterized by touch and sound.
In the lotus of the *uṣṇīṣa*, there is only the sound of emptiness as the single quality.
Having grasped these, the *avadhūtī* emerges through the process of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) in the sequence beginning with earth.
As it was said by the Noble One (Āryapāda): "The element of earth dissolves into water; water dissolves into fire."
Fire dissolves into the subtle element, and wind dissolves into the mind.
The mind dissolves into the mental factors, and the mental factors dissolve into ignorance;
that too proceeds into the luminous state—this is cessation within the three realms of existence.
Through outward flow, the depletion of the elements enters again by way of the sequence beginning with the *uṣṇīṣa*-lotus;
[then] it enters the navel-lotus in the earth element and rests, by way of the sequence beginning with space (*ākāśa*), through the process of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
And it has been said by the venerable Āryadeva: "From the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) comes the great void (*mahāśūnya*), and from the void arises skillful means (*upāya*)."
From that, wisdom arises; from that, the wind is produced.
From wind arises fire, and from fire arises water;
from water the earth is born—this is the origin of all beings.

Thus, through the inward flow and the increase of the bodily constituents, there is the going and coming of the *avadhūtī* from *karṇikā* to *karṇikā*. By process of elimination, this movement occurs within the lotus petals of the *lalanā* and *rasanā*. Below, at the navel, the secret place, and the jewel-lotus (*maṇyabja*), the *śaṅkhinī*—which carries body, speech, and mind and consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* with three, two, and one quality respectively—emerges according to the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*).
Through emanation, she enters.
This very Śaṅkhinī carries the semen from the bliss of women—that is, from the bliss of the passion of sexual union.
The phrase "the latter, the former," and so forth, is the brief indication of the embrace of wisdom and means that will be explained below.
Regarding "wisdom" and so forth: when the *prāṇa* [wind] moves upward, wisdom and means exist as the right and left [channels], respectively.
When the *apāna* [wind] moves downward, they exist in the middle and left [channels], corresponding to the downward and upward flows of the *rajas* (menstrual blood) and semen.

In women, the *śaṅkhinī* alone is called the *caṇḍālī* when it carries the menstrual flow (*rajas*) during the period of menstruation (*ṛtukāla*), and that same channel is called the *khagamukhā* when it carries the semen (*śukra*).

However, the *avadhūtī* is called the *ḍombī* in women when it carries the menstrual flow during the period of menstruation; but for a man, even at the time of the arrival of semen during the period of menstruation, it is called the *avadhūtī* alone.

Through the knowledge of the arising of the mandalas in the left and right nostrils, first according to the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) beginning with earth, and then according to the order of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*).

In the left nostril, according to the sequence to be described, there is the flow of the five aggregates known as consciousness (*vijñāna*), formations (*saṃskāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and form (*rūpa*).
Likewise, in the right [nostril], there is the flow of the five elements known as earth, water, fire, air, and space.

In the center, on the middle path, the sixth mandala of gnosis (*jñāna*) flows together with fifty-six and a quarter breaths, having taken from each of the five mandalas beginning with space eleven and a quarter breaths per mandala.
Within these left, right, and central channels, there is a flow of sixty *maṇḍalas* in a single day and night.

Among them, in the six left petals of the navel lotus—consisting of Aries, Gemini, Leo, Libra, Sagittarius, and Aquarius—there are thirty *maṇḍalas*, because each consists of the five *maṇḍalas* beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*). Likewise, in the six right petals—consisting of Taurus, Cancer, Virgo, Scorpio, Capricorn, and Pisces—there are thirty *maṇḍalas*, because each consists of the five *maṇḍalas* beginning with earth (*bhūmi*).

In that regard, when the wind flows in the right [nostril] during the ascendants beginning with Taurus, then the earth mandala flows for one *daṇḍa* at the root, in the lower part of the nostril. Likewise, on its left side, in the region of the bridge of the nose, is the water mandala;
on the right side, the fire mandala; and in the upper part, the air mandala.
In the center is the mandala of emptiness.
Thus, one mandala flows from each of the two nostrils immediately after each staff (daṇḍa); the meaning is that the fifth mandala flows through five staffs.
As for the left nostril, however, he will explain later.
By the words "in the middle" (*dalamadhye*) and so forth, it is stated that, in relation to that [central channel], [the breath flows] through the two apertures of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
One channel carries how many breaths? By increasing [the count] by three days per month, one should gradually abandon eleven petals over the course of three years.

Thus, on the eleventh petal, through the flow [of the breath], one dries up the elements of the *sattva* constituent consisting of phlegm; however, on the twelfth petal, due to the flow of the right channel, two days of the three days belonging to the second, fourth, and sixth months—having ascended from other petals—are diminished due to the depletion of the *rajas* constituent consisting of the mind. From the drying up of the twelfth petal, as before, one day remains in the *karṇikā* (pericarp) due to the flow of the central channel (*madhyamā*).
Having dried up the wind-natured tamas-element, there is the departure to another existence;
this sequence of illustrations is for the sake of understanding how yogins undergo death through the left-side omen.

In a twelve-spoked wheel with two layers, there are [the following] in the eleven petals starting from the east: three, six, nine, twelve, fifteen, eighteen, twenty-one, twenty-four, twenty-seven, thirty, and thirty-three. However, in the twelfth [petal], there is zero due to the absence of leftward flow. In the outer twelve petals, the months are respectively thirty, twenty-seven, twenty-four, twenty-one, eighteen, fifteen, twelve, nine, six, three, and in the eleventh [outer petal], zero indicating the loss of three months; in the twelfth [outer petal], two days; and on the pericarp (karṇikā), one day.
Thus, there is an increase in misfortune (ariṣṭa) by three days and so forth.
The loss of the auspicious life-force, which consists of the thirty [days] and so forth, lasts for ninety-six years plus six and a half months; this is the period during which the sun and moon flow.
Within three years—consisting of three fortnights that complete nine hundred and three days—the ascent of death occurs in the middle channel.
This is indicated by the passage beginning with "even and uneven," etc.,
referring to the even days from two up to thirty-two, on the right side.

The ascent occurs on odd days starting from the first up to the thirty-third on the left; furthermore, regarding that death, it concerns the ascendant of Taurus or others existing at the time of birth, [calculated] by means of any one of the mandalas such as Earth and so forth.
Likewise, regarding the ascendant of Aries and so forth, the meaning is "starting from that particular mandala" among the mandalas beginning with the void (śūnya).

And this flow, with reference to the destruction of the constituents (dhātu), aggregates (skandha), and so forth of the left and right channels, employs the ablative case (*pañcamī*) by eliding the gerund suffix (*lyap*); thus he states the logical justification.
By the statement "otherwise there is no death," this is what is meant:
for one born under a *samala* [configuration], it flows first through the right [nostril] for two days,
then again for two days in the proper manner, and thereafter through the left for one day and one day in the proper manner.
Four days on the right as prescribed, four on the left as prescribed,
three on the right as prescribed, three on the left as prescribed, six on the right as prescribed, and six on the left as prescribed.
Five on the left, five exactly as prescribed;
likewise thirty-two on the right, thirty-two exactly as prescribed; thirty-three on the left, thirty-three exactly as prescribed.
Here, on the right side, the depletion of the elements beginning with earth occurs sequentially through groups of three days each, starting from two and ending at thirty;
on the left side, the depletion of the elements beginning with space occurs sequentially through groups of three days each, starting from one and ending at twenty-nine;
therein, the depletion of the *sattva* element occurs over thirty-one days.

The destruction of the *rajodhātu* occurs in thirty-two days, and the destruction of the *tamodhātu* occurs in thirty-three days; however, for those born under odd signs (*viṣamalagna*), this flow proceeds in the sequence of one day and so forth— this is the distinction.
Thus, there are three hundred and nine days; above that, there is an ascent of thirty-four days and so forth,
wherein one day is on the right and one day is on the left.
In this manner, it flows for thirty-three days in succession;
thereafter, there is a gradual exhaustion of the five aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), objects (*viṣaya*), faculties (*indriya*), and the functions of the active faculties (*karmendriya*).
Then, for one day in the central channel (*madhyamā*), having dried up the six [categories] beginning with the elements and aggregates, it proceeds to another state of existence (*bhavāntara*).
Having thus understood the signs of death (*ariṣṭa*), he explains the method for deceiving them, beginning with the words "ariṣṭa" and so forth.

In that regard, when the solar *ariṣṭa* occurs, one should assume the vajra posture (*vajraparyaṅka*) and, preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), draw the vital energy (*prāṇa*) from the right side—which consists of the flow of the five mandalas—by pressing the right breast with the right arm, and cause it to circulate in the left;
by this, the solar *ariṣṭa* is averted.
Likewise, from the left [nostril] to the right, there is the cessation of the moon and the ill omen (ariṣṭa).

Similarly, having assumed the paryanka posture, one should settle the mind within the white sixteen-petaled lotus located at the forehead in the *bindu*, preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), and thus settle the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the *bindu*; this is primarily the definition of concentration (*dhāraṇā*).
This alone is the primary method for subduing the *ariṣṭas* (signs of death), and the passage beginning with "avadhūtī" should be interpreted with this very intention.

Thus, having assumed the *paryaṅka* posture, one should meditate upon the *avadhūtī* at the navel-lotus, which has sixty-four yellow petals; in its center, within a moon-maṇḍala, one should visualize the syllable *Aṃ* in the form of a white upward-pointing line, accompanied by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

Therefore, one should always perform the vajra-arising through the lotus of one's own intention and so forth, so that the moon does not go outside, because [this] breaks the movement of the moon and sun which are the causes of untimely death (*ariṣṭa*).
He states the preeminence of this method with the words "not otherwise," and so forth;
having described the upper signs of death (*ūrdhvāriṣṭa*) along with their deceptive appearances, he now describes the lower signs of death (*adho'riṣṭa*).

The *apāna* [vāyu] flows downward in the *śaṅkinī* [channel]; the implication is that it is not only in the *śaṅkinī* channel, but also downward in the two channels carrying feces and urine that the wind called *apāna* flows.

Because death occurs even upon entering that [channel] due to its constant flow of feces and urine, [the author], under the guise of explaining the means of avoiding all portents (*ariṣṭa*), points this out by beginning with "from bliss" (*ānandāt*) and so forth.

By the words beginning with "śukre" (semen), it is shown that from the center of the four-petaled *uṣṇīṣa*-lotus, there is the arrival of semen—consisting of five digits (*kalā*) known as Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā—into the center of the sixteen-petaled forehead-lotus; this is the mutual pervasion (*ubhayavyāpti*). From that [forehead] comes *Nanda* [joy]; from there, into the throat and the heart, comes *Paramānanda* (supreme joy).
This is the pervasion like the full [digit], from the thirty-two-petaled throat-lotus to the eight-petaled heart-lotus. Thus, it is *Paramānanda*.
From that, the joy of cessation (*viramānanda*) arises.

It is the pervasion from the sixty-four-petaled lotus of the navel into the thirty-two-petaled lotus of the secret place; that is the joy of cessation. And that consists of various forms of play characterized by firm embraces, the sound of *śītkāra*, throat-murmuring, and so forth. At the navel and the secret place, however, it is the joy of cessation produced at the very end—a mere experience of bliss characterized by the absence of external conceptualization (*ullekha*), such as the thought, "I am enjoying pleasure."
But the pleasure of passion has not departed from that secret lotus; rather, until the sixteen-fold moon arrives within the eight-petaled vajra-jewel, there is the first innate bliss (*sahajānanda*).
By the power of *dhāraṇā*, due to the absence of outward movement, it is unemitted.
Because of the absence of dispassion—that is, the departure of passion—the semen, which is the bliss residing in the *uṣṇīṣa*, remains firmly established.
That which has not fallen from the vajra-jewel is *nirvāṇa*;
however, because the King of Bliss (*sukharāja*) pervades the space between the *uṣṇīṣa* and the vajra-jewel, he is the *apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*.
For this very reason, he is the Great Passion (*mahārāga*), the Immutable (*akṣara*), the Sovereign by virtue of his preeminence, and the Lord of the Three Realms (*traidhātukeśvara*).
Because it is desired by all with the wish to attain that state,
and because the semen (śukra) is indeed the moon (indu), its arising occurs in the uṣṇīṣa.
On the first day of the bright fortnight, [the flow reaches] the secret place; on the third, it is full.

Thus, through the divisions of bliss and so forth, when the *bodhicitta* has reached the three fullnesses at the secret place, there is the "joy of cessation" (*viramānanda*) and so forth. That sixteenth digit resides at the tip of the jewel-lotus, situated at the very peak of the vajra.
From that point upward, with the arrival of the first day of the dark fortnight, at the time of entering into detachment, the moment of emission (*cyuti*) occurs.
The meaning is that the very moment of death is the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇāpratipad*).

Due to the destruction of passion (*rāga*), in the dark fortnight, the first digit (*kalā*) of the sun, which consists of *rajas*, moves from the tip of the jewel (the *ājñā-cakra*) to the forehead—the place of the sun—due to dispassion (*virāga*); thus, the new moon (*amāvāsī*) is at the forehead.
The sixteenth digit of that sun has gone to the *uṣṇīṣa*-lotus; that very digit is designated as the "lost moon."
Because it is covered by the sun in the form of *rajas*,
there is detachment from the pleasure of passion; that very [pleasure] then goes downward to the nectar of the moon.

At death, at the time of dying, for all embodied beings—gods, asuras, humans, and so forth—the lunar nectar, which is the *bodhicitta*, descends by way of the semen-path below according to the sequential process, due to the habitual practice of the passion of emission (*cyutirāga*).

Likewise, the solar dust ascends upwards; Rāhu, which is ignorance, accompanied by the latent impressions of *avidyā* and conjoined with the vital breath (*prāṇa*), causes consciousness—which is characterized by existence and fashioned by virtuous and non-virtuous karma—to go toward rebirth.
For this reason, the upward movement of the lunar nectar, the seminal element, is taught through the cultivation of the path described above.
The descent of the solar dust (*arkarajas*)— that is, the movement of consciousness characterized by Rāhu— must be directed toward the immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*);
and this was also previously practiced by the Blessed One,
as shown in the passage beginning with "the wool" (*ūrṇā*).
For the Buddhas, however, the full moon of the nectar of the moon—the state of the fifteen digits being completely full—occurs at the ūrṇā on the forehead;
the new moon of the solar dust occurs at the secret place.
Of those two, the moon and the sun, the sixteenth digit resides respectively in the uṣṇīṣa and in the vajra-jewel of the Buddhas.
As it is said in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*: "Standing with the sole of one foot treading upon the surface of the entire earth,
he stands with the tip of his big toe's nail reaching to the summit of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*)."

Thus it is said: that which is reached or attained is the "vajra-word" (*vajrapada*); that word is imperishable gnosis (*jñāna*). The constant worship of this word with the head—until the indestructible gnosis of the Teacher is attained by all embodied beings—that is, by all transmigrating beings—is contrary [to worldly views] and non-abiding.

From this pure body known as the Great Bliss (mahāsukha), designated as the *apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*, the elements such as earth and so forth attain their opposite state, which is freedom from obscuration (*nirāvaraṇatā*). Those other elements are indestructible.

By the power of *dhāraṇā* and by the flame of *caṇḍālī* which proceeds spontaneously, the drops (*bindu*) of body, speech, mind, and gnosis—which hang from the head according to the divisions of bliss and so forth—do not exit externally through the upper [aperture] in succession; thus, being filled with immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*), he speaks of the purification of the four bodies (*catuḥkāya-viśuddhi*) starting with the words "in the jewel" and ending with "from great bliss."

The body-drop (*kāyabindu*), which is encompassed by the pure body and so forth known as great bliss (*mahāsukha*), is the pure body (*śuddhakāya*) due to the exhaustion of the fourth state (*turyāvasthā*);
it abides at the tip of the vajra.
Therefore, the mind (*citta*) is in the jewel (*maṇi*) due to the exhaustion of deep sleep (*suṣupta*).
Speech [arises] at the secret place through the cessation of the dream state; the body [arises] at the navel through the cessation of the waking state.
These—the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa bodies—emanate from the Pure Body (śuddhakāya) by means of the method (upāya).
Since the radiation of these—the dharmakāya and so forth—proceeds downward from the tip of the vajra, that which constitutes their method aspect is established as being below;
however, that of wisdom (prajñā) occurs above.
This he demonstrates with the words "on the forehead," and so on.

The body of this wisdom, called the *nirmāṇakāya*, is established on the forehead; likewise, by the reverse order as before, the *saṃbhogakāya*, *dharmakāya*, and *sahajakāya* of speech, mind, and gnosis-vajra are respectively established in the lotuses of the throat, heart, and navel, belonging to the aspect of wisdom.

Thus, from the body of Vajrasattva, which consists of wisdom and skillful means, there is an emanation of the aggregates and so forth in the form of Vairocana and the other [Buddhas] for the sake of sentient beings;
by this, the limb of recollection (*anusmṛti-aṅga*) is indicated through the realization of the objective.
Having thus indicated the result, he states the means for its accomplishment:
Regarding the passage beginning with "karmamudrā" and so forth: the *karmamudrā* possesses breasts and hair and is the cause of the bliss of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

"Karma" consists of activities such as kissing, embracing, touching the secret parts, and striking with the *vajra*; the *mudrā* is characterized by these and produces a "sign" (*pratyaya*). Here, the "sign" is defined as the characteristic of fleeting bliss (*kṣarasukha*).
A *mudrā* is so called because it bestows joy (*muda*), a specific form of bliss, and delight;
it refers to the *jñānamudrā*, which is conceptualized by one's own mind,
has the nature of goddesses such as Viśvamātā, and is that which was previously experienced.

The knowledge of the cause of the bliss of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is characterized by the cultivation of previous states such as laughing and smiling; the condition (*pratyaya*) here is characterized by the pleasure of touch.

Furthermore, she is both great (*mahatī*) and a seal (*mudrā*), hence a "Great Seal" (*mahāmudrā*). Her greatness, moreover, consists in being endowed with the excellence of all aspects, and not being limited or partial.

She is called a "seal" (*mudrā*) because one is sealed by this Vajra of Bodhicitta. Here, the condition is the manifestation of one's own mind, free from the phenomena imagined by one's own mind, preceded by signs such as smoke, accessible to the yogi like a reflected image (*pratisenā*).

The *phalamudrā* (fruit-seal), however, perpetually assumes the joy (*rati*) of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), which is characterized by the gnosis of supreme unchanging bliss, through the yoga of immovability from its prior state; thus it is a "seal" (*mudrā*). Its greatness consists in both the greatness of abandonment (*prahāṇa*) and the greatness of realization (*adhigama*). Therein, the greatness of abandonment is characterized by the direct realization of the natural luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), whose nature is the abandonment of all habitual tendencies and all obscurations.
The greatness of realization, however, has as its essential nature the direct realization of the body known as *yuganaddha*, which consists of all the completely pure Buddhas.

The direct realization of the mind—which is free from all stains such as darkness and cold—as being empty like the sky and possessing the single flavor of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), is itself the attainment of all the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*).
This is because all the qualities of a Buddha exist therein in the form of the power to accomplish the welfare of the entire world.

For this very reason, they call the body that is the support of these qualities the "Dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*). Furthermore, if [the Dharma-body] were not manifest there, then even when establishing a cognition, the undesirable consequence would be unavoidable that upon the manifestation of a jar, one would also have the attainment of a cloth and so forth.
Furthermore, the view of enumeration (*saṃkhyā-darśana*) would indeed be faultless;

moreover, the perception of the entire collection of aggregates, elements, and sense-bases as unconstructed—like an illusion, a dream, a city of gandharvas, or a reflected image—is called the vision of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*).

And that very conventional truth, consisting of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), is the luminous and utterly pure mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) and so forth, as well as the host of deities such as Vairocana who are supported therein, and the maṇḍala of the celestial palace and other supports; this is what is proclaimed in all the *tantra-rājas* as the supramundane maṇḍala.

Because it has the nature of all the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*), this very [reality] is called "Yuganaddha" (the yoked pair), having as its nature the non-duality of the two truths; therefore, the *dharmakāya* itself is precisely the *yuganaddhakāya*,
which is distinct from both the *sāmbhogika* and *svābhāvika* [kāyas], and is to be personally realized by yogis.

And it was said by the venerable Āryamañjuśrīpāda in the *Tantrottara*: "That which has not arisen is the Truth; the white mass of virtuous qualities is the Dharmakāya of the Victors. From the Dharma arises the Saṃbhogakāya, the totality of all sounds. The collection of the primary and secondary marks is the Nirmāṇakāya. The Dharmakāya is the supreme bliss beyond syllables. Therefore, there is no defining characteristic of these bodies. That which is here [described] by the Master named Nāga, who has attained the state of bliss—is neither one nor many, being the support for the great perfection of the welfare of self and others; it is neither non-existence nor existence, like space, of equal flavor, and its nature is difficult to discern."
I pay homage to that incomparable Dharmakāya of the Jinas— untainted, changeless, auspicious, peerless, all-pervading, free from conceptual proliferation, and to be realized within each individual—

which manifests in the midst of the assembly a great and manifold splendor as the fruit of hundreds of well-performed deeds for the sake of delighting the wise; and I pay homage here to that Sambhogakāya, which, established in the great kingdom of Dharma, proclaims throughout all worlds the continuous and noble sound of the True Dharma of the Buddhas, which is transcendent and inconceivable.

I bow to the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Munis, which, for the sake of maturing sentient beings, appears in some places blazing like fire, and in others is seen utterly tranquil at the wheel of Dharma of perfect enlightenment; which proceeds in manifold forms through various means that remove the fear of the three realms of existence; which follows the course of the ten directions for the great purpose of all;

which is liberated from the conduct of the three worlds, equal to space, and the very nature of all phenomena; and which is pure, peaceful, secluded, and consists of supreme bliss, accessible only to yogins.

I pay homage to the body of the Victors (jinānām), which is difficult to understand, difficult to contemplate, most beneficial for oneself and others, all-pervading, causeless, the peerless bliss, and the singular embodiment of non-conceptuality.

Because of the statement, "The evil dharmas have been conquered by me; therefore, I am indeed the Victorious One (Upaga-jina)," they are called "Victors" (jināḥ) because they have conquered the four Māras. I pay homage to their body, known as Great Bliss (mahāsukha), which is luminous due to being free from all obscurations like space.
The meaning is that I prostrate to the fourth body, characterized by the gnosis of supreme immutable bliss.

"Unequaled and equal" means that because it is the nature of the fruit— attained through the sequence beginning with "motionlessness" (*niṣpanda*) and reaching the ultimate limit of excellence— it is unequaled and unique compared to the pleasures of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas;
yet it is equal because of the single-flavor nature (*ekarasa*) of all phenomena.

"Free from the conduct of the three worlds" means it is liberated from the conduct of the three worlds— namely, the pleasure characterized by smiling, gazing, and so forth— and thus abandoned by it; otherwise, even divine pleasure would become the reality (tattva).
It is stated in the *Mūlatantra*: "The reality born from the two organs is known as the bliss of the passionate deities;
the bliss of the Buddhas is imperishable, free from the conduct of the three worlds, devoid of laughing, gazing, and so forth, and abandoned by all dualities."

Free from cause and effect, appearing as the three worlds yet non-dual; it is the supreme syllable, free from vibration, attained through the worldly pleasures arising from laughter, the seizing of hands, embracing, and the union of the couple, and is like the sky in its pervasive reach.
One whose movement and realization are equal to and like the sky is "thus" (tathā).

Just as the sky, though all-pervading by virtue of its omnipresence, is not attached to any object whatsoever and is devoid of defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), so too the Blessed One’s knowledge, although it has the entirety of the knowable as its object, is not established in any phenomenon (*dharma*) and is devoid of defining characteristics.
As it is said in the Āgama: "With knowledge that is non-reliant, you behold all fields."
O Nirālamba, who possesses the conduct of all sentient beings, homage be to you!

And by Indrabhūtipāda, in the *Jñānasiddhi*, it was said: "That which is non-abiding like space, all-pervasive, and devoid of characteristics—that is declared to be the supreme reality, the unsurpassed Vajra-knowledge."
And elsewhere it is said: "Like space, it is non-abiding, all-pervading, devoid of characteristics,
indefinable, and formless— this is the characteristic of reality."
Alternatively, "one whose movement is equal to space" (*gaganasamagati*) refers to the body of great bliss (*mahāsukhakāya*);
because it is devoid of color and shape, its meaning is that it is like space, free from all appearances.
And it is said: "That body which belongs to all Buddhas is without appearance,
without support, unborn, unconditioned, pure, and free from existence, non-existence, and so forth."

In the *Śrītantra*, it is said that "the wisdom-vajra of the Jina is like a crystal gem," and by the venerable Candragomin: "That which is like the utterly pure sky, yet perceived by those clouded by the darkness of ignorance as if covered by clouds, is perceived by the Jinas as the true reality."

Thus, "the nature of all phenomena" refers to the fact that all phenomena— such as the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), whether stable or moving entities— and indeed everything included within the remaining three realms, arise from causes and conditions like space; their nature is such that, because they originate from it and are ultimately resolved in it, they possess the single form of *tathatā* (thusness), which is the nature of great bliss, free from all conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) such as existence and non-existence.
And it has been said by the venerable Vajragarbha: "When the mind is free from conceptual construction, there is no meditator, nor is there an object of meditation;

there is no mantra, nor is there any deity's empowerment, because of the nature of the absence of conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). It exists precisely as the nature of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), in a form wherein all stains of conceptual construction have completely subsided."
And by the venerable Candragomin: "Suchness is his dharmakāya; it is the nature beyond the range of conceptual constructions.
It is the lineage (anvaya) of all sentient beings and of the welfare of sentient beings.
It is the existence and non-existence [of things], impermanence and permanence, and both multiplicity and unity."
Purity and impurity, as well as awakening— all these are conceptualized therein;
for it is there that all states of being arise, like waves in the ocean, like reflections in a mirror, or like the objects of dreams within the mind.
That which is like the pure sky, yet perceived by those clouded by the cataract of ignorance as being covered by spots,
is perceived by the Victors as it truly is.
In this [work], the forms of the universe, which are the very essence of reality,
attain a state of single flavor, just as rivers do in the ocean.
This very body of such a kind is the Dharma-body of this Protector;
it is the domain of omniform, perfectly pure, complete enlightenment alone.
Thus [it is said]: the *dharmakāya* is the body that is the basis and cause of all perfectly pure Buddha-qualities. "Purity" means being untouched by defilements.
"Peaceful" means free from the transformations of the eighteen elements.
And it has been said by the noble Vajragarbha:
"By its own nature, form does not exist," and so forth.
The intrinsic nature is self-cognizing; it is not the seer, nor is it the visual consciousness.
Likewise, it is not the sound, nor the hearer, nor the auditory consciousness. Likewise, it is not the taste, nor the taster, nor the gustatory consciousness.
Thus, there is no contact, no toucher, and no body-consciousness;
likewise, there is no dharma-element, no grasper, and no mental consciousness.
In this way, the jewel of reality, which is free from the transformations of the eighteen elements, should be meditated upon by the yogi of reality.

"Solitary" (*vivikta*) means being distinct from the obscurations such as the meditative absorption on the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-samāpatti*). Precisely because it is free from all afflictions, it consists of supreme *Śiva* by virtue of its nature as ultimate auspiciousness and its being the cause of auspiciousness; thus, it is accessible only to yogins. Yoga is the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅga-yoga*) that has reached the limit of its excellence. Those who possess that yoga are "yogins," who have attained the state of the Great Vajradhara; [the state] is accessible only to them. Therefore, by the fact that its realization does not depend on anything else, he reveals its quality of being personally realized within oneself (*pratyātmavedyatā*).

It is difficult for yogis to comprehend because it is to be realized only at the culmination of the excellence of meditating on the path of smoke and so forth, which proceeds with reverence and without interruption.
It is difficult to analyze because, although its nature consists of a cognition superior to that produced by learning and reflection (*śruta-cintāmayajñāna*), it is impossible to delimit.
It is "the most beneficial for oneself and others."

The meaning is as follows: because it is endowed with the perfection of one’s own welfare (*svārthasaṃpad*), characterized by the abandonment of all obscurations along with their latent predispositions (*savāsanāsarvāvaraṇaprahāṇi*), it is exclusively for one’s own benefit; and because, through its empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the welfare of others is accomplished without remainder by means of the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) according to the inclinations and lineages of those to be trained (*vineya*), it is exceedingly for the benefit of others.
It is pervasive (*vyāpin*) because it lacks restriction of place and time, pervading all objects such as the minds of others.
It is signless (*nirnimitta*) because it is devoid of causes consisting of the Action Seal (*karmamudrā*) or the Knowledge Seal (*jñānamudrā*).
It is non-conceptual because it is free from the duality of conceptualizing the apprehended object and the apprehending subject;

it is unique and non-dual because its nature is the single form of ultimate truth, as there is no second [truth] here, namely the conventional truth—thus it is the singular embodiment of non-conceptuality. And by the venerable Puṇḍarīka: "The body endowed with the excellence of all aspects [appears] according to various inclinations."
It is perceived by sentient beings through its own intrinsic nature as having the characteristic of a transformation.

That body characterized as the Enjoyment Body (saṃbhogakāya), which manifests its own sovereign power through the sounds of all sentient beings, exists solely by virtue of the inclinations of those beings.
That which is neither impermanent nor permanent, neither characterized by unity nor multiplicity,
neither an entity nor a non-entity— that is the supportless Dharmakāya.
Indivisible from emptiness and compassion, free from both passion and dispassion, this is neither wisdom nor means; it is the other body, the svābhāvika-kāya.
And in the *Svadarśanamato-deśa*: "The infinite mass of my forms is my supreme nirmāṇakāya;
the infinite mass of my sounds is my supreme sambhogakāya."
The infinite mass of Dharma is proclaimed by me as my Dharmakāya;
the infinite mass of bliss is my supreme, imperishable Sukhakāya.

A "piṇḍa" is a heap; likewise, it is proclaimed as a body (*kāya*) and a collection (*sañcaya*). Even in works such as the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, the *dharmakāya* is established as distinct from both the *svābhāvikakāya* and the *sambhogakāya*.
The subject at hand is now stated: for one who has received the instruction, first there is the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) which is favorable.

Through meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), by the destruction of the highest-of-the-high degrees of conceptualization, there is an increase in the lowest-of-the-low degree of imperishable bliss (*akṣarasukha*).

Likewise, by means of the support of the knowledge-seals (*jñānamudrā*), such as the goddesses Viśvamātṛ and others, through the diminution of the highest degree of conceptualization, there is an increase in the lowest degree of imperishable bliss.
And it is said in the *Śrītantra*:

"At the beginning of service, there is the action-seal (*karmamudrā*), for the purpose of increasing this innate bliss of the Victor; therefore, she is of the nature of the sun, possessing bliss-bestowing feet, a crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*), and complete limbs," and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) is included.

By taking as an object the *dharmamudrā*, which has the nature of the reflection of smoke and other [signs] that are the preliminary forms (*pūrvarūpa*), there is an increase of the supreme unchanging bliss (*akṣarasukha*) through the destruction of weak afflictions (*kleśa*). Subsequently, by the practice of the *mahāmudrā* known as the universal reflection (*viśvabimba*) of the subsequent form (*paścādrūpa*), there is an increase of the supreme-unto-the-supreme unchanging bliss through the removal of even the subtlest obscurations along with their latent predispositions (*savāsanāvaraṇa*).
[Objection: But how can unchanging bliss, which is devoid of addition and subtraction, undergo increase? To this he says:
"For there can be no further growth for that which has already grown.
For the growth consisting in the abandonment of obscurations occurs sequentially, like the purification of water, gold, or space.

And such growth—characterized as stainlessness (*vaimalya*) resulting from the abandonment of all obscurations along with their latent tendencies (*savāsanā*)—could not belong to one who is already "grown," that is, one who is endowed with the growth consisting in the state of perfection.

Thus, for the sake of removing the obscurations that are to be cultivated gradually, that by which they are further diminished—namely, the "state of being diminished" imagined for that which has been diminished—that too does not exist, because it is eternally arisen.
If this is so, then since there is an absence of both increase and decrease, how is it that the path and so forth are not rendered futile?
To this he says: "of phenomena whose nature is non-existence."

Those phenomena such as old age and so forth, which lack intrinsic nature, are "phenomena devoid of intrinsic nature"; their arising and their destruction are merely illusion (*māyā*) and not reality.
By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), it is implied that even worldly convention (*lokasaṃvṛti*), characterized by setting, rising, and so forth, is merely illusion.
Thus it says: "They do not go to destruction," and so forth;
for this very reason, they do not arise by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This universe is devoid of intrinsic nature, characterized solely by existence and non-existence.
It has the form of existence because it performs purposeful action on the conventional level;
it has the characteristic of non-existence because it is empty in reality.
He speaks of the cultivation of the flow, vibration, and so forth,
beginning with the words "one's own wisdom" (*svaprajñā*).
This refers to the state of the bliss of awakening (*bodhisukha*) when embraced by one's own wisdom, such as the action seal (*karmamudrā*) and others.

The state of vibrating bliss (*spandasukhāvasthā*) is attained through the *jñānamudrā*. The term "vibrating" (*spanda*) also includes the syllable that effects the emission (*srāva*). When these two states of bliss are directly realized, they serve as the means for achieving worldly accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*), characterized by mastery over the realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and form (*rūpadhātu*).
The cultivation of the unchanging syllable through the Mahāmudrā, however, is the means for accomplishing supramundane siddhi, which has omniscience as its characteristic.

Regarding the passage beginning with "in the channels of body, speech, and mind," and so forth: by the power of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), during the fourfold bliss, the four channels of body and so forth are established as the four parts pervaded by the moon-like seminal essence (*śukra*).
Among these, the cultivation of body is in the forehead, the cultivation of speech is in the heart, and the cultivation of mind is in the secret place.

The unification—the gathering together—of the drops (*bindu*) of body and so forth within the *vajramaṇi* is the cultivation of gnosis (*jñāna*). This limb of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is indicated by two and a half verses.
He explains the binding of the four drops with the words beginning "prajñā" and so forth.

By means of the knowledge of Caṇḍālī, the drops— which have been melted by the passion of wisdom (prajñā)— are, according to the aforementioned sequence, brought from the head, that is, from the forehead, to the place of fullness.

The binding of those who have entered the jewel-lotus—that is, those who have gone to the jewel-lotus—is, in the ultimate sense, by means of the binding of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is unchanging bliss (*akṣarasukha*), and by means of the meditation on reality (*tattvabhāvanā*). Having thus established, according to the stated sequence, that the increase, decrease, and so forth of unchanging bliss are unreal, he confirms that very point through a worldly analogy, beginning with "Just as the risen moon," and so on. Just as the moon, having risen, gradually reaches fullness through its phases (*kalā*).

For the world, which is like the full moon, the "fullness" consists solely in the removal of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); there is no actual cutting away or filling. For that [moon] is eternally full, yet it is conventionally designated as "waning" or "full" through the covering and uncovering of darkness.

Likewise, the knowledge of the Imperishable (*akṣara*), having arisen within the diamond-jewel (*vajramaṇi*), gradually attains fullness in the *uṣṇīṣa*-cakra above, through the stages (*bhūmi*) to be described—beginning with *muditā* and characterized by the distinctions of being "motionless" (*niḥspanda*) and so forth.

The removal—that is, the departure—of the afflictions and so forth, as well as the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the obscurations of the afflictions, the knowable, and meditative attainments, is designated by the word "full" (*pūrṇa*).
There is no cutting off of knowledge, nor is there its filling.
As it is said in the Āgama: "But for the Buddhas, [knowledge] is eternally arisen; it is not for those whose minds are defiled by ignorance."
And by the venerable Saraha it was said: "Victorious is the one King of Bliss, causeless and eternally arisen for the worlds;
at the time of whose description even the Omniscient One became impoverished of words."
Having stated the example for filling, he states the example for cutting:
"Just as in the middle," and so forth.

Just as the moon situated in the center of the mandala is not stable at the full moon because it increases gradually by way of the rabbit-form which has become the seed, the meaning is that it is not eternally full.

Likewise, because the latent tendencies of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra-vāsanā*), which are characterized by perishable pleasure, increase gradually, the mind also does not remain stable in imperishable pleasure (*akṣara-sukha*).
Since there is an absence of passion and its cessation, as well as birth and its termination, there is the non-dual imperishable pleasure.
Demonstrating an illustration under the guise of the union of the external and internal, he says:
"Arising," and so forth:
just as the white fortnight is the gradual arising of the digits of the moon starting from the first day (pratipad),
and the black fortnight is the gradual waning of those digits.
Those two are established and accessible to the world, but the sixteenth digit situated between them is not so, because it arises for only a single moment;
likewise is it with the moon of semen (*śukrendu*).

When, however, for yogins the jewel of the *bodhicitta* becomes fully awakened as the imperishable (*akṣara*) in a single moment and remains eternally unmoving, then that *cittavajra*, by means of its non-fluctuation (*niṣpanda*), fills all moments within the *vajramaṇi*; that is, it fills the two million, one hundred and sixty-eight thousand breath-moments, flowing without interruption.

And it is said in the *Paramārthasevā*: "When, by the power of meditation day and night, the mind gradually comes to abide in the central channel—that infinite form, perfectly pure, non-dual, and the unique trident—I bow to that Vajra.

Thus, for this Mind-Vajra, there is no abiding in passion during the bright fortnight, nor is there any departure [from it] during the dark fortnight, because it is free from both the extremes of passion and dispassion."
Therefore, that which stands between the two halves of the fortnight, having entered the full moon, is non-dual and non-abiding.
As it is said in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*: "Awakened in a single moment, the manifestor of all moments;
partless, beyond calculation, the holder of the pinnacle of the fourth dhyāna."
In the Hevajra [Tantra] as well: "O Āi, there is neither end nor middle; for me, there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa.
This is that supreme great bliss, neither other nor self;
it is the proclamation of the sequence of saṃsāra."
Regarding the phrase "of that": because the sixteen digits (*kalā*) of the moon, which has become the seed, are full, it is "full" within the *vajra-jewel*;

however, through lack of means (*anupāya*), due to detachment and the consequent destruction of passion (*rāga*), there is a loss of digits—the destruction of fifteen digits. Starting from the *vajra*, as there is a decrease, there is a further filling up of the sun, whose nature is *rajas*, in the *uṣṇīṣa*.
Again and again, by means of the yoga of the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) and so forth, there is an arising in the *uṣṇīṣa*.

Furthermore, within the vajra-gem there is fullness; due to detachment, there is a loss of digits (*kalā*), but for embodied beings there is no loss of gnosis. Gnosis is the sixteenth digit, and for that there is no loss.
Moreover, it has been said: "All sentient beings have the essence of the Tathāgata’s gnosis.
Furthermore, through the loss of gnosis, there would be nothing but death.

He explains the meaning of the word *pūrṇā* with the words "Great Bliss" (*mahāsukha*) and so forth: that which is the nature of great bliss belonging to this *bodhicitta* is called *pūrṇā*. This alone must be stabilized by yogins. Apart from the stabilization of great bliss, there is no other state for embodied beings that serves as the cause for the creation and withdrawal characterized by the arising and passing away of that great bliss. For if this moon of bliss is not stabilized during the *pūrṇā*, it arises and perishes again and again.
Regarding this, he states an illustration:
"by its two sides," and so forth; just as the moon [is measured] by its white and black phases, and the sun by its northern and southern solstices.

By day, because one observes the increase and decrease in the form of the sun's waxing and waning, through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), this stable great bliss becomes full. Through the twelve stages (*bhūmi*), there is a gradual fulfillment from the secret place up to the crown protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*). In each of the wheels (*cakra*) from the secret place to the crown, the attainment of the stages occurs by doubling [the count] through the three hundred and sixty breaths that are blocked from flowing or leaking.
That which is imperishable is so called because it transcends the two sides of passion and dispassion, which consist of arising and ceasing.
Then, having abandoned the two sides, it is filled with the stages (bhūmis),
possessing twelve aspects and sixteen aspects of the meaning of truth.
He explains that by means of the stages (*bhūmi*), and so forth; [it is] by means of the stages.
Samantaprabhā, Amṛtaprabhā, Vajraprabhā.
Ratnaprabhā and Padmaprabhā are the performers of the Buddha's work.
The incomparable simile is wisdom.

The light of omniscience is to be personally realized; it consists of twelve aspects through the cessation of the twelve transits beginning with Aries and Taurus, and by means of attaining the twelve stages (*bhūmi*).
The supreme non-duality,
because it lacks the characteristics of wisdom and means,
is neither wisdom nor means.
Because it is stated in the *Śrītantra* that "this is the body of the co-emergent," the imperishable [essence] consists of sixteen aspects,
due to the exhaustion of the sixteen worldly digits (*kalā*).

This mind, which is complete in all its aspects and consists of the vision of reality as it is—beginning with the single object (*ekārtha*) and so forth—is the nature of the non-dual dharma. Because of the absence of both sides, that single object is the "Great Passion" (*mahārāga*) beginning with dispassion (*virāga*). This is the fourth moment of consecration.
As it is said in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*: "The Great Passion beginning with dispassion, possessing all colors, blazing with light."
That Buddha, seated in the vajra posture, upholds the Dharma of the Buddhas' assembly;
and that [Dharma] is unsullied by the latencies of the two sides of passion and dispassion.

The meaning is that when the multitude of phenomena (*bhāvagrāma*) has entered into that syllable, it is "the imperishable" (*akṣara*); thus, in the Teacher who holds the imperishable vidyā, there is the manifestation of all phenomena in all their aspects consisting of bliss.
The word "just as" (*yathā*) provides a clear example, and the purpose of another example is also evident.
Just as a collection of minerals such as mica and others, when consumed by the mercury (*rasa*), attains the state of mercury;

and when the seeds of gold and so forth have been digested (*jīrṇa*), they attain the state of seed at the time of the fruit characterized by the piercing (*vedha*) of the eight metals—being free from pride through the power of piercing millions and more once they have been digested—so too is the illustrative application (*dārṣṭāntika*): the entire aggregate of phenomena (*bhāva-samūha*), consisting of both the stable and the moving, when consumed by the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*), attains the state of the supreme syllable, which is the single flavor of great bliss, stainless like the sky, and naturally luminous (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*).
And consequently, he becomes the bearer of the essential nature of all aspects,
because his form consists of the manifestation of all phenomena;
by means of the example of poison, he states the pervasiveness of non-conceptual great bliss.
Regarding the phrase "he does not feel the bite," etc.:

when the poison has reached its full state of pervasiveness, the one bitten feels no sensation or pain at the site of the bite, nor anywhere else on the body; nor does he perceive objects such as forms through the gates of the senses. Likewise, when the mind has reached its full phase and attained pervasiveness, the yogi does not perceive the sublime bliss in the *vajramaṇi*, nor anywhere else.
It does not [enter] the objects by way of the sense-faculties;
rather, even though it is situated in one place, it pervades as far as the pores and joints of the body. Regarding the example of mercury acting upon iron, he says:

"The bliss stabilized in one place within the diamond-jewel (*vajramaṇi*), when the mind is heated by the blazing flame of Caṇḍālī through the yoga of the *kartṛmudrā*, *karmamudrā*, and so forth, should pierce the body in its entirety."
The two verses beginning with "yathā" are clear because they bring about the state of being identical with that;
"yathā" refers to the afflictions such as latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) and passion (*rāga*).

There exists a certain great gem such that by its touch, stone attains a state of blazing radiance and becomes a luminous jewel. How much more so, then, should the existence and power of primordial wisdom (jñāna) be considered from the perspective of ultimate reality and the ultimate truth? It is certainly not the case that there is no piercing of the mind merely because it is defiled by adventitious stains; rather, this must be investigated with certainty, even as it is clearly evident to ordinary people through the example of the seminal element (śukradhātu).
With three verses beginning with "The reality of afflictions and so forth is not," he negates [their existence];
first of all, they are not adventitious,
because it would follow that even one free from passion would be subject to passion.
Nor do they arise from a cause existing prior to the mind, because such a cause does not exist;
for afflictions and the like are produced by the mind, nor are they causeless, as they would then be as ineffective as a sky-flower.
Nor are the afflictions (kleśas) of the nature of the [mind] itself, because that would entail their indestructibility; or, if they were destroyed, it would entail their extinction like a lamp.
Here, he illustrates this with the example of copper:

if this impurity were adventitious to the copper, then the copper was previously free of stains. Since the copper existed long before the impurity, from what source or cause could that impurity have arisen?

If it were produced without copper, then even a sky-flower would have come into existence. Furthermore, if it remained as an imperishable entity within the copper, then it could not be removed even by *siddharasa* (mercurial elixir). Therefore, all this does not cohere with reason. Thus, the true meaning here is this: this stain is produced together with the copper and perishes through contact with the mercury; it was not there before, nor after, nor is it present apart from it. In its state of stainlessness, it exists as gold.
In this way, he also demonstrates that for the mind—
as well as for those [other factors] beginning with "likewise"—
there is the state of knowing the path of emptiness, smoke, and so forth, which is to be personally realized within oneself.
And it was said by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna in the *Dharmadhātustava*: "The sun and moon, though naturally stainless, are indeed obscured by five impurities:
by clouds, mist, smoke, the mouth of Rāhu, and the dust of pollen.
In this same way, the luminous mind is obscured by five impurities."
Through sensual desire, ill-will, sloth, restlessness, and doubt— just as a garment soiled by various stains becomes clean when cast into the fire,
where the stain is burnt away but not the cloth.
Thus, the mind is luminous, yet it is defiled by stains born of passion;
when the stain is burned away by the fire of gnosis, that luminosity itself is not burned.
Whatever sūtras have been spoken by the Victors that provide nourishment for emptiness [are intended for this].
By all these [means], there is merely the removal of the hair [of ignorance], not the destruction of the element;
just as water hidden within the earth remains pure,
so too does knowledge remain pure when hidden by the *kuśa* grass.
And it has been stated by the venerable Āryadeva:
