"One should behold with the eye of wisdom that which is instantly freed from darkness, luminous, exceedingly pure, having the nature of perpetual light, and characterized as the ultimate truth."

By the verse beginning with "rasa" and so forth, it is stated that for one who is liberated, there is no further rebirth into cyclic existence, because [the nature of reality] is the luminosity of the intrinsic nature of gnosis; thus,
[the text says] "no," and so on.
From the destruction of passion (rāga) arises evil; from that, hatred toward one's dearest is born;

from hatred comes delusion (moha), and from that, the mind suffers as if struck by its own thunderbolt, falling into a state of stupor. Consequently, the mind is always engaged with other objects—such as all manner of improper food and drink—and being thus mocked, its happiness destroyed, it falls away throughout six births.
Evil arises from the destruction of passion because it consists in the exhaustion of compassion;

for what reason is this? Because toward one who is most dear—a beloved woman—hatred arises, which is the destruction of love and consists in the exhaustion of loving-kindness (*maitrī*); this is to be connected respectively with each [term].
From hatred comes delusion, which is the destruction of exhilaration and consists in the exhaustion of sympathetic joy (*muditā*); fainting is characterized by the destruction of bliss.

[Objection: "If equanimity (*upekṣā*) consists in the exhaustion [of all feelings], then because the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) would be absent, there would be only evil; how could there be merit?

For is it not the case that compassion (*karuṇā*) is characterized by the increase of passion (*rāga*), loving-kindness (*maitrī*) consists in the destruction of hatred (*dveṣa*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*) consists in the exhaustion of delusion (*moha*), and equanimity consists in imperishable bliss (*akṣarasukha*)? [Reply: Is this not found in the *Buddhakapāla*? As it is said: "One should be endowed with the view of compassion and the embrace of loving-kindness."
When the self is engaged in friction with a supreme woman through joy,
that single moment of observation at their union is known by me as equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Thus, for one joined to the yoga of cultivation, how could one be bound by passion?

"Veśanīyam" (to be entered) refers to the fact that the immutable bliss (*akṣarasukha*) transcends the path of speech due to the cultivation of the path; he says "one cannot speak," etc., because one knows it for oneself upon attaining sexual union in youth.
For those devoid of meditative concentration—
those lacking the concentration on emptiness— there is no happiness of mind in dispassion; therefore, dispassion should not be practiced for the sake of that which is not happiness.
He demonstrates that death itself is the cause of saṃsāra through a continuous succession by saying "of death," and so forth;
thus, in the manner described, there arises the production of detachment among sentient beings.
"Not otherwise" means that if for them the arising of detachment does not have death as its cause,
then their existence— that is, their cyclic existence— cannot occur in any other way.
Therefore, the meaning is that death itself is the cause; since this is so, one should abandon attachment to death.
As it is stated in the *Pañcalakṣābhidhāna*: "By the cessation of ignorance regarding the imperishable, there is the cessation of formative forces (*saṃskāra*);
by the cessation of formative forces, there is the cessation of consciousness (*vijñāna*)."
Through the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; through the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases;
through the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact.
And with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling;
with the cessation of feeling, there is the cessation of craving;
and with the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of arising.
Through the cessation of arising, there is the cessation of existence;
through the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of birth;
and through the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of old age and death.
The cessation of the aggregates and elements is known as pacification;
likewise, through the cessation of the body, there is the cessation of the vital breath,
and through the cessation of the vital breath, there is the cessation of the bodhicitta.
Through the cessation of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), there is the cessation of emission;
through the cessation of the moment of emission, Buddhahood [is attained] for all embodied beings.
Likewise, through the cessation of the hair [of the head], there is also the cessation of karma.
Through the cessation of karma, there is also the cessation of suffering;
that arising of a sprout would not occur— without the arising of a seed, the arising of karma never takes place.
Without its arising, the arising of suffering also does not occur;
without suffering, the yogi remains happy and constantly acts for the benefit of sentient beings—
this is because he has abandoned the pleasure of death.
By the words "the lustful one" (*kāmuka*) and so forth, he describes the effort toward the bliss of the syllables (*akṣarasukha*);
[he states] "suffering characterized by passion and dispassion," and so forth regarding the semen (*śukra*).

Because when the semen—the support—is emitted, there occurs the destruction of the detachment from the bliss that is the supported; therefore, great bliss (*mahāsukha*) is to be accomplished through the non-emission of that very semen. Furthermore, this distinction between support and supported persists only as long as fullness has not been attained in the *uṣṇīṣa*.
When fullness is reached and the mind attains a state of non-emission, then the characteristic of support and supported no longer exists.
[The author] now describes the state of stainlessness (*vaimalya*):

Regarding the passage beginning with "akṣara" and so forth: "akṣara" refers to the knowledge of supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*). That from which [the body] arises is the "unborn-arisen" (*akṣarodbhava*) body—the body consisting of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense-faculties (*indriya*), and so on. Of that body which has arisen from the supreme unchanging, the "ūrṇā-wheel" is the forehead-wheel (*lalāṭacakra*); because it goes there, the sixteenth digit (*kalā*) residing in the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣaga*) is stated by implication to be its supported (*ādheya*).

The moon is transformed from the vowels beginning with *a*, and the sun is transformed from the consonants beginning with *ka*. The support (*ādhāra*) for these two—the union (*samāyoga*), the merging (*mīlana*), and the state of flowing through the central channel (*madhyamā-pravāhitva*)—is the conjunction of the *ālikāli* [vowels and consonants] on the left and right. Furthermore, the supported (*ādheya*) is not the form of the lord of the mandala transformed from the syllable *hūṃ* and so forth; rather, the support is the moon and sun situated within the central cavity (*varaṭaka*) of the crown-jewel (*uṣṇīṣa-maṇi*), and the supported is the form of all-pervading great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

As it is said in the *Vimalaprabhā*: "One foot [of the mantra] is in the vajra-jewel, which is the dust (*rajas*) and the sun; the second is in the crown-jewel, which is the semen (*śukra*) and the moon."

Having bowed with his head to the beloved of his Lord—the indestructible, indivisible, and ever-practiced [state] together with the three worlds—it is said that by means of this, the *pada* (the state) of the Lord’s *bodhicitta-vajra*, the glorious *Kālacakra*, is reached; that *pada* is the imperishable gnosis (*jñāna*).

It is practiced and established for the cessation of ignorance upon the diamond-jewel (*vajramaṇi*), on the ground-circle at the sun of passion (*rajo'rka*) in the stage of non-abiding *nirvāṇa*, within the element of gnosis (*jñānadhātu*). That which is "one" refers to the right [foot], whereby he stands treading with the sole of one foot.

In the *uṣṇīṣa*, which transcends the bliss of existence (*bhava-sukha*), in the semen (*śukra*) and the moon, in the toenail of the big toe, in the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*) whose nature is the primordial erotic power (*kāma-kalā*), there is the second, which is the left.

Having ascended to the peak of the Brahma-egg (*brahmāṇḍa-śikhara*), it is always—in all three times—uncut by the sword of ignorance and nescience because it transcends the veil of hair; it is indivisible by the extremes of subject and object because it has passed beyond the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-dharmatā*); it is desired because its nature is great bliss (*mahāsukha*); it is situated in the jewel (*maṇi*) at the place where what was to be done has been accomplished; and it is accompanied by the three worlds because it is free from worldly conduct, remaining in the *uṣṇīṣa* at the far limit of saṃsāra.
This is what is meant:

having prostrated at the feet of that Lord, the Gnosis Body (*jñānakāya*), whose nature consists of the six channels obstructed above and below and the six elements; whose lotus feet have been worshipped by the three realms; who, through the state of being free from obscurations, belongs to both the white and black fortnights which constitute existence; who, with his two feet consisting of emptiness and compassion—the twenty-two lunar mansions—whose nature is that of the moon and sun, and which block the paths of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, has pervaded the full moon and the new moon; he is the sole lord of the world—at his feet one should bow.

In the *Paramākṣarajñānasiddhi*, by the word "syllable" (*akṣara*), the knowledge of the bliss of the supreme syllable is meant, [and] Vajrasattva; likewise, because it serves as a protection for the mind, the mantra is also called the "knowledge of the supreme syllable. And in the *Mūlatantra*: "Because it serves as a protection for the elements of body, speech, and mind, therefore..."
The meaning of "mantra" by the word "mantra" is the knowledge of emptiness, the imperishable;
the mantra consists of merit and knowledge, having the nature of emptiness and compassion.

Likewise, the inner science of the self is called by the Victors the *prajñāpāramitā*, naturally luminous, the *mahāmudrā*, whose nature is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), the state of fullness that is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the *dharmadhātu*, and the innate body (*sahajatanu*).

These two are beyond the range of the sense faculties produced through dependent origination, yet they are the range of the divine senses; they are the mothers of the Buddhas and Vajrasattvas, whose intrinsic nature is supreme unchanging bliss (*paramākṣarasukha*); they transcend the nature of atoms (*paramāṇudharmatā*), and are like a reflection in a mirror or a dream; they possess the essential form of supreme unchanging bliss.

In this context, the syllables— form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— are said to be the five great voids when free from obscuration; likewise, the elements of earth, water, fire, air, and space, when free from obscuration, are said to be the five syllables.
The six syllables are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, each being unobscured and devoid of grasping its respective object;
likewise, the spheres of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (dharmadhātu) are also unobscured and are said to be the six syllables.
These aggregates, elements, and sense-bases have become a single, unified flavor.
The drop (*bindu*) becomes empty, and that drop, being unchanging (*acyuta*), is called the supreme syllable (*paramākṣara*). The supreme syllable is also the letter *A*;

from the letter *A* arises the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksambuddha*), who is Vajrasattva, consisting of wisdom and means, the neuter state, and is called the Innate Body (*sahajakāya*), because he consists of both knowledge and the object of knowledge due to the non-duality of cause and fruit.
And that Blessed One Kālacakra is the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*), spoken of as the lotus of bliss.
And it is said in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*: "The progenitor of the meaning of all mantras, the great bindu, the syllableless;
the five-syllabled, the great void, the bindu-void, the six-syllabled."
And in the *Mūlatantra*: "That which is designated by the syllable A is proclaimed as the Great Immutable Dharmadhātu, the Vajra-womb of the Lords of Victors, the cause of body, speech, and mind.
For example: the Blessed Buddha, the Perfectly Awakened One, is born from the syllable A."
The letter A is the foremost of all phonemes, of great significance, the supreme syllable;
it is indeed the great vital breath, the unarisen, devoid of speech and sustenance; it is the pinnacle of all causes for verbal expression, luminous within all words.

That in which the perfection of body, speech, and mind possesses the nature of the indivisibility of the three vajras is proclaimed as the vajra-womb (*vajrayoni*) of the bodies of the Victors (*jinakāya*),
since from it there arises the manifestation of the Buddhas and their qualities such as all-pervading sovereignty.
"That supreme [state] is called the 'Arising of Dharma,' consisting of merit and gnosis"—

having thus indicated the limb of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he now describes the relationship between cause and effect from the perspective of conventional reality, beginning with the words "the image" (*bimba*).
The causal basis (*hetu*) is the reflection (*bimba*) possessing all characteristics, which has arisen from the empty space;

the result (*phala*) is the bliss born from the immutable semen (*śukra-akṣara*). It is sealed by that result—the untainted bliss—and is of the nature of bliss because even the cause is of the nature of bliss.
And by such a cause, the untainted bliss is likewise sealed, because that too has the nature of non-referential emptiness; thus,
this pair is emptiness and compassion.
He says it is not without characteristics:
"emptiness," and so forth.
The mind that maintains the image of emptiness with an object is the cause.
The fruit is the upholder of compassion that is without an object.
That which is the non-differentiation of these two—emptiness and compassion—characterized by oneness, is called the *bodhicitta* that is unchanging (*acyuta*);
it is not something else produced by the action-seal (*karmamudrā*) or the knowledge-seal (*jñānamudrā*), characterized by emission and vibration.
And he says that this is free from both annihilation and cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).

The *bimba* is free from *nirvāṇa* in its insubstantial form, and it has transcended *saṃsāra*, which is characterized by perishable pleasure; it is the imperishable, uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) great bliss. The union of these two—the imperishable and the *bimba*—is non-dual, supreme, and unsurpassed.
Therefore he says:
"free from eternalism and nihilism. He states the proof for this as follows:
"Non-existence," and so forth.
There is no non-existence—that is, no annihilation—of the *bimba*, which is the manifestation of one's own mind in all its aspects; why?
Because its characteristic is that it arises from non-existence (*abhāvodbhūtalakṣaṇāt*).
Because from the absence of existence—that is, from the void, which is like the surface of the sky alone—there arises for each individual the manifestation of the three times and the three realms;
and as it will be stated here in the root text: "By means of the image arisen from space, when cultivated by oneself in such a manner.
For that which abides in the syllable, there is no arising of untainted bliss; how could there be?
Because it has the characteristic of being produced from existence;
that is, because it possesses the characteristic of a reflected image appearing as something produced from existence.
And this will be clarified by the passage beginning with "because it is unarisen due to the cause of wisdom."
Alternatively, because of the upward movement of the seminal essence (*śukra*) from the jewel (*maṇi*), there arises a world-transcending, untainted bliss (*nirāsrava-sukha*).

Non-existence and existence—characterized as described above—are the images of these two, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*), which have the nature of the conventional and ultimate truths. Their union, their blending, is the Vajrayoga.
It is called "the pair" (*yuganaddha*), and it is imperishable (*akṣara*).
This alone is the reality.
As it was stated by the venerable Āryadeva in the *Sūtaka*: "O Blessed One, that which is real is the reality; what is this that is called 'real'?
That which is non-contradictory is real."

What is this so-called "contradiction"? It is that which contradicts the meditative absorption (samādhi) whose nature is the method of reality (bhūtanaya). What is this so-called meditative absorption whose nature is the method of reality? It is that characterized by the non-dualization of the two truths.
That samādhi consists of the method of reality.
What, O Blessed One, is this so-called "two truths"?
They are: first, conventional truth, and second, ultimate truth.
For this very reason, it is said to be "completely free from form and formlessness.
For in a *pratisenā* (magical reflection), such as a body perceived in a mirror and the like, there is no characteristic of form because of the absence of a collection of substantial atoms;
nor is there a characteristic of formlessness, because that which is being perceived cannot be denied.
Therefore, the reflection does not come from existence (saṃsāra) nor does it go to extinction (nirvāṇa), for it is the imperishable [reality] embraced by one another.

Peaceful and unchanging because it is devoid of the fluctuations of the senses, this very state is the neuter ground (*napuṃsakapada*) consisting of both [aspects]. It is supreme and most excellent because it is unique to the entire world. Now, since the innate (*sahaja*) arises from the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), the innate possesses the nature of being produced by a cause, and the Great Seal likewise possesses the nature of being a cause. Thus, both cause and fruit do not transcend one another. Therefore, [an objection is raised]: "Let the Action Seal (*karmamudrā*) and the Wisdom Seal (*jñānamudrā*) be the cause; what indeed is the distinction of the Great Seal? To this he says:

"Wisdom," and so forth: Wisdom is characterized by the reflected image (*bimba*); it consists of the realization of all aspects and is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*). Furthermore, it is not produced from a cause, nor is it born, because its nature is unconditioned (*akṛta*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Even that which is called "the fruit born of wisdom" or "produced from wisdom"—that too is not born from a cause; it does not arise from the cause of wisdom. Why? Because it is not born from the cause of wisdom, since wisdom itself is not born from a cause. How, then, could the fruit known as the "innate" (*sahaja*) possibly be born from a cause, especially since the very discourse on causes has already been refuted?

Therefore, for this reason, that imperishable knowledge which is wisdom (*prajñājñāna*) is not produced by a cause; and consequently, because the relationship of cause and effect does not exist, the cause is not "sealed" by the effect, nor is the effect sealed by the cause—thus they do not exist even in relation to one another.
Nor is the cause sealed by the effect, nor is the effect sealed by the cause—thus they do not exist even in mutual dependence. Why is this so?
He says: "The cause," and so forth.
Since cause and effect are conventional because they are dependently originated, whereas that [reality] is supramundane and without beginning or end;
therefore, the reflection known as the "yoke-pair" (yuganaddha), which is mutually sealed and non-dual, is neither arisen nor ceased, being devoid of production and destruction.
And it has been said:
Whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise, this true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) remains constant; for that reason,
the wisdom aspect (prajñābhāga) of the image which is non-dual in both respects is eternally unarisen due to its primordial quiescence,
whereas the means aspect (upāyabhāga), because it is to be individually realized, is perpetually manifest.
Even from that, there is neither the state of cause and effect nor mutual sealing.
Regarding the state of being mutually sealed, he states another argument beginning with "of the unborn," and so forth.
Because an external object distinct from the form of cognition is impossible,
one's own mind alone is perceived as differentiated externally by way of the forms of the three realms.
There is nothing other than one's own mind at that time for the yogin, because the conceptualization of the distinction between self and other has ceased.
And it is said in the *Hevajra*: "In an instant, one becomes a single embodiment of the heavens, the immortals, and the netherworlds;
one cannot be obstructed by the conceptualization of self and other."
Regarding the phrase "the division of external objects of knowledge":
having set aside the external object of knowledge, the conclusion begins with "not from this" (*ato na*) and so forth.
The illustration begins with "what does it cut? and so forth.
One might object: "Since Mahāmudrā is unborn, its fruit is also impossible; for no one ever experiences the fruit of any phenomenon whatsoever that has not arisen. To this he says:
"The barren woman," and so forth.
Even though she is unborn, the pleasure that is experienced during the time of a dream upon union with the daughter of a barren woman [is nonetheless felt].
Therefore, through the practice of the mandala arising from space, the innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) in the form of the fruit is indeed experienced by yogins.

For that which is not produced by the faculties of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*) is not perceived by those who do not know reality (*atattvavid*), even though it is like the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), unproduced, like space, free from obscuration, and abiding in all beings.

Now, was it not said by the Tathāgata: "In the absence of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*) devoid of the union of the two organs is not self-cognizable because of its non-emission (*acyutatva*)"?
How can one, having formed an attachment through one's own mind toward that which appears as one's own mind, make that very mind free from obscuration and enjoy the gnosis of great immutable bliss?
[This is impossible] because there is no body composed of an aggregation of atoms. This alone is a contradiction, like the sentence: "Devadatta, having mounted his own shoulder, goes to the village."
In this regard, someone might have the following intention:

"Therefore, it is said here that for those who are dull-witted and consist of a collection of atoms, wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*)—which is self-cognized (*svasaṃvedya*)—does not occur through mind-only (*cittamātra*) alone in the absence of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (*skandhadhātvāyatana*). Why is that? Because of the power of adventitious mental impressions (*āgantukacittavāsanā*).
Here, what are called the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases are adventitious mental impressions; by the influence of these, the mental impressions of pleasure and pain enter the mind."
When examined from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), this body has no minor affliction whatsoever by which suffering would enter the mind.

It is well known throughout all the worlds that in that very state, another body—consisting of mental impressions (*cittavāsanā*) and devoid of a collection of atoms—is perceived as traveling to another place.

When that body, while traveling to another place, is subjected to an affliction such as being attacked by thieves, suffering enters the mind because of that affliction, and one cries out because of that suffering.
This is a great marvel: even without a physical body and without thieves or other such causes, a cognition of suffering arises that is self-cognized.
Likewise, in a dream, when the mind experiences the enjoyment of great passion, pleasure enters the mind.
Thus, even without a wondrous body and without the enjoyment of passion, a cognition of pleasure arises for sentient beings within the mind that is self-cognized.
Even this limited knowledge cannot be investigated by the wise;

how much less can the wise fools conceive of the omnibeneficent (*samantabhadra*) gnosis of great imperishable bliss, which is personally realized by yogins, transcends the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of cyclic existence, and arises from the latent tendencies of nirvāṇa?
Furthermore, regarding that which is called "the non-duality of wisdom and means," he states that even that does not exist in the ultimate sense.
"Neither wisdom," and so forth.

There exists no separate heap of either wisdom (*prajñā*) or means (*upāya*) by which the *bodhicitta* might be distinct from them; because that state is unknowable to immature yogins, it is called "innate" (*sahaja*) due to its being the innate reality (*sahajatattva*) through the intellect of wisdom. Because one has attained the state of being completely filled with bliss, it is the definitive realization (*nirṇaya*) free from all obscurations—such as passion and other afflictions (*kleśa*), as well as the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*)—since there is an absence of contact with hands and so forth.

Because it is devoid of the apprehended and the apprehender, it is free from objects and sense faculties. Because it is all-pervasive, it is present everywhere; because it possesses the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatva*), it abides within all beings. Because it transcends the nature of atoms even throughout the three times, it cannot be cut by the blade of ignorance and lack of knowledge. Because it has transcended the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-dharmatā*), it is indivisible by the categories of subject and object, and is thus free from division. It is "self-arisen" (*svayambhū*)—these three verses constitute the summary of the six qualities of the supramundane being. Because it is without arising or cessation, it is self-arisen. Because it effects the welfare of the world, it is of great purpose.
In the six chakras from the secret place to the uṣṇīṣa, there are respectively those named Vajrasattva, Mahāsattva, Bodhisattva, Samayasattva, Vajrayoga, and Kālacakra.

Regarding their explanation: "Vajra" and so forth—since the vajra is the empty-form (*śūnyabimba*) and is therefore indivisible, it is of great significance; that which is the Great Teaching (*mahodeśa*), the *sattva* known as the unity of body, speech, and mind in the realms such as the desire realm, is indicated as the supreme unchanging (*paramākṣara*). Thus, he is Vajrasattva.

Alternatively, "Vajra" refers to the indestructible gnosis of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), which is the single essence of body, speech, and mind; "Sattva" refers to the oneness of the three realms of existence. The supreme immutable (*paramākṣara*) is the unity of these two. It is designated as "Great" (*mahā*) because it is full of great bliss, and as "Great Passion" (*mahārāga*). Furthermore, that Sattva is designated as "one who brings joy to all beings" (*sarvasattvaratiṅkara*) because he is full through the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*); thus, he is the "Great Being" (*mahāsattva*). Alternatively, by the word "Great" (*mahā*) here, the supreme immutable bliss is meant; the Being who is full of that and also full through the stages is the "Great Being."
Because he is immovably established in the wheel of Dharma, which consists of emptiness and compassion for the sake of awakening,
and because he is victorious over the hosts of hatred in the form of the afflictions and so forth, he is designated as "Great Hatred" and the "Great Foe.
Consequently, he is a "Sattva," that is, a Bodhisattva.

Because he is the consumption in the form of non-falling within the bliss of the *samaya*—the seminal essence (*śukra*) known as the moon-nectar—he is designated as "Great Delusion" (*mahāmoha*) due to his victory over delusion, yet he is the destroyer of the delusion of the foolish; therefore, he is the *Samayasattva*.
Because he is the union with the *prajñā*, the *bimba*, and the immutable drops (*bindu*) of the *vajras* of body and so forth, he is their oneness.

Because he has conquered anger, he is taught as Mahākrodha; because he has conquered Māra, he is taught as the enemy of Kuṭṭamāra. Thus is the Vajrayoga. Since that Time (Kāla) is Great Bliss, the Blessed One—out of that very means, never abandoning the welfare of sentient beings who are called "crooked" (vakra)—is therefore taught as Mahālobha, the destroyer of fleeting greed. Thus is Kālacakra.

In the wheel of the six-spoked *ṣaḍnāḍī* form, these Vajrasattvas and others are each of six types. Therein, at the lower spoke in the form of the *śaṅkhinī*, there is imperishable gnosis (*jñāna*); at the southern spoke in the form of the *rasanā*, imperishable sensation (*vedanā*); at the upper spoke in the form of the *avadhūtī*, imperishable consciousness (*vijñāna*); at the western spoke in the form of the *viṇnāḍī*, imperishable form (*rūpa*);
and at the eastern spoke in the form of the *sūtranāḍī*, imperishable formations (*saṃskāra*).
In the subsequent spoke of the form of *lalanā*, there are the six aggregates known as "syllables" (*akṣara*);
these same six are the six families (*ṣaṭkula*) corresponding respectively to the elements beginning with earth, which are bound by syllabic knowledge (*akṣarajñāna*).

In this way, there is the non-emission of the imperishable through the six sense organs beginning with the mind, as well as the six objects beginning with sound; by implication, this refers to the imperishable emission of the divine sense organs— the hands, genitals, anus, and feet— and likewise, by implication, the imperishable emission of their respective objects.

These thirty-six [deities] correspond respectively to the activities of the organs of action—namely, grasping, walking, speaking, excreting, and procreation—and are as follows within the mandala: Vajrasattva known as Mahākāya, Ratneśa known as Mahārāga, Akṣobhya known as Mahākrodha, Vairocana known as Mahāmoha, Amoghasiddhi known as Mahādveṣa, and Amitābha known as Mahālobha;
as well as Prajñāpāramitā, Pāṇḍarā, Vajradhātvīśvarī, Locanā, Tārā, and Māmakī.
Samantabhadra, Kṣitigarbha, Vajrapāṇi, Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhī, Ākāśagarbha, Lokeśvara;
Śabdavajrā, Rasavajrā, Dharmadhātuvajrā, Gandhavajrā, Sparśavajrā, Rūpavajrā;
and Śumbha, Prajñāntaka, Uṣṇīṣa, Yamāntaka, Vighnāntaka, and Padmāntaka.
The consorts Mahānīlā, Ajamminī, Raudrākṣī, Śumbhinī, Mahāvīryā, and Māninī; and this Acittacittavajra, who pervades the thirty-six deities,
possesses six faces— Mahākāma and the others— due to the cessation of the veils of passion and so forth, and because he is the Wrathful King.
Because it is terrifying due to the fear of the Lord of Death (Mṛtyumāra) and others, it is "Bhīma.

The body purified by the six families of the aforementioned knowledge and so forth is the "Body Maṇḍala. This Body Maṇḍala consists of the three—the Secret Faculty Maṇḍala, the Speech Maṇḍala, and the Mind Maṇḍala—and is the Six-Family Maṇḍala. Through the cultivation of that path, one should purify it and accomplish the state of Vajrasattva and the state of Acittavajra for those who are primordially pure—the aforementioned three Vajras of Wisdom and Method. This treatise titled *Sekoddeśa* has thus been explained; it sets forth the practice of the ten initiations and the practice of the initiation of the supreme immutable [syllable].
The Blessed One said: "This [teaching], which illuminates the family of channels (nāḍīkula), has been clearly explained in brief according to the instruction of the Teacher Vajrapāṇi.

May this pure moonlight of the knowledge of consecration (sekendu-jñānacandrikā), which clarifies the excellent subject matter and removes the darkness of all obscurations, dispel the suffering of the world."
Thus ends the commentary on the *Sekoddeśa*.
This is the work of the venerable Naḍapāda (Nāropāda).
